Easy shore dive in a sheltered cove, very shallow and good for training.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards.

Underwater: As its a sheltered cove dive anywhere and look for small life in the seaweed. Take a compass and when you finish the dive head north. There is supposed to be a tunnel near the west corner at the entrance to Lulworth Cove. Lulworth Cove tunnel

This is a very shallow dive so a 10-litre cylinder is plenty for diving here. The seabed is covered in seaweed and is good for photography. In John Howland's book "Treasure from British Waters" it mentions fifteen gold coins found in Lulworth Cove. Toilets are near to the carpark

sites.name: Luna Kirk
sites.access: Take the A970 north from Lerwick. As you near Voe you need to turn right onto the B9071. At the Vidlin crossroads go straight on and Lunna Kirk is down a little turning to the right approximately 3 miles further on.
sites.parking: There is plenty of parking outside the kirk. Kit up and walk through the gate and down the grassy slope to the shore about 50 yards
sites.entryExit: . A simple walk in entry/exit with plenty of large rocks to use for putting fins on.
sites.airFill: Malkoff Ltd . Other than that contact the local dive club Zetland SAC 01806 588261
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: None
sites.notes:
Luna Kirk is a scenic Shore dive in Vidlin Voe, Shetland.

Suggested experience: Novice/Open water

Underwater: Keeping slightly to the left of the bay swim out over the weed. (Diving at low tide will mean this is a little shorter). Swim out until you are roughly level with the point this should be around 10-12 m and the sandy bottom should appear. Turn left and swim over the rocky reef until it is time to return. At the base of the reef, 17-20m is a sandy bottom. I didn't explore how deep it goes down here but swam along the bottom of the reef looking at the life on the sandy bottom then returned higher up.

You can also shore at Mavis grind and Spiggie beach

sites.name: Manse point
sites.location: N56 41.082 W5 10.416 Postcode PH49 4JP Google map
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the M8 cross the Erskin bridge onto the A82 and turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. At Tyndrum bear to the right still on the A82 over Rannoch Moor into Glencoe. On entering Glencoe you will see Loch Leven on the right, Along this road ½ mile on the left is a church and Manse point is across the road. Google
sites.parking: There is no parking across the road now but it is possible to get onto the lochside through a gap in the roadside barrier if you are careful.
sites.entryExit: Walk down the stonny path onto the beach and out to the point. It's a longer walk when the tide is out.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Isles of Glencoe Hotel · Cafe: West Laroch.
sites.hazards: Currents, this is a slack water dive, if you don't get it right you can get swept up or down the loch and a long surface swim back to the shore.
sites.notes:
Manse point is a good shore dive on the point in Loch Leven

Suggested experience: Advanced sport diver.

Underwater: Head left as you face the water and you will see small walls covered in life. If you keep the main wall to your left choose your desired depth and head along the wall, the wall gradually steps up to shallower depths. You can then turn back on yourself and follow the reef back into the bay.

This is a great site for U/W photography due to the light and water movement. You can also dive a few miles along the road at the Kentallen wall and The slates Don't forget to use the comments at the bottom of the page to let other divers know what its like to dive here.

sites.name: Malinbeg
sites.access: from Donegal: 61 Km 1 Hr 7mins Google
sites.parking: There is a right turn off the road through Malinbeg (downhill towards the ruined tower) about thirty metres past the hostel. There is plenty of parking about a minute down the road.
sites.entryExit: Enter and exit the water at the pier.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Mary Murrins at Bruckless
sites.notes:
Scenic shore dive

Suggested experience: Novice

Underwater: There is a sea stack at the entrance to the south-west which is usually the focal point for the dive. The bay runs north-south making it pretty easy to navigate. To return to the pier swim off the stack towards the nearest Easterly sandy patch, head North following the edge of the sand and after 100m change direction West where you should surface back at the pier wall.

A very scenic dive with overhangs around the base of the stack, lots of the usual life you get on the west coast and some unusual, Atlantic triggerfish have been seen here. This is also a good location for a night dive. Two street lamps on the cliff overlooking the quay light up the underwater terrain and act also as navigational marks.

sites.name: Martins Haven
sites.access: Heading west, follow the M4 all the way to the end. Join the A40 to Haverfordwest and continue on the B4327 Dale Road. Before Dale, turn off and take the road through the village of Marloes. This road leads to Martin's Haven. Google
sites.parking: There is a National Trust car park at the top of the hill. As you arrive let the guy at the gate know you're diving and he will allow you down with the car to drop off the heavy bits of kit.
sites.entryExit: The beach can be reached via a concrete track 150m down from the car park. Entry and exit to the water is from a gently sloping stony beach.
sites.airFill: Divein2pembrokeshire Dive Pembrokeshire Haven Diving Services
sites.accommodation: Haverfordwest tourist information , 01437 763110. Foxdale Camp Site
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Lobster Pot Inn in Marloes · Cafe: None close to here
sites.hazards: Danger of strong currents outside the bay and the Skomer ferry operates out of Martin's Haven during the summer months so use an SMB.
sites.notes:
Shore

Suggested experience: Trainee to experienced diver

Underwater: Best to stick to the edges of the bay which both have walls as the middle is flat and sandy. The west of the bay is deeper to 30m at the exit of the bay and 15m on the east. There tends to be more fish life in the east and you get more bottom time.

There is a no-take policy and are fines for divers found removing certain species here. The viz here can get very bad after storms so it best to check that it's been calm for a week or so and avoid diving here in northerly winds as it blows straight into the bay. On a rising tide its a very good night dive, particularly when the tourists have all left. There are toilets and a small visitor hut on the short walk from the car park down to the shore. It's best to stay away from the boat jetty as it gets used all day so an SMB is recommended.

sites.name: Mellon Charles
sites.access: From Glasgow or Edinburgh head for Perth then Inverness Cross the Kessock bridge and stay on the A9 until the Tore roundabout take the second exit and follow the A835 and A832 to your destination.
sites.parking: Park at the end of the track looking out to the old pier.
sites.entryExit: Kit up at the car and walk down the beach into the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Shore Croft Hotel. · Cafe: None close to here.
sites.hazards: The pier is occasionally used by fishing boats who tie up briefly to drop or retrieve holding pots for lobster, crab & wrasse – usually towards the end of the day. Keep an eye out for swimmers and, SUPs and kayakers too.
sites.notes:
Shore dive on an old Submarine boom pier with lots of sealife

Suggested experience: Ocean diver

Underwater: Snorkel out (90m) on the surface to the pier or take a bearing and Fin out.

Park around the edges of the hardstanding (Helicopters very occasionally land here), Do not block access to the slipway. Note this is MOD land and camping overnight here is not allowed.

sites.name: Mavis grind
sites.access: Mavis Grind itself is the narrow isthmus that joins Northmavine to the mainland of Shetland, preventing it from becoming another island. It is here that you can reputedly stand on the shore of the North Sea and throw a stone into the Atlantic on the other side. Follow the A970 northwards away from Lerwick. Continue following it through Voe and on to Brae. Around 1mile after Brae is Mavis Grind. There is a huge sign on the rock announcing that you are in Northmavine and if you go past that, you have gone too far. The dive site is on the right of the road opposite a large layby
sites.parking: There is a small space you can pull into just above the beach or there is a large lay-by on the opposite side of the road
sites.entryExit: Very small, bay with a shingle beach. Large rocks to use for putting fins on.
sites.airFill: Malkoff Ltd contact the local dive club Zetland SAC 01806 588261
sites.accommodation: Lots of places for wild camping around Shetland and registered sites.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.notes:
Mavis grind is a Scenic Shore dive on the narrow isthmus that joins Northmavine to the mainland of Shetland

Suggested experience: Novice/Open water

Underwater: This dive can be quite dark and gloomy so a good torch is a must. Swim straight out over a band of kelp where minute sea stars cling onto the crinkly blades, and tiny scallops perform their comical jerky dance with almost frenetic energy as they try to escape. The sandy, shingle sea bed quickly starts to slope quite steeply on this dive. Keep slightly over to your right where the large rocks are thickly covered with thousands of fluted sea squirts. However, this is not the only variety; I counted five different types, including the very beautiful gas mantle sea squirt all growing on and around these rocks here. Most of the life on this dive is between 10-20m, below that visibility is poor.

sites.name: Meanish reef
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the M8 cross the Erskin bridge onto the A82 and turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. At Tyndrum bear to the right still on the A82 over Rannoch Moor into Glencoe. Cross the bridge and up to Fort William, take the A82 and A87 to the Kyle of Lochalsh. Cross the bridge to Skye and take the A850 and A863 to Dunvegan. Turn southwest onto the B884 to Meanish Google
sites.parking: There is plenty of parking at the end of the road to the pier. (See pic below)
sites.entryExit: At low tide enter at the slip or high tide off the rock and exit on the stony beach.
sites.accommodation: Dive & sea the Hebrides or Kinloch Campsite B+B
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Stein Inn (very good food) · Cafe: None
sites.hazards: Swell caused by wind from the north and Offshore SW wind if you need to surface swim for any reason.
sites.notes:
Meanish reef is an excellent shore dive on a submerged reef which is covered on top by a huge kelp forest

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: Jump in off the pier and swim to the reef (see dive map) head out on 350 - 360 Deg From the shore to the reef or from the pier follow the cliff round to the point and head out on 345 - 355 Deg.

This is probably the best shore dive on the Isle of Skye.

sites.name: Meadfoot beach
sites.access: From Torquay harbour, take the main road to Babbacombe. Take a right-hand turn just 100 yards from the harbour and this takes you to the beach.
sites.parking: Park in the Car park. Google
sites.entryExit: its an easy walk down the path across the stone and shingle beach into the water, but take care as it can be slippy.
sites.airFill: Dive Torquay Nautique Teign Diving Centre
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: A great beach Cafe
sites.hazards: To Follow
sites.notes:
Meadfoot beach is a good shore dive in a sheltered bay

Suggested experience: Novice upwards...

Underwater: Head out to the rocks and this is the main part of the dive, search in all the cracks and gully's and you will see lots of good sea life.

The visibility is reduced here when the sea is choppy. This is a site where an SMB must be used as there can be a lot of boat traffic. Avoid diving here when you have strong easterly and southeasterly winds.

sites.name: Menai straights
sites.access: From Birmingham154 Miles 2 hrs 40 Mins Google map
sites.entryExit: You can enter Anglesey via either bridge and make your way to the bottom of the Menai bridge (the north of the two) on the Anglesey side
sites.airFill: Mike's at Trearrdur Bay. Anglesay divers
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: : The Anglesay arms · Cafe: None close to here
sites.hazards: The Menai Strait should be avoided on spring-tides when currents can reach up to eight knots and watch for surface traffic.
sites.notes:
: The Menai Straits is a great drift dive if you dive with someone who has experience in doing it right.

Suggested experience: Experienced diver.

Underwater: You will drift SW for about 20 minutes, then about 5 minutes of slack and then the current reverses and takes you NE back to the start. A good indication for the right time to enter the water is to wait until the water level is within a metre off the end of the wall. The seabed is a mixture of gravel, bare rock and boulders. There is a wreck called the Conway between the two bridges in an area known as The Swellies - it's closer to the suspension bridge & on the mainland side of the Straits.

The telephone cable runs across the straits between the two yellow markers, it's about 4 inches in diameter and easy to spot. It's a good idea to locate the telephone cable and simply follow it until you are about 15m and then let go and drift away. On the return journey watch out for the cable again and when you hit it follow it SE back towards your entry point.

sites.name: Memorial cove
sites.access: 5hr 40min From Glasgow head up to Fort William and continue on the A82 through Spean bridge to Invergarry onto the A87 to the A890 Continue on A890 . to the A832 to B8057 to your destination.
sites.parking: Car park for memorial cove on private land but access to the public.
sites.amenities: Farmhouse at the start of the private road.
sites.entryExit: Rock slab entrance into kelpy pool, exit same place or onto boulders. Note we tried this site a few times in a very calm weather week but deemed it unsafe to enter until the last day. Need flat water and S or E wind for safe access due to how exposed the site is.
sites.hazards: Few abandoned pots with lines caught next to the island. Turn W early enough to prevent passing the island. Gas management due to the length of dive- we consumed approx 3000l each.
sites.notes:
Shore dive around a rocky headland and around the island, with beautiful walls and gullies.

Suggested experience: Sport Diver (due to navigation).

Underwater: swim out NE over kelp 3m depth to a shelf, descend and follow the wall on the left running NW starting at about 6m to 20m. The terrain becomes rocky with sand to the right sloping down to about 22m off in the distance. Scorpionfish spotted here. Following the island around until an NW heading. At about 35 min run time ascend up the boulders going W towards the gap between the islands heading SW. (depth here 17m ascending to 6m). Through the gap is lots of boulders to poke around in, Lions Mane Jellyfish here. When the SW heading is blocked head E to SE over rocks at 12m back to the wall onto the sand and go S back to the entry/exit points.

sites.name: Millshore
sites.access: Its on a shore road between Pennan and Gardenstown Google
sites.parking: Just off the road facing the bay or through the gates at the picnic tables.
sites.entryExit: Enter the water on the beach and exit in the same place.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Pennan Inn · Cafe: Millshore pottery at the car park.
sites.notes:
Easy shore dive

Suggested experience: Suitable for trainees

Underwater: Dive to the west on the reef running along the foot of the cliffs (left facing the sea) it's not deep but has plenty of life. The seabed is white sand and the rocks along the shore are covered in kelp and seaweed. You can also enter the reef from Millshore and come out on the other side of the reef into the next bay

Contact Ellon SAC for local information. Its a good site for photography

sites.name: Midway
sites.access: From Glasgow travel west on the M8 onto the A82 then turn left onto the A817 turning right at the roundabout onto the A814 and continue north. The parking is in a cut in the hillside (see picture below) with water running down the cliff. Google
sites.parking: Parking for up to six cars in the cut in the cliff Google The parking here is now fenced off and now its a problem.
sites.amenities: Finnart oil terminal / The Village Inn, Arrochar
sites.entryExit: Step over the crash barrier 10m towards Arrocher from the car park and walk down the slope to the tree. The tree roots make steps to the shore. There are a couple of well-placed rocks to sit and put on your fin’s. There is kelp to 3m depending on the tide Exit on the left of the wall looking towards the shore from the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Village Inn , The Arrochar Hotel · Cafe: : Pit Stop Diner, Arrochar
sites.hazards: Fast cars and bikes on A814, Depth
sites.notes:
Midway on Loch Long is a steep 60 Deg small stone slope.

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: The dive site is a steep 60 deg slope to 53m with seaweed to 3m and small stones and broken shells. you can pick your depth and head up or down the Loch.

sites.name: Milton rock
sites.access: 24 miles 50 mins Google
sites.parking: Parl in the car park along the front as near to the path as possible Google 100 meters past the beach cafe.
sites.entryExit: Kit up at the top of the beach at the path to the beach and it's a simple walk into the water. Milton rock can be seen in the picture below at the bottom of the path.
sites.airFill: None close Aquanauts Dive Centre Deep Blue Diving Sandford and Down
sites.accommodation: Self-catering Hope and anchor Bed and Breakfast
sites.nearbyFood: Cafe: Beachhouse in the summer.
sites.hazards: Navigation under the water.
sites.notes:
Scenic shore dive around an offshore rock.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards.

Underwater: Surface swim out to the rock as there are gully's in between that makes navigation a nightmare. The seaward side of the rock is the deepest but on the way back explore the gully's as there is a lot see, and the remains of an unknown wreck.

The parking can be crowded on sunny summer days. There are public toilets 200 meters from the path to the sea.

sites.name: Mevagissey
sites.location: N50.269758 W-4.782604 Google map Postcode PL26 6QT
sites.parking: You can park on the north side of the harbour and kit up there but parking is extremely restricted so we park the cars on the south side.
sites.entryExit: Walk to the end of the pier and down the steps. You can either cross the harbour entrance and do the north cove or dive around the south harbour wall (although there are usually numerous fishermen on the south wall). You can drop dive kit off on the north side of the harbour and enter via a small beach area shown in the picture below.
sites.accommodation: The Headlands Hotel Holiday Cottages B&B
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Harbour Tavern and The Ship Inn. · Cafe: Tea on the Quay The Squirrel's Nest
sites.hazards: Occasional boat traffic
sites.notes:
Shore dive in reefs and gully's

Suggested experience: Sport Diver.

Underwater: Follow the reefs and gully's which are lined with dead men's fingers and toped help. There are spider crabs, pipefish, wrasse, velvet swimming and edible crabs here. When you have to finish your dive, retrace your route back to the north wall of the harbour.

A good night dive can be had on the south wall of the harbour but navigation can be difficult unless you know the site. Don't dive here during the day because of fisherman. It is important to inform the harbour master you are diving.

sites.name: Midletters
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the A82 turn left at Tarbet onto the A83, through Arrochar and over the rest and be thankful, turn left onto the A815 just after Strachur, Turn onto the A886 towards anchor point etc and continue along the lochside. Go past the war memorial on the right and as the houses peter out the countdown markers for 40mph for the traffic coming the other way appear on the opposite side. Next to the third marker (see pic) is a grassy verge. Google
sites.parking: There is plenty of room on the grass verge to park in single file for several cars.
sites.entryExit: Down the concrete ramp and a gently sloping shingle beach.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Creggans Inn · Cafe: Strachur
sites.hazards: There are no major hazards here.
sites.notes:
Midletters shore dive on Loch Fyne is a gentle slope with small rocks scattered around with large pieces of sugar kelp.

Suggested experience: Site has an easy entry and is good for novices. Shingle beach so no slippy stones and convenient rocks for donning fins.

Underwater: Swim out over a band of kelp and then it's just a gradual muddy/silty slope. Few small rocks scattered around and large pieces of sugar kelp with things hiding underneath

sites.name: Mingary pier
sites.access: From the Corran Ferry follow the A861 until you get to Salen then pick up the B8007. Follow this twisty road along the lochside and round Benn nan Losgann until you reach Kilchoan. Drive through the village. Google
sites.parking: Either in the ferry car park or just above the slip next to the fence.
sites.entryExit: Time this dive so that you are not on or near the slip when the ferry is arriving or departing.Fortunately the ferry is not too frequent allowing a reasonable window for a dive. Probably easier to enter and exit the site during high tide as there is a considerable amount of kelp over the rocks for some distance at the bottom of the slip. Also, the depth under the pier will be better.
sites.accommodation: As you leave the Lochside at Ardslignish and follow the very scenic road round Benn nan Losgann there are many beautiful spots for wild camping B+B Bunkhouse
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: There can be a considerable amount of surge on the reef around the corner from the pier. Be wary of currents as this dive is nearer to the mouth of the loch which reputedly has some very swift currents
sites.notes:
Mingary pier is an easy shore dive under and around the pier legs.

Suggested experience: Any

Underwater: As soon as the ferry departs enter the water swim over the kelp where iridescent rock cook swim about in small shoals and swim down to the pier legs. There are loads of things growing on and under the pier legs here. Spiny and common sea stars, huge prawns hiding in cracks, cup corals and dahlia anemones. Swim down the sandy sloping seabed to about 10m and then turn right to find a rocky reef. Although this does have some kelp growing on it this is not very thick. Snakelocks anemones, stalked jellyfish and decorator crabs live on the kelp here and a few dead men's fingers, while urchins are scattered about and the odd lobster can be seen quickly reversing into its hiding place as you arrive

There are some public toilets here.

sites.name: MOD Reef
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the A82 turn left at Tarbet onto the A83, through Arrochar and over the rest and be thankful and turn left onto the A815 Its 7.4 miles to the turnoff to MOD Reef from the junction of the A83 and the A815 and first right past Ardnish cottage. It’s 100m down this road. Google map
sites.parking: Don’t park on the grass in front of the houses, park in front of the MOD building. There are logs along the side of the road now making parking harder. Its possible to drop off kit and park at the top of the road.
sites.entryExit: Enter at the end of the metal slip and to exit come back along the shore until you see cables heading down the slope. The cables take you to the end of the slip.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Creggans Inn . · Cafe: Strachur
sites.hazards: Some surface traffic.
sites.notes:
Shore dive on a boulder slope with sandy patches.

Suggested experience: Suitable for all divers

Underwater: From the end of the slip swim down to 10m and turn left keep at this depth until you reach the reef. The reef goes down to 38m and then it slopes down to 52m. If you want a shallow dive the reef extends along the shore for 50m.

Thornback rays in late July.

sites.name: MY Alastor
sites.location: 54 27.06 N 05 37.71 W Google map Postcode BT23 6PA
sites.access: Distance from Belfast 19 Miles 45 Mins The Alastor is on the East side of Strangford Lough. From the A22 on the East of Strangford lough follow the Ballymorran Road (2.5 miles south of the Balloo House) to a T junction, turn left, then right at the top of the hill. Follow the road to Ringhaddy Quay.
sites.parking: Park in the lay-by before the pier. Do not block access to driveways or the slip. If the layby is full park considerately along the road before the layby, tight to the hedge to allow access.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Balloo House .
sites.notes:
Shore dive on a Motor Yacht

Underwater: Utube Utube Contact me

Popular shore dive. The line reaches wreck on the port side of the stern deck, which sits upright and is quite complete, making navigation easy. After exploring the stern deck, swim forwards over the superstructure There are lifeboat davits on either side of the funnel. The funnel (a mock-up to conceal the much smaller exhaust inside) is intact, and often a Conger eel can be found living at its top. Around the funnel base, several compartments and cabins can be seen from above. Continuing forward, the superstructure beams can be seen, having collapsed inwards. Nothing remains of the bridge. The spacious foredeck leads to the atmospheric bow. One notable swim-through is possible in the after part of the superstructure, which passes through a bathroom, entering and exiting through the doorways at the ends of the port and starboard galleries. Limited penetration is possible elsewhere, the hull of the wreck being filled with silt. Visibility can vary from <1 m to a stunning 10+ m (rare), usually, 2 to 3 m can be expected. Finish with a pint in the Balloo House .

sites.name: Mullion cove
sites.parking: The car park is on the right just before you get to the sea Drive down and dump your kit off at top of slipway as it is a bit of walk fully kitted from the car park.(510m)
sites.entryExit: Enter the water down the steps at the end of the harbour watching out for boats and stay to the right. You can do a jump entry from the end if it's a high tide.
sites.accommodation: Criggan Mil B+B Seaspray cottage Seagull self-catering
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Mullion Cove Hotel · Cafe: Porthmellin Cafe
sites.hazards: Boats entering and leaving the harbour.
sites.notes:
Mullion cove is a scenic shore dive just outside the harbour. Webcam

Suggested experience: Novice upwards

Underwater: Swim out of the harbour over a stony bottom and head right through an area covered in kelp with loads of big rocks and gully's to explore and out and around the small Island.

Don't dive here if the winds are from the south. You can launch a rib here and dive Mullion Island as well. An SMB is essential here due to boat traffic.

sites.name: Newhaven West Breakwater
sites.access: Newhaven is located between Brighton and Eastbourne on the A259 Coast Road, or by following the main A27 & heading along the A26. Once in Newhaven follow the signs into Newhaven Town Centre, from South Way turn left into South Road (police station on the corner) which leads into Fort Road, this leads to the car park for the sandy beach From London take the M25, M23, A23 the A26 into Newhaven then follow the direction above
sites.parking: Park in the large car park at the top of the breakwater. Open 8am-5pm Pay and display and free at night.
sites.entryExit: Its a long walk (100m) down to the stony beach into the water beside the breakwater. The blocks at the bottom of the wall are good to sit on and put on your fins.
sites.airFill: Brighton dive centre Newhaven Scuba Centre
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Hope Inn · Cafe: The fort tearoom
sites.hazards: Entry/exit when there is a swell
sites.notes:
Newhaven West Breakwater is a shore dive along 705 meters of boulders at the base of the Breakwater and on the chalk reefs.

Suggested experience: Novice with an Instructor.

Underwater: In the shallows it is shingle this leads onto areas of shallow chalk gullies then following the wall takes you to concrete boulders that protect the wall. You will probably see shoals of whiting and pouting, also flounders, wrasse and pollack. In and around the rocks crabs and lobster.

The viz here drops to near zero if there have been long periods of south-westerly winds.

sites.name: Newry beach
sites.parking: Park on the layby above the Maritime Museum – the parking at the bottom is for the museum patrons only. Drop kit and park at the top.
sites.entryExit: Easy entry by walking down the beach, Holyhead Harbour Master (01407 606700) should be informed about any diving activity in the harbour - he is happy to entertain divers so long as they inform him.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Victoria Inn, The Boathouse Hotel · Cafe: Holyhead Maritime Museum
sites.hazards: Overhead traffic – permanent SMBs recommended
sites.notes:
Newry beach is a gently sloping shore dive

Suggested experience: Ocean Diver with good buoyancy control

Underwater: We went in on the far left side of the beach, headed straight out towards the mooring buoys, turned 90 degrees right, finned for a short time then turned 90 degrees right again to head back into shore

Best dived at high tide as finning over pebbled seabed prior to getting to the muddy bottom. At low tide, the light is supposed to be better. Anglesey Divers use this beach for training so it might be wise to check with them to see if they are running any courses – the site could get very busy!

sites.name: Newquay
sites.alternativeNames: Lifeboat Slip, Little Fistral, Spy Cove, The Zeds, The Gazzle
sites.access: Travel through Newquay towards Fistral Beach, when on the headland road turn right half way along the road and drive down to the car park. Google
sites.parking: Park in the Pay and Display car park close to your chosen entry point.
sites.entryExit: : There are 4 different entry points, all best at high tide. The first is Spy/Seal Cove just behind the boulders on the right-hand side, before the car park. The next is the old lifeboat slip itself. The next is to the right of the toilets, there's a slope that is cut into the rocks in a Z shape. The other is on the other side at Little Fistral.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Beach Bar on Fistral beach or the Red Lion next to the Harbour · Cafe: None
sites.hazards: If it's anywhere near spring tides do not venture close to the end of the headland, currents can be strong there.
sites.notes:
Newquay is a great place to shore dive with lots of places to dive in one place.

Suggested experience: Open Water

Underwater: There are 4 different dives. From Seal Cove go right for a small cave, go left for a small gully and sand/reef. From the slip right to the gully, the left is a sand/reef. from the Z's right or left for sand/reef. From Little Fistral, if there are no waves out to the right along the reef.

Newquay can get busy in the summer months.

sites.name: Newtons Cove
sites.access: From the A354 heading south for Weymouth. Straight through North Quay roundabout onto Rodwell Rd/A354 Turn left onto Rodwell Ave and at next roundabout turn right into Newton-road and continue to the sea.
sites.parking: Drop off the dive kit at the small roundabout on Newtons road as you get to the sea and park in the Car park 160m back up Newtons road at the roundabout.
sites.entryExit: From the road walk down to the promenade and down the steps and put on your fins holding onto the rail. It's best to exit here as well.
sites.airFill: Old harbour dive centre Scimitar diving
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The red lion · Cafe: Stone pier cafe DT4 8TX
sites.hazards: Occasional boat traffic, The seabed is silty here so try to stay off the bottom.
sites.notes:
Newtons Cove is a very good shallow shore dive, great for night diving too.

Suggested experience: Novice with good buoyancy.

Underwater: I basically head out on a compass course and come back on the reciprocal course or for the reef its 120m on 30 deg and head along the reef for 15 mins and come back on 215 which usually gets me back close to the exit point.

This can be an excellent night dive as can be seen in this Utube

sites.name: North Landing
sites.access: To get there, drive from Bridlington Head towards Flamborough on the B1255. Keep on this road through Flamborough village towards Thornwick Bay and North Landing
sites.parking: The car park is on the left opposite the North Star Hotel pay and display.
sites.entryExit: The walk from the car park is not far but the steep steps are a bit of a test on the way back to the car park. Enter the water at the right of the bay in front of the disused lifeboat station and exit in the same place.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: North star hotel · Cafe: North Landing Café
sites.hazards: Currents at the head of the bay. Take care leaving the water if there is a swell, it's easy to get knocked over.
sites.notes:
Shore Dive in a sheltered sandy bay with rocky outcrops and the remains of the SS Rosa a steam lighter which sank in 1930.

Suggested experience: Novice also a popular snorkelling site.

Underwater: Keep to the right (facing the sea) and don't go past the head. A part of the SS Rosa's boiler can be seen at low water and other fragments of steel wreckage are visible on the rocks to the west side of North Landing

There is a hand-painted sign saying no diving but this was put up without permission and should be ignored. confirmed by Scarborough Borough Council. Best to dive if it hasn't rained for a few days beforehand or there have not been any heavy winds because the swell picks up. Also if you are night diving you can reverse your car down to the top of the slipway and drop your kit off, remember to park it back in the car park.

sites.name: Nohoval cove
sites.access: Coming south on the M8 from Dublin take the Jack Lynch Tunnel. Take the second exit after the tunnel on to the N28 / R611 to Carrigaline (24km) -Drive straight through Carrigaline (coming off the R611) and keep going approximately 5 km to Minnane Bridge - there turn right for Novahal (3.5km) via the L3210 & L321.
sites.parking: Park at the old ruins as near to the stony path as you can to save carrying your dive kit too far.
sites.entryExit: Walk down 250m stony path to the water's edge and into the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here? · Cafe: None close to here?
sites.hazards: The cove faces south and so should be diveable in anything other than a southerly swell.
sites.notes:
Shore dive in a great small sheltered cove with pinnacles and gullies to the east.

Suggested experience: Novice and snorkelling

Underwater: Snorkel out of the cove over the seaweed into the deeper water drop down to the seabed and head east (left) diving around the pinnacles and further on to the gullies if you have the air to safely return.

The seabed here has Large boulders with white sand between them and is good for seeing Lobster in the slabbed rock formations, crab, sand eels, Dogfish and plenty types of Jellyfish.

sites.name: North strome
sites.access: Follow the A87 along Loch Duich and up to the southern side of Loch Carron. Keep following this round the loch until it turns off up to Loch Torridon. Follow the road through the village of Loch Carron and keep going until you get to Strome. Look out for the turning on the left that is signed for the castle. Google
sites.parking: Park above the slip keeping in mind this is quite busy, particularly at weekends in the summer with vehicles reversing down to the water. Google
sites.amenities: None close to here. This e-mail address is being protected from spambots. You need JavaScript enabled to view it
sites.entryExit: Use the handrail to put on your fins and enter the water at the end of the slip, and exit at the same place.
sites.accommodation: There is a small campsite in the middle of Loch Carron. I understand they are extremely helpful. Jo Rowley has used this and would probably recommend it. Sanachan bunkhouse
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: The tides roar through here like a steam train, the flattened kelp in the middle and rows of heaped up sand across the channel are all evidence of this. One to be avoided on springs. Be aware of what the tide is doing all the time, don’t get so immersed in taking photos etc that you miss the tide picking up and end up with it running so fast it pushes you past your exit.
sites.notes:
Very good shore dive on Loch Carron which is now a Marine Protected Area.

Suggested experience: Some experience or a novice diving with an experienced diver

Underwater: At slack, swim straight out into the middle of the loch where the mearl beds are covered with black brittle stars, gobies, butterfish and gravel sea cucumbers. From here you can explore up or down the loch, circling round and use the incoming or outgoing tides to bring you back to the jetty as slack finishes.

I haven't stayed there but the Loch Carron Hotel does a great Gammon and chips! Take lots of insect repellent if you are visiting during the midge season.

sites.name: Oddicombe
sites.access: Oddicombe is situated on the Eastern corner of the southwest peninsula, approx. 30 miles South of Exeter, 30 miles East of Plymouth on the Northern edge of Torbay and easily accessible from Torquay Harbour by following the many road signs. The main motorway networks link the southwest from the M6/M5 and the M4 with these main routes connecting around the Bristol area. All routes link directly to the end of the M5 and virtually link Torbay directly from the end of the motorway network.
sites.parking: Parking is on the side of the road heading down to the beach.
sites.entryExit: To dive Oddicombe it is best to enter the sea at the north of the cafe. (left facing the sea)
sites.accommodation: Royal hotel & carvery 31 Babbacombe Downs Rd, Torquay TQ1 3LQ
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Three degrees west · Cafe: Three degrees west
sites.hazards: Swell
sites.notes:
Oddicombe is a good shore dive on a Reef and Wall.

Suggested experience: Ideal for newly qualified to the U/W photographer.

Underwater: Head out East until you are at the bottom of the beach 3-4 meters deep! at this point, you want to head North following the line of the beach. you will come to some rocky outcrops where you can spend your whole dive! There are lots of small critters! anemones, Lobster and lots of Nudibranch species for the photographer! For a second dive, You can pass the rocks and keep heading North until you hit the wall! you can then follow the wall around for as long as you want! there are lots of cracks and crevices to explore with many more small critters to find. In the winter it's more open than Babbacombe meaning you get the sun most of the day which is nice after getting out from the cold sea!

Oddicombe Beach is a great dive for the winter when the winter season allows parking. This usually runs from the end of October through to March!

sites.name: Old cemetery 1
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the M8 cross the Erskin bridge onto the A82 and turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. At Tyndrum bear to the right still on the A82 over Rannoch Moor into Glencoe. Turn right after crossing the Ballachulish bridge onto the B863 and past the Loch Leven Hotel and the old cemetery with a loop in the road across from it and this is the car park area. From Glasgow 79 miles – about 1 hour 55 Min's
sites.parking: The Car Park Area has room for more than 10 cars.
sites.entryExit: Very easy access, just walk down to the shore from the picnic site, be careful as it's a bit slippy when wet.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: In Glencoe village · Cafe: Loch Leven Seafood Cafe
sites.notes:
Old cemetery 1 is a shore dive on Loch Leven, and old wooden wreck opposite the cemetery.

Suggested experience: Suitable for trainees and qualified divers (can be less than 20m)

Underwater: Swim out at about 30degrees to the East (left) of your entry point (the coarse gravel to the left of the wee stream, that's on your right) and drop to 4-5m and you'll find the wee wreck. A swim/dive further out, left or right and you'll find more bits and pieces of wreck associated with the wee wreck. There are some carved/ chiselled stone beams to the right of the immediate area of the timber, these might have been cargo. They are quite big. At this depth (15-18m depending on the tide) there is a field of Phosphorescent sea pens Exit can be afforded pretty much anywhere along the shore except midway, but it's only a short surface swim either way.

Don't forget to use the comments at the bottom of the page to let other divers know what its like to dive here.

sites.name: Old cemetery 2
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the M8 cross the Erskin bridge onto the A82 and turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. At Tyndrum bear to the right still on the A82 over Rannoch Moor into Glencoe. Turn right after crossing the Ballachulish bridge onto the B863 and past the Loch Leven Hotel and the old cemetery with a loop in the road across from it and there is a layby on the left. Google
sites.parking: The Lay By across the road has room for 10 cars.
sites.entryExit: Very easy access between the two rocks. Top arrow shows the dive site.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: In Glencoe village · Cafe: Loch Leven Seafood Cafe
sites.hazards: Cold and visibility if there are a lot of divers.
sites.notes:
Old cemetery 2 is a gentle shore dive and wall dive.

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: Enter the water and head down to 6m and turn right and head along until you come to the wall. Spend most of your bottom time here exploring.

This dive site is in a very quiet area and would be good for Barbi and campfire.

sites.name: Oxwich bay
sites.access: From Swansea head south-west towards Mansel on the A4118 for 11.5 miles then turn left at signpost marked Oxwich and Slade. Continue through Greenway park to Oxwitch. Total of 13 miles and 33 mins.
sites.parking: Park in Oxwich Bay Car Park or in the Oxwich Bay Hotel car park for a night dive when its quiet.
sites.entryExit: Enter the water at the south of the beach. (the right looking at the sea)
sites.airFill: Dive in2 Pembrokeshire West Wales dive centre Pembrokeshire Coast
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Oxwich Bay Hotel (good barbie in the summer). · Cafe: Oxwich Bay Cafe.
sites.hazards: Fishing lines and Fishing.
sites.notes:
A shallow wreck dive from a sandy beach which is also a popular snorkelling site for spearfishing.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards

Underwater: Head out staying close to the cliff on the surface until you see a large white arrow and the letter W painted on the cliffs This is where the wreck lies parallel to the cliff.The middle section of the hull is visible at low tide and looks like a fence.

The Solor was an 8,262-ton Norwegian motor vessel which was hit by a torpedo from U-825 in the Irish Sea. The Solor is now a popular dive site and is known for Conger Eels, spiny spider crabs, Triggerfish and Kayak fishing.

sites.name: Old Swimming Pool
sites.access: From the A1 travelling south at a roundabout marked (Dunbar A1087) turn left for the A199 then to next roundabout and turn right for the A1087 through West Barns and in Dunbar turn left into Marine road and continue to the end. From Edinburgh 30m and 40 mins.
sites.parking: There is ample parking on Marine Road, opposite the great Rocks Hotel.
sites.entryExit: Two ways to access the dive is either walk across the rocks and jump entry into about 4-6ms, following the rocks on your right-hand side until you come to exit point or swim in from the shore crossing over the small wall over a sewer pipe (no longer used), this leads you into a gulley, turn left and follow the rocks, keeping them on your left-hand side. To exit, it can be a bit disorientating, the first gulley that looks like it will take you back to shore is a dead end, follow on for a couple of minutes to the next gulley, this will take you back to the pipe, then over a small wall back into the old pool area, then a short walk up the steps, this is murder as they are different heights, take your time.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The rocks The Rocks Hotel has a wee beer garden, perfect for buying a cold/hot drink or a bite to eat, can recommend their bowls of soup after a dive. Previous owners have indicated its okay to use their toilets, but it's up for new management so would have to check before using. · Cafe: Probably on Dunbar high street and certainly takeaways there open till at least 11 pm
sites.hazards: Swells with a Northeast wind.
sites.notes:
Good s hore dive in the rocks and gullies near the old swimming pool.

Suggested experience: Novice in good conditions.

Underwater: There is a fantastic system of gullies all along the reefs seaward side, as well as some on the shore side. On the north-west side of the reef you'll come across a break in the reef, called coral canyon, around the back of this there is a large hollow at 15mtrs. Look carefully into all the nooks and crannies for small crabs, fish, the occasional octopus and lobster. Swim for 30 mins depending on your air and turn back.

This dive site is very exposed so its best done after a week's calm weather.

sites.name: Pendennis point
sites.access: Travel through Falmouth, take the road to the docks. Drive past the docks around Pendennis Castle, go past the car park a few hundred metres until you see a layby on the left.
sites.parking: Park in the layby as close to the start of the layby as possible. Google
sites.entryExit: A few metres from the bottom of the layby in front of where you park are some granite steps leading down to the rocks. The rocks are fairly easy to cross and slope into the water.
sites.airFill: Atlantic scuba Cornwall divers in Falmouth or Seaways dive centre in Penryn.
sites.accommodation: Falmouth has plenty of hotels within 1m of the site
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: There are some pubs around, the most popular is the Chain Locker about 1 mile away by Customs House Quay · Cafe: Ice creams and cold drinks available at the car park, there are plenty of cafes in Falmouth
sites.hazards: Boat traffic in summer increases
sites.notes:
Pendennis point is a good shore wreck dive on the remains of two Uboats.

Suggested experience: Open Water

Underwater: To see the U-boats you need to go left, roughly northeast. The biggest piece is in a direct line of sight from the second set of steps. A bit further along there is a gully with a small cave at the end.

2nd most popular dive in Cornwall. The U-boats that sank here were the UB86 and UB112,

sites.name: Overstrand
sites.access: From Norwich head north on the A140 turn left onto the A149 turn off at Crossdale street and follow signs for Overstrand onto Pauls Ln onto the Cliff Top Cafe.
sites.parking: Park as close to the top of the path as possible or in the Pay and display which have toilets 100m along the road.
sites.entryExit: Its 150m from the top of the concrete path down to the sand and 40m across the sand to the sea depending on the tide but it seems to be further on the way back up the path. If you have a trolly its ideal for here as its a good path down to the beach.
sites.accommodation: Ivy Farm holiday park Overstrand campsite
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: Cliff top Cafe
sites.hazards: Viz here is very weather dependent, and can drop to zero quiet fast after onshore winds, but remaining clear into the Autumn if SW winds continue.
sites.notes:
Overstrand in Norfolk is a varied dive in rock holes and chalk gullies.

Suggested experience: Novice with good conditions

Underwater: The chalk reefs here have fingers emerging from the sand sloping downwards, Straight north is an abandoned pipe to the west there is an area of rock with large and small holes that look as if they had been drilled, to the east is an area with chalk boulders.

The viz at Overstand beach is usually 3-4m but best at high slack water. You can also dive the Sheringham gullies 7 miles and 20 mins west of here.

sites.name: Picnic site
sites.access: Google Leaving Glasgow on the M8 cross the Erskin bridge onto the A82 and turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. At Tyndrum bear to the right still on the A82 over Rannoch Moor into Glencoe. On entering Glencoe you will see Loch Leven on the right, cross the bridge and after a few miles turn left Google down into the car park.
sites.parking: In the car park.
sites.entryExit: Dive 1: The car park and picnic site have a path down to the glaciated rocks on the point. The entry is the small pebble beach to the right (North) of this (entry bay). Dive two: from the entry bay a pebble spit runs out 100 yards north, at low water, this is exposed. Walk to the end of this
sites.airFill: Puffin divers Oban & The underwater centre
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Corran Inn · Cafe: Fort William
sites.hazards: No major Hazards.
sites.notes:
Easy shore dive on Loch Linnhe seven miles south of Fort William which is often used for training.

Suggested experience: Novice up...

Underwater: Dive 1: Head straight out over a 3m shelf and down the slope to 6m, this brings you to the steep edge of a mud slope covered in multi-coloured brittle stars. This continues down to at least 25m where the angle appears too shallow (though the loch is much deeper). Scallops (few), queenies, anemonies and usual burrowing worms. Dogfish reported. A gentle drift when lower down the slope took us southwards. A few large dragonettes. Coming back up the slope we encountered an overhanging wall at 8m, covered in life (and mono-filament line and hooks) which we followed to the end of the dive surfacing at the point. Shoal of saith on the kelp here as well as leopard gobies. Others reported following this reef further and surfaced in the middle of the bay to the south.

This is a good site for a club training day, good parking and plenty of room.

sites.name: Pettico wick
sites.access: From the A1, turn off for Eyemouth on the A1107 and turn left onto B6438 and left again before St Abbs
sites.parking: Car park at the top of the hill on the left just before the lighthouse.
sites.entryExit: As the pictures below, enter off the end of the ramp.
sites.mobileSignal: No reception at sea level but OK at the parking area.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: St Abbs · Cafe: St Abbs
sites.hazards: Path to the dive site and currents to the north.
sites.notes:
Pettico wick is a wreck and reef shore dive.

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: In the center of the bay there is a small tunnel ( Utube ) in a depth of 7m in a rock called Wick Gault. There is also a wreck here called the Ringholm (Odense) (N55 54.90 W02 09.19) and the only sizable part left is the boiler.

This dive site is usually done when St Abbs is blown out but it can be a great dive.

sites.name: Pittulie
sites.access: Come off the A90 or A98 onto the B9031 into Sandhaven and along the shore road to the last house until you see a small car park on the shore side of the road.
sites.parking: There is room for 6 cars leaving room for access to the house.
sites.amenities: There are no public phones near here.
sites.entryExit: Walk along the grass at the back of the houses then Its a very easy entry/exit down the concrete slip.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Arc Pittendrum Bar · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.notes:
Pittulie near Sandhaven is a gentle shore dive with plenty to see in shallow water.

Suggested experience: Novice in good conditions

Underwater: Contact me

sites.name: Platcock rocks
sites.parking: Drive round to the old pier and if you are lucky you can get a space here if not drop off the kit and park on Melbourn road Google
sites.entryExit: Enter the water at the end of the path to the point and exit in the same place or up the steps at the back of the pier.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Auld Hoose · Cafe: Number 12
sites.hazards: Surge and waves from the northeast.
sites.notes:
Shore dive on the point of North Berwick.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards

Underwater: You can explore around the point and head south to the pier or explore around the point heading east into the gully and back.

It's best to dive here when there have been two weeks of low winds. Otters are often spotted here so maybe someone could get an u/w shot.

sites.name: Port Gaverne
sites.access: Port Gaverne is next to port Isaac on the north coast of Cornwall, follow signs to Port Isaac, drive past the car parks to the bottom of the hill, that is Port Gaverne
sites.parking: Parking is limited, there are about 5 spaces on the verge and about 10 on the road.
sites.amenities: Port Gaverne has a pub with a phone, otherwise Port Isaac
sites.entryExit: Enter the shore on the right and head out to the Island, no surf unless the wind is North-West or strong West
sites.mobileSignal: Orange works so do most networks
sites.accommodation: There are plenty of hotels & guest houses all around including 2 in Port Gaverne and dozens in Port Isaac.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: 100m from the water Link · Cafe: There was a tea van in Port Gaverne but it appears to be closed now, so Port Isaac has plenty
sites.hazards: Port Gaverne is an active fishing port, keep an SMB up and stay close to the North or South sides.
sites.notes:
Scenic shore dive.

Suggested experience: Open water/novice

Underwater: Follow north side along until you reach the gulley (Nort-West), the gully is noticeable from the sand from 2 places as there are 2 small gullies running to the main gulley. The main gulley is the gap between the headland and the island. Once through the gully, I always check everyone's air. If you have plenty left you can head anti-clockwise around the island and back along the north side (South-East). You can also dive the south side, it is a series of rocky outcrops and is worth a dive while you're there.

Don't forget to use the comments at the bottom of the page to let other Divers know what its like to dive here.

sites.name: Port Mellon
sites.access: Google Leave Exeter on the A30 - A391 - B3274 - B3273 Mevagissey
sites.parking: Park in the rising sun hotel carpark if you just have one car and remember to go in and buy a snack.
sites.entryExit: Walk down the slipway and enter the water on the sandy beach exit at the same place. See the picture below.
sites.airFill: : Atlantic scuba or Cornish diving in Falmouth or Seaways diving in Penryn.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The rising sun · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: Occasional boat traffic
sites.notes:
Port Mellon is a very easy shore dive under the cliff in good conditions

Suggested experience: Novice

Underwater: Keep the cliff on your left shoulder along the bottom and explore all the cracks in the cliff, there is plenty to see and photograph. Continue around into the bay at the back of the cliff and retrace your fin strokes at a shallower depth back into the bay.

Very easy dive best done at a high tide, but look out for occasional boat traffic

sites.name: Port Erin jetty
sites.parking: Park on the road opposite the jetty.
sites.entryExit: Simply walk down the stairs onto the jetty and down the stairs at the end into the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: FORAGING VINTNERS · Cafe: Cafe Delicious Waterside Bistro
sites.hazards: Swell from the west.
sites.notes:
Port Erin jetty on the Isle of man is an easy shore dive from the jetty near the Lifeboat Station.

Suggested experience: Novice and suitable for training.

Underwater: Info to follow Contact me

sites.name: Port Na Happle
sites.access: Port Na Happle is in the very north of Northern Ireland near Port Stewart.
sites.parking: There is parking for 15 cars in the car park
sites.entryExit: From the car park walk down the stairs and along the path and back towards the house then down to the gulley.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Anchor bar. · Cafe: Bob & Berts coffee house The three Kings
sites.hazards: entry and exit point at shore require caution due to rocks covered in kelp. Easy to lose footing. It's possible to enter the water by giant stride at the end of the natural pier but exiting the same way is difficult
sites.notes:
Port Na Happle at Portstewart is a shallow gully sandy in the middle and small cliffs along the sides.

Suggested experience: Novice to the experienced diver.

Underwater: Utube

There are plenty of crabs and dogfish to be seen in the seaweed at the edges of the gully with flatfish in the middle sandy areas.

sites.name: Port Quin
sites.parking: There is a small free (donation if you're feeling generous) national trust car park, with a couple of benches and tables to the side. Google
sites.amenities: There are no public phones here.
sites.entryExit: A 50m walk and you are on the slip, at high tide the water is on the slip, but being a shore dive leaves you a long swim to get any depth as can be seen in the picture below at low tide.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Port Isaac · Cafe: The Salt Pig in Port Quin
sites.hazards: There are no major hazards in the cove.
sites.notes:
Port Quin is a gentle shallow shore dive in a protected cove.

Suggested experience: Novice in good conditions.

Underwater: On both sides, there are reefs with some life. From the slip to the mouth of the cove it's around 400m, the beach has either a rocky entrance at HW or sand at LW, so LW a shorter swim, long walk. Across the entrance of the cove is a large reef with quite a lot of life. If you go south you have a wall dive getting to about 15m HW, with a few gullies around the corner and if you swim far enough and the sand is low, there are the remains of a fishing boat in a small cave. If you go north, there is a large reef, again with gullies and quite a bit of life.

If you are feeling fit, or have a DPV, another 200m out the is the Cow & Calf. I dived this a few weeks ago from my boat, after following the edge of the reef around, it took 69 minutes to get 3/4 of the way around. The side closest to the land has huge boulders and big recess's for fish to hide

sites.name: Portencross
sites.access: Head west on the M8 turn off onto the A737 turning right onto the A760 to Largs. Turn left onto the A78 south towards West Kilbride for 8 miles and turn right onto the B7048 to Portencross, the carpark is clearly on the left as you enter Portencross
sites.parking: Enter the carpark under the goalpost in the middle of the picture below and park on the far left facing the sea or along the road to dive the pier.
sites.entryExit: From the left of the car park as you face the sea go through the gate and walk 15 meters and enter the water at the clearing. See the pictures below…. or enter the water at the point marked exit on the picture below to dive the pier.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Largs marina · Cafe: Nardini in Largs
sites.hazards: A west wind turns the site into a dangerous washing machine with an excessive surge in the shallow water and waves breaking onto the rocky shore.
sites.notes:
Portencross is a shallow dive near the castle.

Suggested experience: All grades of diver

Underwater: Head out till you reach 8m (about a 100m) and turn right and head north for 200m and exit beside the castle or return to the entry point. To the south of the Castle, the seabed is rocky, in Summer there is lots of kelp. North of the castle mid-way between the castle and the pier, the seabed is sand. An east wind will hold the sea flat, a west wind turns the site into a dangerous washing machine with an excessive surge in the shallow water and waves breaking onto the rocky shore. The pier is popular with some Scotsac branches for the sport diver "jump entry" skill assessment, it's quite high. A shallow dive around the pier north of the castle can be good for creatures and critters. (see picture below)

This is where the famous Portencross galleon sank in 1740 a few hundred yards off Farland head, possibly one of the Spanish Armada. One of the cannons used to lie beside the castle till a few years ago. There is another report that says the wreck is straight out from the castle in 60ft of water. The diver reported, that from the size of her guns, she appeared to have been a capital ship; and a very large chest was perceived fixed upon deck. The operation succeeded so far, that some fine brass guns were brought up, and a smaller iron one, which still lies upon the beach.

sites.name: Porth Ysgadn
sites.access: From the north down the coast road (B4417) onto the (B4354) or the east on the (B4354) to the coast on the (A497) onto the (B4412) (B4417) turn right 0.7 miles after Tudweiliog and head to the end of the road which is easily recognised from a distance by a derelict house and chimney on the headland.
sites.parking: Park next to the bench at the end of the road or in the car park shown below.
sites.entryExit: Its a 3 min walk down to the slip and enter the water at the end of the slip.
sites.airFill: You don’t really need nitrox fills for this. You can get air fills from Anglesey divers Vivian
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Lion pub · Cafe: Pen Y Bryn Cafe
sites.hazards: Don't go past the mouth of the bay when the tides are ebbing or flowing.
sites.notes:
Shallow shore dive with walls at either side, gullies and sandy seabed.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards, good for training.

Underwater: Its a small horseshoe-shaped bay so navigation is easy. Head out along the south wall then over the mouth of the bay and back, going in and out of the small gully's. If you look in the middle of the bay use an SMB as the bay is popular with dive boats, water-skiers and lobster boats. For novices keep to the rocks along the northern side of the bay as it never has any current.

This dive site is best done after a few days of calm weather on a flooding or high tide. Forget about diving here on a bank holiday as it can get very busy unless you are here early.

sites.name: Porth Colmon
sites.access: From Porthmadog Head west towards A497, Exit the roundabout onto Penamser Rd/A497, At the roundabout, take the 1st exit onto A497, Turn right onto B4354, Turn right to stay on B4354, Turn left onto A499, Slight right onto A497, At the roundabout, continue straight onto B4412, Turn left onto Lon Terfyn/B4417 and continue to Porth Colmon.

sites.notes:
Porth Colmon in north Wales is a very easy shore dive, good for novices and snorkelling.

Suggested experience: Novice, Photography and Snorkeling.

Underwater: Stay within the cove and the current is easily manageable or if its slack water you can explore east towards the beach. Don't go to the west unless you are confident the tide is not a problem.

As with most of the dive sites here you will see spider crabs, plumose anemones, snake locks anemones, small gobies. This is a lovely dive site for all divers, from complete novices to photographers and divers who enjoy wildlife.

Shore dive (high tide best)

Underwater: Head out from the bay east or west staying close to the edge of the bay to avoid any possible boat traffic and look in all the gullies.

Best done after a long spell of low winds as is exposed to the prevailing wind. In June you get plankton blooms like most dives around here. There are lots of gully's and cracks to explore and as it's not deep so you get good bottom times. It's also advisable to use an SMB in the bay as boats do use the bay. There are toilets 25m from the beach

The less experienced can stay on the inside and potter around in a number of pools with plenty of crannies to shelter all manner of fish, crabs and lobsters, plus the usual encrusting growth. The more adventurous or energetic head to the outside of the reef, where it is deeper and there are caves and large boulders, and less kelp due to the north exposure.

Porthgain in Pembrokeshire is an easy shore dive just outside the Harbour.

The wreck of the Dan Beard can be dived from here, Launching from the slip. (51°56'00.0"N 5°29'00.0"W) You can also dive the Blue Lagoon 2.7 miles and 10 min south of here.

A popular training site for divers

sites.entryExit: The beach is a long walk from the car park so drive as far down to the beach as you can and drop off your dive kit then take your time and two trips to carry your kit to the shore. Its an Easy entry into the water by walking down the beach...

Prussia cove is a good scenic shore dive used for snorkelling as well

Suggested experience: Novice upwards...

Underwater: Keep to the east which is your left facing the sea and swim in and out all the gully's and return the same way. The seabed is sandy with rocks and seaweed. This dive site is famous for Tompot Blennies, Squat Lobsters, Rocklings, Squid, Cuttlefish, Dogfish as well as the usual wrasse and Pollack. In the centre of Prussia Cove, there is the wreckage of HMS Warspite a Queen Elizabeth-class battleship which sank under tow to the breakers yard.

About 50m off the beach is the best diving, around a rock called the Enys. There is also an island to the south-east, which has a long tunnel passing through it.

Shore dive

Underwater: Head south to the rock and explore in and around the rocks and cracks staying close to the rock. The currents get stronger as you go further from the shore.

It's best to dive here with somebody who has dived here before. It's also advisable to have good shore cover when diving here.

sites.name: Ratagan
sites.access: I ts 61 miles from Fort William (90 mins) Take the A82 up the side of Loch Lochy, At Invergarry turn left onto the A87 to Sheil bridge turn left onto the old military road, Turn right for Ratagan from here it's 0.4 of a mile along the coast road.
sites.entryExit: Its a very easy walk down the stony beach on the west of the youth hostel into the water.
sites.airFill: 5Bells at Loch Carron, Dive and sea the Hebrides on Skye, or carry your own
sites.accommodation: Ratagan youth hostel Kintail lodge hotel (Bunk Rooms and Bunk House), The youth hostel makes a good base for a dive holiday
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Kintail lodge hotel · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: Silt
sites.notes:
Ratagan is a gentle silty slope at the head of Loch Duich famous for its sea pens and Firework anemones.

Suggested experience: Sport diver with good buoyancy

Underwater: The first 20-30 m out from shore (depending on tide height) are shallow over cobbles and gravel with wrack over most of it. Then you get a bank of cobbles that starts to angle down at about 40 deg slope. The slope is muddy, silty with gravel and small cobbles throughout down to about 20m depth, then it changes to almost entirely mud. Tall sea pens start at around 20m depth and proper forests of them at around 30m. You get phosphorescent sea pens and slender pens too and the occasional fireworks anemones. There's a chance of a ray. There is no bottom topography to speak of, so I generally go straight down the slope to whatever bottom depth I choose, then either come back up the slope in a zig-zag or along at a tangent west or east and then back up to avoid going over the same ground. As always with Duich, careful with fins near the bottom or it'll be pitch dark and zero viz in a jiffy! If caught out by disturbed sediment, feel along the bottom in a random direction and you will suddenly come out of the dust cloud again!

The sea bed is very silty here so good buoyancy is essential. You can also dive Ardearg cemetery and the Boathouse just along the coast roa d.

sites.name: Queenie Reef
sites.access: To the south of the upper basin in Loch Creran; Follow the ‘local traffic’ road at the roundabout before the bridge Google
sites.parking: There is a large lay-by at the steps which can become full of divers at busy times. There is another lay-by just to the west which is easily walkable back to this site if needed
sites.entryExit: Access is easy down the steps from the layby, entry is also easy on a gently sloping gravel beach. Utube
sites.airFill: The only option within a reasonable distance is Puffin Dive Centre in Oban, air fill £5 from the self-serve fill 24hrs.
sites.mobileSignal: O2 Vodaphone T-mobile and Orange works
sites.accommodation: Seabank farmhouse Oban… Corran House SYHA
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Creagan Inn is very close and has food. If staying in Oban there are plenty of options.is very close and has food.
sites.hazards: There are no hazards associated with this site; the only thing to beware of is the silty bottom which is prone to bad visibility if kicked up as is common with shore dives in Scotland. The site can be dived in any tidal and weather conditions every day of the year if you want to as it is so sheltered. Visibility is better when it has been calm for a few days though. This is a special area of conservation so respect the area and do not touch the Serpum Vermiscula,
sites.notes:
Sheltered, shallow shore dive on a silty seabed with rock formations, areas of rocky reef and horse mussel beds.

Suggested experience: All diver grades, suitable for training if care is taken with silt reducing visibility and around the worm structures

Underwater: See the map below. The normal approach is to follow the rock formation to the left, keeping the rock on your left as you swim out; this ends at about 12m and then heading off at 45 degrees to the right of the direction you followed the rock formation will bring you to another ledge which drops down a few more metres. If you are new to this site, bring a compass as it is possible to become disorientated when attempting this. All the rocky areas are covered in life and there is also a lot to see exploring the silty bay between the rock formations.

Loch Creran is one of 2 locations in Scotland plus another in Ireland where the tube worm Serpula vermicularis grows in dense groups, forming small biogenic reefs. The worm itself isn’t rare but this reef-forming behaviour is known from very few areas. These reefs are fragile and clearly shouldn’t be disturbed - be careful with novice divers. There are far fewer aggregations at this site than there used to be (probably in part due to careless fin kicks) but you can go looking elsewhere within Loch Creran. You can also dive Cregan bridge 600m from here.

sites.name: Rhoscolyn
sites.access: A55 over the Meni bridge onto Anglesey, onto A155 At junction 3, take the A5 exit to Valley Turn left at B4545 Turn right at Ffordd Caradoc.
sites.parking: There’s a Pay&Display car park just behind the beach, however, it’s not big so arrive early in sunny summer.
sites.entryExit: Simple entry on the beach or the boat slip on the right of the bay.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The white eagle · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: Speedboats and jet skis. An SMB is recommended for diving here if you dive in the bay.
sites.notes:
Rhoscolyn is a scenic shore dive good for snorkelling as well

Suggested experience: Novis

Underwater: Head out looking in all the cracks in the shore to your right until you get to the Island where you are in a gully and then keep the wall to your left and go round the Island. When you get back to the gully keep the shore to your left and return to the shore.

This is a great area for a club dive trip its good for photography with good viz and if you have a RHiB with you there are a few wrecks as well as scenic diving.

sites.name: Rosehearty
sites.access: Head north on the A90 into the toll of Birness turn left onto the A592 into Fraserburgh and then the A98 to Rosehearty.
sites.parking: Park at the picnic site in North Street just past the ex RAF lookout tower. which is also good for a surface interval if you are doing two dives. See picture below.
sites.entryExit: Rough rock and boulder access to entry/exit site. The gully is the most common entry/exit point. Just step off and clear the gully and drop down to 7 - 8 m this takes you into a North-South running channel, (see picture below) Even at low water exiting the water is easy as there are natural steps at the end of the gulley only difficult on low spring tide.
sites.airFill: local dive club can provide air fills (orca diving club) message through Facebook.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Masons Arms as you enter Rosehearty opposite the golf course and the Bay hotel in the main square. · Cafe: None close to here so take what you need.
sites.hazards: rough rocky/boulder access and difficult exit if there is a swell.
sites.notes:
Shore dive with plenty to see.

Suggested experience: Suitable for all grades.

Underwater: Three swim-throughs approx. North-East of the main entry point. There are a variety of dive routes by following the rock faces, one of them being the Pinnacle. You can exit the first gully and head North-West till you come to two pipes lying on the seabed from here you go west following a rock face then as it breaks there is a small gully which you follow slightly up then down again to another deep gully bottom covered in large boulders explore this gully and back at the start follow the northerly side round and at the end of this is more boulders and in the summer months is full of wrasse then retrace your steps back to the pipes from there South-East takes you to the gully.

sites.name: Royal Adelaide
sites.parking: Park in the car park next to the Chesil Beach Centre. Google map
sites.amenities: 300 m on the left as you go towards Weymouth
sites.entryExit: From the cafe, walk straight to the top of the beach and find a red stone block. Walk about 40 paces North and go directly to the water. The most reliable way to hit the wreck is to follow the seabed on a compass bearing. It's a tough walk so carry as little weight as possible. The exit here can be dangerous if there is a swell.
sites.accommodation: The Aqua Cottage Ferrybridge Inn or Weymouth tourist information, 01305 785747.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Ferrybridge Inn · Cafe: Quiddles Cafe
sites.hazards: The walk over the stones to the water's edge, swell and exiting the water up the pebble slope.
sites.notes:
The Royal Adelaide was a 1500 ton steel sailing ship blown onto the beach in November 1872. and she was carrying a general cargo including casks of rum, brandy and gin.

Suggested experience: Strong sport diver.

Underwater: The Adelaide lies about 90 metres from the shore, at the edge of the pebbles If the seabed starts to undulate you've gone too far so head back to the shore.

In September till October, you can see tame triggerfish around the wreck which swim towards divers and is a great shot for the Photographer. Carry as little weight as possible, a 10 or 12-litre cylinder is enough to dive here. The bell has been recovered from the wreck. There are toilets here.

sites.name: Rumbling Kern
sites.access: From Alnwick 7 miles 16 mins Google
sites.parking: About 200m from the sea the road veers sharply left (north) whilst a farm road leads off to the right and a track passes straight on through a gate towards the sea. Park on the verge of the farm road taking care not to block the gate. Access to the sites is through the gate and along the track.
sites.entryExit: From the sandy beach climb the rock here (pick below) then its an easy walk over the rocks. and enter and exit the water in the gully.
sites.nearbyFood: Cafe: None close to here.
sites.hazards: Entering and exit with high waves.
sites.notes:
Shore dive over rocky ridges.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards.

Underwater: There are several reefs running paralleling too the shore.The reefs are about 30-50m apart and the third and fourth reefs out are usually the biggest (up to 2.5m high) All the reefs have a vertical wall with the kelp covered tops sloping eastwards into the sand. Pick a reef and follow it along and back. There is an arch about 150m out from the shore on the third reef and there are bits of the sub G11 that was broken up for salvage just north of here.

Its a bit of a walk with dive kit from the car to the dive site. The area between the rocks and the grass is a sheltered area and is great for a BBQ.

sites.name: Salen Pier
sites.access: Follow the A849 towards Tobermoray when you reach Salen turn right and follow the road to the pier. Google
sites.parking: Ample parking for residents of the House and Lodge passed the cattle grid and parking for visitors near the old pier so just park considerately.
sites.entryExit: Enter the water by walking down the small rock beach to the left of the pier facing the sea.
sites.mobileSignal: Vodafone, O2 and Orange work well.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Glenforsa Hotel The Mishnish
sites.hazards: Currents see above
sites.notes:
Salen Pier is an interesting shore dive around and under the pier. Webcam

Suggested experience: All grades.

Underwater: Swim out at the end of the pier it suddenly drops to 8m and it is here there is most life. There is a rock and concrete base to support the end of the pier and this covered with life. Initially, there seems to be very little but on further examination, you will find some well-concealed scorpionfish, nudibranchs, cup corals, sea squirts, and tiny sea stars. Going to the left or right of the pier there are rocks, some covered with kelp with a few crabs etc, but not a great deal of life. Swimming straight out there is little but the flattened kelp on the seabed hints at the speed of the currents that rush down here, so something to beware of. This is not a fantastic site in comparison to many but for someone who likes small marine life or the macro photographer, there is plenty here.

The pier is privately owned by Peter and Susanne who have Salen Pier House which sleeps 13 and 4 in the Lodge. The pier has a gate across it and has been extensively renovated. The slipway is private and non-residents should contact Peter and Susanne in advance. Residents of the House or Lodge have free access.

Scarfskerry haven is a good shore and wreck dive.
