sites.hazards: Steps down to the shore and slippy seaweed at the shoreline.
sites.notes:
The Creggans shore dive is a long silty slope on Loch Fyne.

Suggested experience: Trainee

Underwater: dive to the right, taking you in front of the pier. This site seems to be barren with only a few small boulders but there are lots of small life and some bigger rays at the right times of the year.

sites.name: Thirteen mile reef
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the A82 turn left at Tarbet onto the A83, through Arrochar and over the rest and be thankful, turn left onto the A815, from this junction its 8.7 miles to the A886 then for 4 miles to the turnoff for the B8000 then for 9.8 miles to Thirteen-mile reef. ( Half a mile past Gortein point and just passed triple reef) At Thirteen mile reef the telephone pole at the side of the road has a No 29 on it. Google map
sites.parking: Park in the passing place, leaving plenty room for cars to pass.(see picture below)
sites.entryExit: Walk through the gap in the Bushes as in the picture below and down the rocks to enter the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Creggans Inn · Cafe: None close to here.
sites.hazards: Can be a long swim back to shore if following it all the way down. Entry and exit can be tricky if there is a bit of a swell. If there is a flood or ebb tide you have to work hard to stay on the reef.
sites.notes:
Shore dive in Loch Fyne with a wall and boulder slope to 40m,

Suggested experience: Experienced sport diver

Underwater: head straight down to 22m and turn right until you come to the wall. Wall runs down to about 36m where it turns into a boulder slope we stopped at 40m. There is a nice big mushroom anchor and chain that hangs over the wall at about 25m.

Often mistaken for Triple reef .

sites.name: Thornwick bay
sites.access: To get there, drive from Bridlington Head towards Flamborough on the B1255. Keep on this road through Flamborough village towards Thornwick Bay. Google
sites.parking: Park at the top of the cliffs you pay £1 to park all day in the booth on the access road. This road is not in good condition and you have to go slowly.
sites.amenities: In the cafe above the bay.
sites.entryExit: When you get kitted up, head down a lot of steps onto the beach into the cove, There are now some metal steps at the bottom to make it easier to get onto the beach, walk to the right-hand side and walk into a small cove. this is the best and the most accessible way to get into the water.. You can walk or swim depending on the tide straight back onto the beach Utube
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: North star hotel · Cafe: At the car park above the bay.
sites.hazards: The long walk down to the beach and be aware of a strong current which runs around the point and the long climb up the stairs back to the car.
sites.notes:
Shore Dive

Suggested experience: Novice also a popular snorkelling site.

Underwater: Keep to the right (facing the sea) and head out towards the point but turn back before reaching there.

Best to dive here when it hasn't rained for a few days beforehand or there haven't been any heavy winds because the swell picks up.

sites.name: Tod head lighthouse
sites.access: Todhead Lighthouse is located just South of Stonehaven and North of Montrose on the coastal road route of the A92. It is clearly signposted and easily seen from the main road. A small bumpy road takes you down to Todhead Lighthouse Google
sites.parking: Park near the lighthouse
sites.entryExit: Take the steps down to the water on the north side of the lighthouse and out towards the rocks beyond the wall on your left. Go past the first opening and enter in the second opening There are quite a few steps so it makes sense to “travel light” if possible.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None near here. · Cafe: None so take everything you need
sites.hazards: Be careful not to stray too far offshore because the current can be strong and will take you to Montrose (it has happened!).
sites.notes:
Tod head lighthouse is a very good shore dive in good conditions

Suggested experience: Experienced shore diver.

Underwater: After entering at the second opening you should drop down to 10 metres onto a wreck and follow the coast in a southerly direction in a narrow gulley to a wee cave and then the arch.After looking at the arch its time to exit. As with most of the sites on the east coast, the area can be quite silty but it is very nice in clear conditions.

Catterline has a large seal population so you should get the odd sighting here.

sites.name: Torpedo post
sites.access: Follow the A83 past Arrochar and Conger Alley Dive Site, and take the turn left into the Ardgartan Visitor Centre. Continue over the Croe Water bridge and turn left towards Ardgartan Hotel. Continue along the single-track road past the hotel, and once you reach the first houses on your left, parking is approximately 150m past these.
sites.parking: Park in the small layby ensuring that you leave enough room for other traffic to use as a passing point. The layby has space for two cars maximum, with further parking possible just along the road if intending on just dropping off gear
sites.entryExit: The approach to the site is fairly steep and challenging. It is recommended that you kit up at the parking site and descend the slope towards the shore that is 100m away. Once you reach the edge of the shore, head northwards 30m approximately until you reach the entry point resembling the image below. Entry into the water is easy from this point.
sites.accommodation: Ardgartan Hotel , Forest Holidays - Ardgartan Argyll
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Slanj Bar & restaurant · Cafe: Three Villages Cafe , Arrochar Tea Room
sites.hazards: Challenging approach from the parking site to the shore with areas of bog and slip/trip hazards.
sites.notes:
Shore dive on the north-west coast of Loch Long

Suggested experience: Sport/AOW

Underwater: Heading straight out from the shore, you will fin through a small kelp field for about 3m. This gives way to a gravel/small stone slope down to approximately 10m, where you then encounter a boulder reef that extends down to about 22m. Within this boulder reef, there are numerous huge boulders that must have fallen as part of a landslip at some point in time. As a result, they have formed some fascinating features; including overhangs and a small tunnel (although, it is not advised to swim through this). At approximately 15m, there is also a torpedo that is sitting vertically in the ground and is now providing a small habitat for life; this can be used as a marker for the exit point. Deeper on from the boulder reef is a sandy silt slope that starts to taper off from 26m. Dotted about this area are numerous Firework Anemones and plenty of Langoustines. Return by zigzagging back up the boulder reef (exploring the huge boulders that are covered in life) until you find the torpedo again. From here, it is straight back up to the exit point.

To the knowledge of the author, this is a new site that could benefit from further exploration in all directions.

sites.name: The slates
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the M8 cross the Erskin bridge onto the A82 and turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. At Tyndrum bear to the right still on the A82 over Rannoch Moor into Glencoe. On entering Glencoe you will see Loch Leven on the right, Along this road ½ mile on the left is a sign for Lochside Cottages on the right in west Laroch, turn in here.
sites.parking: JCBs have dug up the parking area and it is not possible to park here just now.
sites.amenities: Swallow Isles of Glencoe Hotel (100meters from dive site)
sites.entryExit: Walk down from the car park between the old slate buildings and enter the water on the left side of the large rocks
sites.accommodation: The red squirrel Glencoe Mountain Parkview B+B
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Isles of Glencoe Hotel (100m from dive site) Laroch · Cafe: West Laroch.
sites.hazards: Depth 50+ Meters
sites.notes:
Suggested experience: Sport diver + Training area

Underwater: On entering the water there is a fair bit of weed 0-3 meters, which is great for spending a few mins on your safety or deco stops when you have been to depth at the point. Then there is a sand and silt slope to 12 meters. Keep the slate and boulder slope on your left side and follow the point at your chosen depth into the next bay and exit before the small pier. The whole of the point is made from old slate from the quarry and there are so many things to see here it's not possible to list them. Don't forget to look up as there are shoals of fish here. If you do go to the bottom of the point its 50m and from there on its a long flat seabed, I don't think its worth it unless you are on a rebreather.

This site has lots of life and is good for pictures. As well as two dives here there is Manse point just along the road. You can also dive the quarry behind the village. Google map Also a few miles along the road is the Kentallen wall Don't forget to use the comments at the bottom of the page to let other divers know what it's like to dive here.

sites.name: Torpedo station
sites.alternativeNames: Torpedo Station/pier, Ardgartan Loch Long Access is blocked just now
sites.parking: Park at the side of the road next to wire fence before the abandoned house, the pier is visible through the trees. Leave plenty of space for passing cars.
sites.entryExit: : Entry point is just through the trees next to parking spot (be careful as it’s very slippy!!) enter/exit the water at the side of the metal fence that enters the water at muscle beds.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Village Inn · Cafe: Petrol station Pitstop diner
sites.hazards: Viz can be poor.
sites.notes:
The Torpedo station on Loch Long is a silty slope under and around the pier

Suggested experience: Suitable for trainees

Underwater: This dive is best done at high tide. From the entry point fin round in a circle to meet the end of the pier, take your time as there is a fair amount of marine life to see if you look closely for it. This site has lots of old jars, bottles, shoes, corrugated roof panels, gloves, car tyres and general wreckage from the pier.

You can also dive on some of the torpedoes near here. T orpedoes

sites.name: Toscaig Pier
sites.parking: Park on the right facing the pier.
sites.amenities: Red phone box half a mile back from the pier. Google
sites.entryExit: Easy entry down the left side of the jetty at High Water or there is a path leading in about 100 M North which is accessible at all states. It just means lugging the kit a bit further, then a shallow 100m at the start/end of the dive or you can do this... Vimeo
sites.accommodation: Wild camping and Lochcarron Hotel Glen Uig Inn Castle cottage B+B B&B
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Lochcarron Hotel Glen Uig Inn Applecross Inn · Cafe: Waterside cafe
sites.hazards: Slippy rocks at low – mid tide. Otherwise, the site is suitable for training. No currents experienced on several dives between Low water and final dive one hour before HW
sites.notes:
Good little scenic dive off the remains around the Pier on Loch Toscaig.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards

Underwater: Keep the wall on your right and head South. There is a fair bit of life on the wall with literally hundreds of Spider Crabs. The wall peters out past the jetty and becomes a sandy, silty slope down to about 30 metres but scallops are a possibility. We didn't see much else in the silt other than a small Nudi.

Quite a trek but, if you are in the area, it's well worth the effort

sites.name: Torpedoes
sites.access: T ake the A82 up Loch Lomondside to Tarbet. Take the LH fork onto the A83 and pass through Arrochar driving around the head of Loch Long.
sites.parking: You can park 350m down the road in the Succoth car park. Google
sites.amenities: At the Esso petrol station at the head of the Loch.
sites.entryExit: On leaving the car park walk along the shore road and the trees will stop and when they start again just back from the waterfall on the other side of the road, step over the barrier and walk down to the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Village Inn · Cafe: Arrochar tea room
sites.hazards: Fast cars and Poor visibility.
sites.notes:
Shore dive in Loch Long around old WW2 Torpedos.

Suggested experience: Novice with good buoyancy.

Underwater: As the positions of the torpedoes have not been mapped, you will have to explore.

The Torpedo Range operated on the loch from 1912 to 1986, and in 1944, approximately 12,565 torpedoes were fired in the Loch, which works out at an average of 48 runs per day. Photo below of the Torpedo testing station by courtesy of arrocharheritage.com Other dive sites near here are the Torpedo station Twin piers and Conger alley

sites.name: Trevaunance Cove
sites.access: Trevaunance Cove is just under a mile from the centre of St Agnes. The village is within easy striking distance of Redruth and Truro and around 12 miles from Newquay. From all directions it is easiest to turn of at the main Chiverton Cross roundabout on the A30 and take the B3277 to St Agnes. From here head into the village and past the church and down the hill. At the roundabout here turn left, following the signs for the beach / Trevaunance Cove. Follow the narrow Quay Road down a wooded valley for a half a mile to the cove.
sites.parking: There are two car parks on the left as you approach the beach. (£1.50)
sites.amenities: Red phone box in the bottom car park.
sites.entryExit: Very easy walk down the ramp onto the rocky beach then onto sand into the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Driftwood Spars · Cafe: Breakers Beach Cafe
sites.notes:
Trevaunance Cove is a great shore dive on the north coast of Cornwall.

Suggested experience: Novice in good conditions.

Underwater: To the north/east it's mostly sand with occasional rocks and to the west, there is more to see as there are more rocks with sandy patches.

There are public toilets opposite the bottom car park. Trevaunance Cove can get busy in the summer months.

sites.name: Totaig
sites.access: As you descend down Glen Shiel, A87(on the way to Kyle of Lochalsh), take the left signposted Ratagan over the wee humpback bridge, take the next right to Ratagan, pass thru and continue driving past Letterfearn (single track road) Google
sites.parking: Park at the wide open area before the gate. You can take your gear down in the car and pick it up from the slipway after the dive but you must park back up at the open area. The area by the house is private property and must be kept clear. Google
sites.entryExit: The old (very slippy) ferry slipway. Enter and exit here.
sites.airFill: 5 Bells Diving at Loch Carron, Dive and Sea Hebrides on Skye, or carry your own
sites.accommodation: Kintail lodge hotel (Bunk Rooms and Bunk House), Ratagan Youth Hostel
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Kintail lodge hotel (nice pint of Ember, Strongbow, Stella. Meals quite expensive (but good)… (Scallops as a main £18.50!) · Cafe: There is a cafe further up from the Kintail Lodge on the way to Kyle of Lochalsh (but can’t rem its name)
sites.hazards: Current if you get the tide times wrong. No exit other than large rocks to climb out over if you don't return to entry/exit point. Very slippy on the slipway and there's also quite a drop where the surface wall ends.
sites.notes:
Shore dive on the point of Loch Alsh

Suggested experience: Ocean Diver (experienced), Sports Diver, Dive Leader, Master Diver etc

Underwater: Keep the cliff face on your right on the way out and on your left on the way back. If the current picks up, then keep close to the cliff to keep out of the flow.

sites.name: Trefin cove
sites.access: From Swansea Get on M4 from the B4489 thru Carmarthen then M4, A48 and A40 to Letterston then follow signs to Trefin.
sites.parking: There is parking for six cars at the top of the path
sites.entryExit: Walk down the stairs onto the path down to the stony beach (155m)
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Ship Inn in Trefin.
sites.hazards: Some surge and light currents possible. Also swells.
sites.notes:
It's a shallow shore dive (2-5m)

Suggested experience: Trainee upwards.

Underwater: ead North towards the rock islands and explore that area. There is a tunnel swim through the large island. Rock gullies interspersed with grey sand, large boulders.

Cove faces W. Around to the right (N) there is a rock island with a tunnel through the middle (you can walk through it at low tide). Bottom features include large rocks, gullies, kelp and other seaweeds, flat rock beds and gritty grey sand. Likely fauna includes various species of crab, jellyfish, wrasse, pollack, sand eels, grey mullet, anemones.

sites.name: Treaddur bay
sites.alternativeNames: Ravenspoint Gully. This dive site is not in use due to parking issues and the dive shop is currently closed.
sites.access: A55 over the Menai bridge onto Anglesey, At junction 2, take the A5153 exit to Penrhos/A5 Turn left at A5153 at the roundabout, take the 1st exit onto Kingsland Rd/B4545. Continue to follow B4545 and turn left into Ravenspoint rd. the bay is opposite Diving services and Google
sites.parking: Diving services dive centre car park £5 or park just around the bend up the hill about 200-300 yards free.
sites.entryExit: There is beach access in front of the dive centre down the steps shown below, and an easy walk into the sea.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Restaurants Pubs & Inns
sites.hazards: Speedboats and jet skis. An SMB is recommended for diving here
sites.notes:
Shore dive (high tide required)

Suggested experience: Novis

Underwater: Take a compass bearing to the HUGE house opposite and that takes you to/from a very nice reef about 80m out - about 15M at high tides and plenty of life.

Best done after a long spell of low winds as is exposed to the prevailing wind. In June you get plankton blooms like most dives around here. There are lots of gully's and cracks to explore and as it's not deep so you get good bottom times.

sites.name: Trefor pier
sites.alternativeNames: None still called Trefor pier after it's been demolished.
sites.access: From Caernarfon, drive along the A499, signposted Pwllheli, for about ten miles, shortly after driving through Clynnog Fawr the village of Trefor is signposted. Turn right and as you approach a small green (with a big glass bus stop) follow the signs on the right for Traeth (Beach), follow the narrow road between the houses to the beach at the bottom of the hill. It is a narrow road, so be prepared to move over for cars coming up the hill!
sites.parking: : Parking is not usually allowed on the breakwater unless it’s very quiet (the warden will sometimes let you get away with it) but you can unload the dive kit and park the car in the nearby car park, where there are also toilets and an emergency telephone. Google
sites.entryExit: : Kit up on the breakwater, by the picnic tables, unless you’re diving on low tide the steps here lead straight into the water (If you are diving on low tide, you’ll have to walk out along the bottom of the breakwater wall and put your fins on when you get to water!)
sites.airFill: You don’t really need nitrox fills for this! In fact, you hardly need air! You can get air fills from Anglesey Divers or Vivian Dive Centre in Llanberis. (Or if you’re really nice to me I’ve got a compressor………..)
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The nearest decent pub for me would be the Newborough Arms in Bontnewydd, on the way back to Caernarfon, good food at a decent price, but there are plenty all along the Pwllheli road. · Cafe: None near here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: : Keep a lookout for any fishermen - they will cast their rods directly out there now and you don't have the protection of the pier anymore.
sites.notes:
Trefor pier is a shore dive where the old wooden pier used to be.

Suggested experience: This is a lovely dive site for all divers, from complete novices to photographers and divers who enjoy wildlife.

Underwater: : It is a case of compass work now - nice and simply North out, south home. There are a few rotted pier legs on the seabed, with lots of life attached, although the majority have been cleared away. Some cobbles and pebbles - good for a little mooch. Swim back to the harbour wall and ascend or follow the wall back underwater - take care as usually kids crabbing!

Use an SMB if there are fishermen about.

sites.name: Triple reef
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the A82 turn left at Tarbet onto the A83, through Arrochar and over the rest and be thankful, turn left onto the A815, from this junction its 8.7 miles to the A886 then for 4 miles to the turnoff for the B8000 then for 9.8 miles to Thirteen-mile reef. ( Half a mile past Gortein point) Triple reef lies between Gortein point and Thirteen-mile reef at Triple reef the telephone pole has a No.34 on it.
sites.parking: Park in the lay-by next to the telephone pole; there is enough room for 3 cars. Google
sites.entryExit: Follow the path down onto the rocks be careful climbing down the rocks as it can be slippy. Entry and exit can be made difficult at low tide and if there is a bit of a swell.
sites.accommodation: The Creggans Inn Kanes Hote l
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Creggans Inn · Cafe: None
sites.hazards: Entry and exit climbing up and down the rocks
sites.notes:
Triple reef on Loch Fyne is a shore great dive on three reefs.

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: The first reef lies directly off of the shore and drops down to about 12m. The second reef lies slightly further north and runs from 15-25m. The third reef lies about 35m and is quite featureless. The best life is found on the top reef.

sites.name: Trinkie
sites.alternativeNames: The Trinkie is actually the outdoor swimming pool nearby.
sites.access: Leave Inverness on the A9 heading north over the Kessock bridge and stay on the A9 till you enter wick, then take the fourth street on the right Northcote St, at the end of the street turn left into Macrae st and turn 1st right into Kinnard st and head straight on to the end of the road by the sea. Google
sites.parking: Park at the end of the road.
sites.entryExit: Walk down the rocks just before the end of the road. Google
sites.airFill: Caithness diving club Make a donation to the upkeep of the compressor, They have nitrox as well Divenotheast
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Crown bar
sites.hazards: Swell,
sites.notes:
The Trinkie is a very scenic dive with walls, gullies and caves.

Suggested experience: Experienced to 25m in open water.

Underwater: Contact me

Visit a distillery

sites.name: Twin piers
sites.access: Take the A82 up Loch Lomond side to Tarbet. Take the LH fork onto the A83 and pass through Arrochar driving around the head of Loch Long. Two miles out of Arrochar is an old burnt out pier on your left....just past here is a small pier sitting on its own.
sites.parking: Park up on the grass at the fence off the main road. Google
sites.amenities: Phone at the entrance to Ardgarten campsite and the Esso petrol station
sites.entryExit: Step down at the concrete blocks and walk down to the water. There is now a metal ladder at the side of the blocks making it easier to get to the water's edge.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Village Inn · Cafe: Pit Stop Diner, Left after the Arrochar hotel heading north Three Villages Cafe , Arrochar Tea Room
sites.hazards: Fast cars and bikes on A83, Silt can cause poor visibility.
sites.notes:
Twin piers on Loch Long is a gentle shore dive around two offshore piers.

Suggested experience: Suitable for trainees upwards

Underwater: Head off to the left at 45 degrees to your entry. There is first the of the wreckage of an old truck that fell off the end of the pier (chassis and wheels with tyres still on) then, head in the same direction to 15m and then correct your direction to stay at that level, you'll come across a reef rock. Turn to your left and you'll come across a small fishing boat wreck about 20ft long IIRC, just a hull now. Up to you how you return, but if you head for 8-5m you'll know when to stop, at the piers.

If its busy here, you can dive along the road at Conger alley . the Torpedo station the Torpedos , or Finnart

sites.name: Wembury Beach
sites.alternativeNames: None This dive guide is a work in progress
sites.parking: There is a large pay-and-display car park 20m from the beach.
sites.entryExit: From the car park it's 100m walk down to the beach and a simple walk into the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Eddystone Inn The Odd Wheel · Cafe: The old Mill Cafe
sites.notes:
Wembury Beach is an easy shore dive with plenty of sea life.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards.

sites.name: Walpole tidal pool
sites.access: Head east on the M2 then A299 to Margate along Marine Drive to the Eastern Esplanade to the sea. Google
sites.parking: Park in the Hodges gap Promanade car park at the far end.
sites.amenities: In the Jet Ski world Cafe 200m from the pool.
sites.entryExit: Its a very easy walk down the ramp down the stairs into the water as in the picture below.
sites.airFill: Kent Scuba Because of the depth an eight or ten-litre cylinder is plenty.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Plenty in Margate · Cafe: Palm bay Cafe Jet Ski world Cafe
sites.hazards: Only real hazard would be falling off the sea wall onto the rocks below on the seas side on low water ...You can also hear the incoming tide crashing over the outer walls which is a reminder to exit the dive although I have slipped over the outer wall on the tide and dived the outer wall.
sites.notes:
Walpole tidal pool is a protected sea swimming pool which is also used for Snorkeling and diving. There is Lots of marine life ..Jewel anemones, Crab, Squat lobster, Lobster, Oyster and various transient fish that have to wait for the high tide so they can leave.

Suggested experience: Novice to U/W photographer

Underwater: Its a big pool so just explore, best parts are further out at crazy 3-4m depths

The pool is 22,000 square meters and is like diving in a massive rock pool. Do not remove the sea life as it would upset the ecology of the tidal pool. Take nothing only memories and leave only bubbles ...

sites.name: Weasel loch
sites.access: Upon entering Eyemouth, follow signs for the caravan park, heading up the hill to the west. Enter the caravan park and bear right, towards the reception building. Go in & say that you want to dive: you’ll be sold a parking permit (currently £3). Loop around the one-way system until you come to a gate. Google
sites.parking: Pass through the gate & park as far to the left as you can on the large grass area.
sites.entryExit: From the car park, head west past information board to wooden steps. It’s a long walk down, but the steps are in good order. The clamber across the rocks at the bottom is very treacherous at low tide.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Plenty in Eyemouth · Cafe: Eyemouth
sites.hazards: At low tide, Weasel Loch is very difficult to access. The current along the wall can be quite noticeable: be prepared to head east if required rather than fighting it. Some fishing line. Diving boats.
sites.notes:
Shore dive with amazing gullies and rock formations.

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: Weasel Loch is about 8m deep with a sandy bottom: it’s worth exploring at the start and/or end of the dive. Head north and around the headland to the east. A noticeable current will carry you along a very scenic wall which develops into impressive overhangs known as the Grotto. Head north from there for 40m to find Conger Reef (depth 15m). After exploring it, head south to return to the wall. Diver’s Hole is further east (basically a sandy-bottomed depression). At high tide, Leeds Bay can be entered directly, bypassing the headland (Hairy Ness). If air is low or the current too strong, the dive can be exited at Leeds Bay. There are rough steps from the bay back to the car park.

The caravan park gate is locked at 5 pm. If you’re late, you’ll have to rely upon some kind soul with an access card to let you out!

sites.name: West bay
sites.access: From Glasgow 1hr 38mins Ferry timetable and prices Head west on the M8 onto the A8 to through Greenock and Gourock on the A770 to McInroy's point where you get the ferry to Hunter's Quay. From Hunter's quay head south 2.1 miles to West bay
sites.parking: There is free parking at Coal Pier Car Park, around 3-4 min walk, so you could dump your kit at the dive site entry point then go and park at Coal Pier, The car park at the Cafe is restricted to one hour.
sites.entryExit: There are eight steps at the side of the pier leading down onto the ramp that leads to the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Crown , Argyll Hotel · Cafe: Rock Cafe
sites.hazards: Occasional small boat activity in the summer so A flags/good shore cover is advised.
sites.notes:
West bay is an easy shore dive in Dunoon

Suggested experience: Novice and upwards

Underwater: info to follow.

sites.name: West Portholland
sites.access: Drive through the village of Veryan Google
sites.parking: Just up from the beach
sites.entryExit: Enter the water on the right-hand side of the bay (facing the water) and keep to the right.
sites.airFill: Atlantic scuba or Cornish diving in Falmouth or Seaways diving in Penryn.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: In the summer there is a small cafe providing refreshments and home-made cakes.
sites.hazards: No major hazards here.
sites.notes:
Shallow shore dive

Suggested experience: Trainee upwards.

Underwater: Follow the reefs and small gullies as far as your gas allows and retrace your route back into the bay. There are plenty of things to see here.

sites.name: Whale rock
sites.access: From Glasgow / Edinburgh: Approx 3 hours drive. Follow local directions below to Crianlarich. From Edinburgh head North (M9/A84/A85) via Stirling and Callander to Crianlarich. From Glasgow head for Loch Lomond along A82 (turning right at Tarbet) to Crianlarich.From Crianlarich, follow A82 through Glencoe and Ballachulish following signs for Onich / Fort William onto the A830 then left at Lochailort onto the A861 south to Whale rock ( see google map below)
sites.parking: At the big rock on the roadside.
sites.entryExit: Enter the water at the beach with whale rock on the left.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Glenuig Inn · Cafe: None close to here.
sites.hazards: No major hazards
sites.notes:
Whale rock is a very shallow shore dive good for snorkelling as well.

Suggested experience: Novice upwards

Underwater: Keep whale rock on your right shoulder and circumnavigate the rock. Look in all the cracks and gully's as you will have plenty time at this shallow depth.

This is a shallow site and gives you a long bottom time which is great for training and U/W Photography.

sites.name: Widewater
sites.access: From Brighton head west along the coast on the A259 over the river Adur At the first roundabout turn first left onto the Saltings then right onto King's cress till you hit the sea and turn right for 165m and the car park is on the right.
sites.parking: There is a Pay and display car park close to the shore that can take 40+ cars as in the picture below, As you go into the car park turn left, then drive down to the second set of stairs up to the beach and park just before the yellow and black speed bump.
sites.entryExit: The entry / Exit is a simple walk up the stairs to the Cycle path. Cross the Cycle path and walk between the beach huts down the stony beach into the water. If there is a big swell best not to take a camera as you can get knocked about when leaving the water.
sites.airFill: Newhaven scuba Ocean View Diving Services
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: There is a cafe in the car park.
sites.hazards: Surge and Swell with occasional boat traffic so an SMB is recommended
sites.notes:
Widewater is gentle reef dive 80m offshore.

Suggested experience: Sport diver.

Underwater: Head straight out 80m from the shore to the reef which runs parallel to the shore and simply explore the reef. Have a look at the video below.

There is a public toilet in the car park. There is also a shower outside the toilets so you can wash your kit after the dive.

sites.name: Wildersmouth Beach
sites.access: From the east head for Taunton then Barnstaple to Ilfracombe.then follow signs for the Landmark Theatre.
sites.parking: There is a pay and display carpark at the walkway down to the beach or at the theatre 50m from the beach.
sites.entryExit: There is a walkway down to the beach and a simple walk into the water.
sites.accommodation: There are plenty of B+B here
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Ship & Pilot George & Dragon · Cafe: None close to here.
sites.hazards: There are no major hazards here and little or no boats.
sites.notes:
Wildersmouth Beach is an easy shore dive very close to the town in Ilfracombe in a north-west facing cove.

Suggested experience: Novice.

Underwater: Its a small cove so just explore the mainly a white sand bottom with interesting grey rock formations.

This does not seem to be a popular dive site so you will probably have the cove to yourself.

sites.name: Wishing stone
sites.parking: Picture below
sites.entryExit: Off the rocks below the car park
sites.accommodation: The best place to stay when you are diving here is the highlandbasecamp half way up the sound of Mull. They have air, nitrox, trimix and accommodation also Self-catering Morvern Dive Lodge
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Lochaline social club · Cafe: On the pier the at Lochaline ferry
sites.hazards: Currents
sites.notes:
Shore dive

Suggested experience: Novice upwards

Underwater: Swim out over the huge kelp stipes which have snakelocks anemones and a few nudibranch on them and on down a gently sloping seabed of sand and mud covered rocks with dozens of tube anemones on them. Head out to your chosen depth and follow the seabed at that depth coming back slowly ascending to the 6m depth before exiting in the same place you entered.

There are also a few eyelash worms and one or two short peacock worms sticking straight out on the seabed. There are the usual hermits and harbour crabs and also some langoustine and the odd edible crab. Tiny decorator crabs wave their claws at you, and I also came across a slender and a phosphorescent sea pen. A pleasant dive with quite a lot of small life, just what you would expect with this sort of habitat.

sites.name: Blue Lagoon
sites.location: 82 Miles / 1Hr 50 Min Google Its just of the A542 (Horseshoe pass) at the Ponderosa cafe.
sites.parking: Park opposite the cafe on the A542
sites.entryExit: : A steep scramble down a muddy slate slope
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Britannia Inn · Cafe: Ponderosa Cafe
sites.hazards: A remote location with no immediate facilities. The entry is a challenge in itself.
sites.notes:
Blue Lagoon is an Inland quarry dive and work out in one.

Suggested experience: Experienced and fit due to the long walk in and remoteness of the site.

Underwater: Kit up on the larger rocks by the water’s edge, enter the water and head off to the vertical wall on the right-hand side. Quite quickly head off to your left to the deepest part of the lake down to 12m. Quickly the water becomes shallower and you will come across a pile of abandoned cars and vans. After a look at the vehicles, follow the side of the pool to the left where there are large slate slabs, which are home to more sticklebacks. The Lagoon isn't too big so you will soon complete a loop of the lake.

Finding the Ponderosa cafe is the easy part of finding this dive site. Opposite the Cafe are a couple of tracks heading off towards the quarry workings. Follow the track which heads uphill and just before your car gets stuck stop off of the track on the grass. In front of you, there is a footpath which heads between two mounds of slate. Head up the gap and keep on walking away from where you parked. At the top of the slope, there is a quarry road follow this for 500m. On the left, you will see signs which warn of deep water, past this there will be a signpost with no sign, on your left. Find a small narrow gully which should lead to the quarry. It might be an advantage to do this first then go back and collect your dive kit when you know exactly where to go. Good advice for diving here is to use a 7L or 10L cylinder and as little kit as possible.

sites.name: Zarina
sites.access: From the Portaferry pier head north for 1.2 miles on the Lough shore road.
sites.parking: Park at the side of the road as in the picture below.
sites.entryExit: Simple entry/exit over a small seawall protected by rocks and onto a small stone beach as in the picture below.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Portaferry · Cafe: None close to here so take everything you need.

sites.notes:
Shore wreck dive in Ballyhenry Bay, Strangford Lough.

Suggested experience: Novice with a guide

Underwater: From the shore fin out to the buoy and drop onto the wreck.

sites.name: Wishing well
sites.access: From the M8 heading west take the A737 to Saltcoats turn of onto the A760 towards Lochwinnoch and carry on to Largs. In Largs head to the ferry to Cumbrae Leaving the ferry turn left and travel 1.5 miles arrive at the Wishing well.
sites.entryExit: Entry in at the left-hand side facing the sea and there is a cleared pathway into the rocks.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: The Royal George In Millport
sites.notes:
The wishing well is a good shore dive on the Isle of Cumbrae great for small groups of divers.

Underwater: You can go right which is mainly sand and rubble and depths of anywhere up to 30mtrs. If diving to the left work your way down to about 8 meters and then fin over 500 yards, at a depth of around 8-10 meters there are some nice rocks formations holding crab, squat lobster, wrasses, lobster and around that rocky area and down to about 12 meters the Rocks continue. Passed 12 meters it more sandy/silt and the chance of squat lobsters and gurnard.

You can also dive Clashfarland point near here.

sites.name: Blue pool
sites.access: M40 Southam CV47 2QX Head north-east on Gaydon Rd/B4451 (2.9 mi), turn right onto Ropeway (299 ft), turn right onto Blue Pool Vale, destination will be on the right
sites.parking: Access gate off Ladbroke Rd, Bishops Itchington, CV47 2RW. Access to the pool is via a 5-minute walk from where the cars are parked to the poolside.
sites.airFill: Andy @ Diving Cylinder Regulator Services, 148 Coventry Rd, London, Warwick CV34 5HL, 07977 410748
sites.nearbyFood: Cafe: The Blue Pool Nature Reserve & Tearoom
sites.hazards: Some old quarry debris
sites.notes:
Lake, you need permission from Warwickshire Wildlife Trust. Blue Pool is on the site of the former Harbury Cement Works that is made up of several Blue Lias limestone quarries. The rock is a sequence of limestones and shales laid down in the Jurassic period and rich in fossils. In 1927 and 1928 the remains of an Ichthyosaur and Plesiosaur were discovered in the quarries and are now exhibited in the Natural History Museum

Suggested experience: Sports Diver, or above

Underwater: A clockwise swim followed by a trip to the centre will usually show all the sights.

No facilities on site. Toilets at the Butchers Arms pub, and food from Co-op on Chapel Street close to the site. Divers should bring own lunch, water, flask of tea/coffee, and arrive in their undersuits to avoid changing in public as a courtesy to local residents.

sites.name: Beech Hill
sites.access: Located on the east shore of Windermere it's about two miles south of Bowness on the A592.
sites.parking: Travelling from the north on the A592, pass the Beech Hill Hotel and turn right into the pay and display car park. Google
sites.amenities: There are no public phones in this area.
sites.entryExit: Access to the dive site is via 111 steep steps down to the beach.
sites.airFill: Capernwray Blackpool Area Divers Fins also contact KALSAC, Kendal & Lakes BSAC
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: There are no pubs in this area. · Cafe: There are no cafes in this area.
sites.hazards: Silt depth and darkness.
sites.notes:
: Three w recks in one dive, fresh water, Windermere lake.

Suggested experience: Novice with good buoyancy.

Underwater: There are three small wrecks at this site, enter the water and three meters from the shore there is a drop-off, travel north past the hotel jetties on your right (see pic above) a work boat at 17m looking out for the old jetties that had been ditched in the lake. Or head south from the beach and there is the Fair Dinkum at 12m about 8 minutes swim also past the Fair dinkum is a small power boat a further 50m south.

Good Buoyancy and finning technique needed here so you don't kick up the silt and destroy the already low visibility. You can also dive the Vospa on the other side of the lake. There are public toilets by the car park.

sites.access: : Boddam village is 29 miles (47 km) north of Aberdeen and 3 miles (4.8 km) south of Peterhead. There is an unfinished road just south of the Stirlinghill Quarry signpost on the A90 South of Peterhead, head up this road ........ Google

Boddam quarry is a site often used for training and when you get blown out offshore.

Suggested experience: Trainee to the experienced diver

Underwater: Just explore not too big so you won't get lost.

In summer it can become very green with algae reducing the viz to 3-5m. There are rainbow trout, perch, stickleback and a pike.

sites.name: Calvert
sites.access: Steeple Claydon, Buckingham, MK18 2GJ
sites.parking: Small car park opposite Greatmoor Sailing Club.
sites.entryExit: There is a flat surfaced path leading to the shore and pier
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: : None · Cafe: : None
sites.notes:
Two large lakes that was once a brickworks. The 1900 site was chosen because of its proximity to the railway junction where the Great Central crossed the LNWR from Oxford to Cambridge. The brickworks became part of the London Brick Company empire in the late 1920's. The material extracted for brick making was Oxford Clay (aka Flettons), a common material in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire. A very common fossil that can be seen in large numbers at the site is 'Gryphea Arcuata' or Devils ToeNail.

Suggested experience: Ocean diver or above

Underwater: s: Contact me

There is access to toilets, within a spacious club house, and changing rooms. The site also has a number of paths that allow you to explore the woodland and glades that surround the lake and perhaps spot some of the wildlife that is sharing the site.

sites.name: Cawfields quarry
sites.access: From Carlisle east on the A689 onto the A69 its 24miles 36 mins and from Newcastle West on the A69 its 38 miles 1 hr.

Freshwater quarry where you can see perch and stickleback.

Suggested experience: Novice with good buoyancy control.

Underwater: Follow the edge of the quarry and back or use a compass course.

There is a public toilet in the car park and remember you need permission from the parks authority every time you dive here. This quarry has been used for ice diving courses when it gets cold enough. Contact facilities@nnpa.org.uk For a permit to dive

sites.name: Crummock water
sites.access: Google
sites.parking: The parking is about 100m from the water entry point which is, left out of the car park up the road (inclined) to the end of the drystone wall. At the wall take the steps down to the waters edge some 4m below road level. At the bottom of the steps, there is a narrow slate shingle beach edged with a grass bank, where you can kit up from. Google
sites.entryExit: Entry into the water is shallow from the shingle, which quickly turns to large pebble rocks. These can be quite slippery but manageable. You have to walk some 5m out to get to water about 4ft deep. Then it drops off quite steeply to approx 5m deep. Note the bed from here is silt and easily disturbed so good buoyancy is a must. This picture was taken in the winter with a higher water level.
sites.airFill: No shops near here. Air from Clubs
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: In Lorton. or at Buttermere village. · Cafe: None near here so take everything you need (hot flask of soup)
sites.hazards: Cold and visibility also Lake Altitude 99 metres Care should be taken regarding routes leading away from Crummock water.
sites.notes:
Crummock water is a freshwater wall dive but usually very dark.

Suggested experience: Knowledge of altitude diving.

Underwater: Keep the bank to your left follow the contour of the lake for a couple of minutes and you drop over a rock face to a depth of about 11m. Continue to keep the bank on your left (and you'll swim in an arch around a small bay) approx 5 mins. You can see small trout, eels, perch and minnows in the shallow water.

Permission should be obtained from the National Park Authority warden for this lake. Warden is Mark Astley. (01900) 85267 Lake Altitude at 375 feet (99 metres). Care should be taken regarding routes leading away from this dive site.

sites.name: Dorothea
sites.access: Take the A487 to Porthmadog. About 2 miles out of Caernarfon turn left at a roundabout and follow the road into Penygoes. Turn left onto the B4418 and follow the road into Nantle, shortly before Nantle you will see a large lake on your right, just past the lake on the left is a row of houses, turn left along these and follow the track to the quarry. On the way along the track, you will pass the posts of the former gate. Be warned that the track up to the quarry is potholed and will test the suspension of your vehicle.
sites.parking: There is a car park at the top of the site but the ramp to the entry slab is very steep, a serious consideration if you're carrying a lot of kit, and the site can get quite crowded at weekends.
sites.entryExit: When you enter the water you can stand up, then descend down a slope to a small 3m shelf, descend down another shelf to 6m, another slope to 9m
sites.airFill: Air fills can be obtained from Vivian dive centre in Llanberis, but there are no facilities for nitrox or trimix, so if you're here for a weekend you'll need to bring your own.
sites.mobileSignal: mobile phone reception can be variable.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here.
sites.hazards: Temperature and depth.
sites.notes:
Dorothea is a famous freshwater quarry dive.

Suggested experience: Dive to your experiance this can be a dangerous dive.

Underwater: If you swim to the right following the 9m shelf round you come to a wider area where the crane is. You can drop off here and descend to a shelf at 22m where you have a couple of options. From here you can either swim to the left where this shelf widens out, and head towards the first set of pinnacles which have a tunnel through them and some slate huts around their base and either follow the slope down to 40m and the gnome garden, or swim up the slope and back to the exit platform (It's worth noting here that there are two steel cables running up the side of the pinnacle which you can use to ascend to the surface if you don't want to swim back up the slopes) There is also a small sump to the left of the pinnacles which bottoms out at about 35m. If you turn right at the 22m shelf you can drop first to a 40m ledge or continue down into one of the two bottom sumps (about 85m) If you follow the quarry wall around in this direction you can do deeper dives around the bigger pinnacles or take a look at the car stack (People have been dumping cars in here from the same point for years, so the car stack starts at about 85m with the latest additions on top at a depth of about 40m. There are two gnome gardens in about 40m, the most dived of the two has a buoyed rope tied off to it, and from this shelf you can drop over the edge to a long tunnel at 56m, or drop even further into the bottom where there is another tunnel at 90m and beyond that the sump, with a hut and a small blast tunnel, which is closed at the far end. This is the deepest point. Summer temperatures in the shallows can reach 16 degrees, as you descend to 25m it drops to about 9 in the summer and seven in the winter, as you drop to 40m it's a uniform 7 and drop to the bottom it's about 4 degrees. Diving to the bottom is better done in summer when you can at least warm up in the shallows on deco.

Dorothea's reputation as a dangerous quarry is undeserved. You have to swim out quite a way before you come to any drop-offs until you get to 40m, the depth progressions are down slopes, so the bottom is always visible. Obviously, because of it's extreme depths, a diver who goes looking for trouble is going to find it. The vis is usually very clear, although there is sometimes a seasonal algae bloom which can drop the vis, certainly in the shallows, dramatically, to as little as 2 or 3m, this is usually short-lived. It is, however usually dark, except in the shallows on very sunny days, so divers need a torch.

sites.name: Devils bridge
sites.access: From junction 34 of the M6 head towards Kirkby Lonsdale on the A683. When the A683 meats the A65 turn left and Devils Bridge should be visible on your left. Alternatively, come off the motorway at junction 35 and head for Over Kellet and take the B6254 to Kirkby Lonsdale.
sites.parking: : Google Google
sites.entryExit: Get kitted up and then walk through a narrow gate and down on to a small beach upstream of the bridge.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Snooty fox tavern The Sun Inn
sites.hazards: Rocks, Cold, Tree stumps, Branches and it may look calm and easy on the surface but it can turn into a drift dive which can be very tiring fighting to get back to where you entered.
sites.notes:
River dive. Utube

Suggested experience: Sport Diver.

Underwater: The current is at its strongest here so jump in and drift down under the first bridge. After the bridge, the current slackens and you can spend time looking at the fish and in the cracks between rocks for eels. The River shallows rapidly just before the road bridge and after the bridge, there are two areas to exit one above the bridge and one between the bridges.

Best time to dive here is when there has been no rain for a while as it reduces the viz. C heck the forecast for the dive day it's a river so it can rise while you are in the water. Also, there are public toilets on the bridge.

sites.name: Falls of Falloch
sites.access: From Glasgow on the M8 head over the Erskine Bridge and through Dumbarton on the A82 past the top of Loch Lomond. Parking for the Falls can be found 2miles past the Drover’s Inn
sites.parking: There is a small, but busy car park throughout the day due to the steady stream of tourists. As such, if you’re going to dive here go very early. From Glasgow: 50 miles, 1hr 5mins
sites.entryExit: The pool is most easily entered where the stream exits the pool. This requires carrying kit down the steep path to the right of the falls viewpoint
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Drovers Inn · Cafe: None
sites.hazards: Danger of the river going into spate, current of the river, slips and trips on entry and exit
sites.notes:
Steep-sided, freshwater river pool dive at the top of Loch Lomond.

Suggested experience: Sport / AOW

Underwater: It’s a small pool and is best explored around the edges where there are overhangs and small caverns. There is little life including small trout and Anguilla Anguilla, Scotland’s critically endangered river eel.

sites.name: Fron quarry
sites.access: Signposted Fron and Rhostryfan Google The last part is a track and you will need a good ground clearance or a 4x4 to get up it. Don't even think of coming here in a normal car.
sites.parking: Near the end of the track is a hill and park just over the hill.
sites.entryExit: You have to scramble down a 100m long slippy rocky path, a rope is a good idea for this as it is very steep.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None near here. · Cafe: None near here so take everything you need (hot flask of soup)
sites.hazards: Access, Cold, Depth, Altitude, Silt.
sites.notes:
Fron quarry is a quarry dive that is not easy to get to so not dived as often as other quarries

Suggested experience: Qualified to 40m in cold water.

Underwater: Its a small quarry so just explore and surface fin back to the entry point when you have finished your dive. Its a better dive in the winter when the viz is better and the path is not wet.

There are old cars and debris and a blue Buoy at the hut 22m. The best vis normally in the Winter / early Spring. This quarry is at an altitude of 320m so this dive should be treated as an altitude dive.

sites.name: Glynneath
sites.access: From the A465 round-a-bout (McDonald SA11 5NZ), head west towards B4242 for 0.1 mi, turn left onto B4242 after 0.2 mi, turn left after the layby onto a rough road that eventually takes you over a small humpback bridge and under the A465, Keep following until you arrive at a locked gate
sites.parking: Parking is right up against the water.
sites.entryExit: Easy entry/exit from the grass simply walk into the water.
sites.nearbyFood: Cafe: None
sites.notes:
Lake, you need permission from owners and a ‘code’ for the locked gate: 07970722744 There are two lakes at the site, one for powerboating and one for quieter activities (such as diving!). The smaller lake isn’t huge but ok size for a number of divers. Not much depth but good for practice. Not a pleasure dive, there needs to be a purpose. The lakes were created as they were dug out for rock to build the heads of the valleys road and have naturally filled up over time, due to that there’s no fish life although plenty of plants. Adding some fish would be quite nice and would draw in some additional money from fishermen, although there were some kids fishing the bigger lake so I guess that there’s probably some in there.

Suggested experience: Ocean Diver, or above

Underwater: There are a few small boats, a training platform, and some minor objects to explore. Most are near the entry/exit

The water is often very clear with good visibility, although if you knocked the bottom lots of suspended matter would be sent upwards and take a while to settle. No facilities on site. Divers should bring their own lunch, water, a flask of tea/coffee.

Hodge close is a famous quarry and cave dive.

sites.name: Linn of dee
sites.location: N56.988119 W-3.546275 Grid ref NO0689 Google map
sites.access: : The Linn of Dee is a few miles from Braemar, about halfway to Perth on the A93
sites.parking: Leave the dive kit at the bridge with a minder and park In the tourist car park, it's a pay and display....£2. But parking is free if you have a National Trust for Scotland badge. There is also a toilet in the car park.
sites.entryExit: Carry your dive kit down the path at the side of the bridge and down the steep grassy bank which brings you to shelving rocks along the side of the river where you do a stride entry.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: : None close to here take everything you need and don't leave any litter.
sites.hazards: Fast-flowing water that can make diving here very dangerous and cold.
sites.notes:
River dive , Contact the estate office on 013397 31669 before travelling to dive here. Only dive here on a dry day that follows 3 - 4 dry days

Suggested experience: Sport Diver

Underwater: From the entry point swim upstream to the top pool where the waterfall is, called the "washing machine". There are a few large round holes that spin the water. Then work your way downstream until the water is to shallow. The rocks have great patterns and have mica embedded in them and on sunny days they sparkle.

Sometimes there is a dark red tint to the water which is caused by the peat and also means that conditions will be similar to that of a night dive. You can see eels and trout here and if you are lucky the occasional salmon. If you are taking pictures, dive first without the camera and check the conditions first. Don't take anything that is easily broken as you get knocked about in the bowls. A 10L, 232 Bar cylinder is all that is required to dive here.

sites.name: Orchy pools
sites.access: Leaving Glasgow on the A82 turn left at Crianlarich staying on the A82. Staying on the A82 going through Tyndrum to the Bridge of Orchy. Turn left before the bridge of Orchy hotel down the B8074, signposted Glen Orchy. Google
sites.parking: Just beside the waterfall is ample parking for 2-3 cars Google map
sites.entryExit: Short walk for parked cars down schist slabs into the water. Slippery when wet.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Bridge of Orchy hotel · Cafe: Tyndrum Bridge of Orchy hotel
sites.hazards: It is best done at low water when it has not been raining for a week or so to allow you to climb through the pools. In high currents, there is the possibility to get pinned or trapped in undercuts by the water pressure
sites.notes:
Orchy pools is a good river dive in good conditions.

Underwater: Follow the stream up through four swirl pools and through two junctions or necks where you have to drag/climb against the current into the next pool. Keep moving upstream until you get to the waterfall. You will be unable to get beyond this.

You can also dive down the river at River Orchy Don't forget to use the comments at the bottom of the page

Inland site / watersports center,

sites.access: : Leaving Glasgow on the A82 turn left at Crianlariach staying on the A82. Staying on the A82 going through Tyndrum to the Bridge of Orchy. Turn left before the bridge of Orchy hotel down the B8074, signposted Glen Orchy. Continue down the road for 3-4miles till you come to a metal bridge over the river. (see picture below)
sites.parking: : Parking is close to the edge of the road (see pic above)

sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Bridge of Orchy hotel · Cafe: There is nothing near here so take everything you need.
sites.hazards: : Steep entry, The river can be fast flowing after a lot of rain.
sites.notes:
The River Orchy is a very good river dive and I could happily spend an hour looking around here.

Suggested experience: Sport diver

Underwater: Its a small area so just look about. there is a cave near the bridge which is safe to enter and there is room for two divers. Look at the rock formations as they are amazing, perfectly round holes that look like they have been drilled but it's a round stone which has rolled around and worn the hole. There are eels in the rocks at the bottom of the river, and trout and salmon at certain times of the year. Because there is no silt here the viz stays at an amazing 10-15m even with 6 divers in for an hour.

: A different sort of dive. If the river gauge reads over 2 its worth cancelling the dive. You can also dive the Orchy pools upriver.

sites.name: River Tay Bridges
sites.parking: You can park at the fitness centre (Parking at point 1) or down by the wee island (Parking at point 2)
sites.airFill: Dive Bunker Burntisland. Splash Sports Dundee
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: Fair maid · Cafe: Quite a few in Perth
sites.hazards: Strong current at times, I've found you tend to be better diving at low tide since it isolates a lot of the pools and makes it shallower which makes it easier to get onto land if you get in trouble. Also be aware parts of the river can shift and you get debris scattered about the bottom in places. It is probably a good idea to have someone on the shore to keep an eye out if you are in SCUBA kit. Many trees get washed down the river and get caught up in the flora on the banks and on submerged trees and large rocks on the bottom.
sites.notes:
River Tay Bridges in Perth is a River, drift dive between the Smeaton's Bridge and the Queens Bridge.

Suggested experience: Experienced novice for SCUBA, Any experience for snorkelling.

Underwater: at point 2 Heading downstream to a large pool which is fairly isolated and reaches a depth of about 4 meters. There tends to be no current in here (provided the water is below the level of the causeway) and I suspect it would make a good little training area. Alternatively, you can go upstream hugging the east bank to go upstream which will actually cause you to be pushed up the river by a gentle current. You can then go out into the middle of the river and drift back down to your starting point.

This is a great snorkelling site. I have seen, trout, salmon, flatfish, lamprey, eels and all sorts of other things in here. You also can find some interesting things that people have thrown into the river!

sites.name: Waterswallows quarry
sites.parking: Follow A6 East from Buxton. Just before leaving Buxton turn right onto Waterswallows Road. Lomas Distribution has a car park on the right opposite their site. Turn onto this. It used to be possible to drive right to the water's edge but they have now put boulders in place to stop you. It would be possible to push them to one side but when I was there security guard had seen us on CCTV and had turned up within 2 minutes of our arrival. We said we were there to dive and he said he'd turn a blind eye so we just parked where we were. The water is a relatively easy 400-yard walk. It may be worth asking for permission beforehand as not all the security may be so obliging.
sites.entryExit: 400 Yards from the car park. Follow gravel road parallel to the car park and then around to the right.The car park at the side has been partially blocked by a smaller mound but is still easily passable (I saw a Mini drive this route with ease today).This route is up and over the grassed area and then there are no blockades after this, this is now the default main entry to this site I feel.
sites.nearbyFood: Pub: None close to here. · Cafe: None close to here.
sites.hazards: Altitude. The site itself is at 320m so would be classed as an altitude dive. For reference I believe Hodge Close is only 190m From a safety point of view the site is remote, water access is restricted. The water temp even in the summer is about 4-6 degrees (colder than Hodge or Dotty).
sites.notes:
Waterswallows quarry is a typical freshwater quarry.

Suggested experience: Ocean Diver upwards

Underwater: This is a large quarry so not really sure of the best route. Probably best to look at the map and use that as a rough guide.

Planning permission has been granted for a dive site to be set up on this site but not followed through. It should be made clear that this is an altitude dive, it's over 300m above sea level and at the moment there is no access available. The site is of geological importance and this is the reason the site was never allowed to run as a dive site. The basalt rock cliffs are like the Devil's Causeway in Ireland!

sites.name: Minard Isles
sites.alternativeNames: Seal Island, Eilean Fraoch, Fraoch Eilean-E Side
sites.notes:
Minard Isles, also known as Seal Island or Eilean Fraoch, offers a scenic wall diving experience with abundant marine life including seals, sea birds, anemones, butterfish, pipefish, and flatfish. The dive site features excellent walls with plumose and dahlia anemones, particularly on the outside of the buttress and under slight overhangs. Tidal currents create opportunities for drifting over broken rocks and walls, with visibility possibly reduced due to the east-facing wall. Divers can enter at the southern tip and explore rock chutes leading to depths of 45m+ or even 70m for more experienced divers. Overall, this boat-accessible site provides a special opportunity to interact with playful seals and enjoy the diverse underwater ecosystem.

Often referred to as Seal Island, Eilean Fraoch or the Minard Isle is an interesting scenic wall dive site. There is an abundance of marine life, including sea birds, seals, anenomes and a variety of fish including butterfish, pipefish and flatfish to be seen here. There are some excellent walls on this dive with a good covering of plumose and dahlia anemones. 
 
The best life is found on the outside of the buttress making up the wall and under the slight overhangs half way up. As you would expect there are tidal currents around the island, allowing you to drift over broken rocks and past walls. These tidal currents get faster as you reach the surface. The wall is east facing so visibility can be reduced and it does get dark very quickly at depth.
 
Entering at the southern tip, divers can drop down one of the rock chutes to their desired depth. The wall starts at 10m and allows you to dive to 45m+ if you so desire. There is a drop down to 70m close by for those more adventurous and suitable kitted out and qualified. Heading up you will find shallow sand and shell beds from 15m, where you can find scallops. 
 
Only accessible by boat this is a special scenic dive site where the seals will often come and play amongst the bubbles, and sometimes tug on your fins - yellow fins seem popular at the moment!

Tides: This site can be dived at any state of the tide.

sites.notes: History: 10,468 ton tanker built in 1935 by Friedrich Krupp Germaniawerft in Kiel. Owned by Oriental Tankers, Hong Kong. Measured 149m x20.8m x 11.3m and had 912 n.h.p. oil engines and was capable of 12 knots. Torpedoed by a German submarine-93 on 29th January 1941. Four of the 47 crew on board died during the attack. The tanker broke in two and both parts remained afloat. The fore part was sunk by gunfire on February 6th at 56 00N, 15 23W. Attempts to tow the after part failed and it sank off the Scottish coast sometime after 13th February at 58 15N, 07 01W.

sites.name: Eilean C
sites.notes:
A dive site at the entrance to Loch Eriboll on the north coast of Scotland, featuring limestone at 4m, a cave at 25m, and a colourful wall.

Started with a block of limestone at 4m covered in kelp with tiny nudibrancs on the fronds. Vis was about 12m. Descended to a cave at 25m with large boulders at the entrance. Finished with a wall covered in deadmens fingers, anemones, sponges and hydroids.

Biodiversity: Tiny nudibranchs on kelp fronds, shoals of juvenile Pollack, sea hares, velvet swimmers, dahlia anemones, sponges and sea squirts.

sites.name: SS George A. Savage
sites.notes:
SS George A. Savage is a steamship wreck located 22 km SSE from Borrow Head at a depth of 42 metres. The wreck is in a collapsed state with the boiler area and starboard hull plates rising to about 3 to 4 metres above the seabed. The bow, which was reported as upright in 2002, has now collapsed to the port side. The wreckage includes various identifiable features such as the large boiler, engine, debris field, propeller, rudder, anchor winch, and more. Despite being dived in 1997, the wreck is not frequently visited, offering the opportunity for further exploration and potential confirmation of its identity.

This steamship wreck, presumed to be the George A. Savage lies 22 km SSE from Borrow Head.  It lies at a depth of 42 metres (LW) on a stony seabed with the bow orientated to 165 degrees.  The vessel is in a collapsed state with the boiler area and starboard hull plates rising to about 3 to 4 metres above the seabed.  The bow which in 2002 was reported as being upright has now collapsed to the port side.

Although first dived by Isle of Man divers in 1997, it is obvious that the wreck is not often visited.  Much is still to be found and the identity of the wreck confirmed. The name letters may still be on the fallen bow plates, and a makers plate is visible on the photograph near to the portholes and this may be found. The only negative factor about identifying the vessel is that the remains of the forecastle seem very short compared to the forecastle shown in the photograph.

Starting at the large boiler (1) which is surrounded by a jumble of bent and twisted pipes and girders one can begin to get ones bearings.  The two cylinder compound engine (2) lies on its port side behind the boiler and spreading out from this is a tangled debris field partly buried in built up shale.  Square shaped window frames, plates with port holes attached and pieces of copper sheathing (3) lie in this area which is presumably what remains of the bridge and superstructure.  This debris extends towards the stern of the wreck which is badly broken up with the propeller (4) and large rudder lying in a heap on the seabed.  It would suggest that the vessel was torpedoed or mined on the port side abaft the bridge.

Moving forward of the boiler it is obvious that you are in the hold area (5).  The port side plates have collapsed outwards and presumably lie beneath the built up sand bank which covers this area. Alternatively this may be where the torpedo struck, destroying the port side in the hold area. The starboard hull side is more intact, though it is now a skeletal structure, covered in plumose anemones, with most of the hull plates rotted and fallen to the seabed 3 metres below. It is interesting to note that the ribs here are more closely spaced together than usual and are double ribs. This certainly indicates a vessel built to a high strength specification and may show that it was built with a sealed internal hold. The fact that the vessel was transporting pitch may have necessitated a tank like hold but I would have thought that pitch in that era would have been transported in barrels.

Following the line of ribs forward you come to the bow section (6) which is now collapsed over to port lying flattened to the seabed. Like the rest of the wreck this area is completely covered in plumose anemones. At the starboard side it is possible to peer into the bow compartment and surprisingly it contains a strong steel plate which seems to divide the compartment in two along the line of the keel.

Near to the bow the port side plates lie on the seabed and anchor hawse hole is clearly visible.

Returning to the stern the anchor winch (7) lies displaced off to port among a collection of debris and just beyond it is the main cargo winch along with its strengthened base plate. Nearby can be seen pieces of copper sheathing, which may have covered the binnacle, mooring cleats, a section of tiling and what seems like a small donkey boiler. In this area where the sand has built up much lies buried but one small item, an ornate stair tread cover is similar to ones found on the Inkosi and Romeo and would tend to date the vessel to the 1900 period, as would the general construction of the vessel.

Tides: The strong tidal streams in the area and the distance from the Isle of Whithorn mean that for our club this is very much a low water neap tide dive, particularly when the winds are slight to make the journey out easier.  The slack water period seems to start about 40 mins before stated (LW) Isle of Whithorn.

sites.name: SS Ville D' Arlon
sites.notes: History: 7,555 tons Belgian steamship owned by Societe Maritime Anversoise. Built in 1920 by American International Shipbuilding Corporation in Philadelphia. Measured  436.9 x 58.2 x 26.4ft and was capable of 13.5 knots Departed New York via Halifax for Liverpool on 15th November 1940  under the command of Capt. Albert Wilding. On 2nd December the steamer was observed showing "not under control" lights and fell behind the convoy. Nothing was heard of the steamer again and u-boat.net record it as being sunk by the U-47 commanded by Gunther Prien. All 52 crew on board died.

sites.name: HMSm D6 (Possibly)
sites.hazards: Extremely deep wreck at approximately 90 metres, 36 miles offshore with a 4-hour boat transit each way. Very limited natural light at depth. A large net at the bow extends up into the water column.
sites.notes:
The HMS D6 is a British D-class submarine wreck lying at approximately 90 metres depth, 36 miles offshore north of Ireland. She holds several notable distinctions including being the only diveable British submarine in Irish waters and the first British submarine equipped with a deck gun. The wreck lies on her starboard side in brilliant white sand and is relatively intact, making it possible to swim her full length.

The D6 lies 36 miles offshore, requiring approximately 4 hours of transit time each way. The wreck is at approximately 90 metres depth, so bottom time is limited without incurring a long decompression obligation. The downline is best placed at the stern; the wreck can be swum from stern to bow and back. The sub lays on her starboard side in brilliant white sand which provides a striking contrast to the wreck. The wreck is relatively intact and not too big. Visibility can be good but ambient light is very limited at depth, especially on overcast days — boosting ISO significantly is recommended for natural light photography. There is a large net at the bow that sticks up into the water column. The conning tower has fallen over to the side.

History: SUNK BY UB 73 OFF THE COAST OF N IRELAND. (SHIPS OF THE ROYAL NAVY VOL 1).
sites.description: The HMS D6 is a British D-class submarine wreck lying at approximately 90 metres depth, 36 miles offshore north of Ireland. The wreck lies on her starboard side in brilliant white sand and is relatively intact, making it possible to swim her full length.

sites.name: F2
sites.notes:
The wreck dive site known as F2 is located in water just 16-18m deep, making it suitable for divers with entry-level qualifications. It offers an interesting contrast to older Grand Fleet wrecks and is conveniently located near the Lyness Museum on Hoy. The F2 was a German World War Two experiment that ended up scuttled in mysterious circumstances in Scapa Flow. The bow section of the wreck is intact, allowing access through hatches into the bow and forward compartments, while the main gun is still in place. The site is said to be fairly sheltered, allowing diving in all weather conditions and at any tide state. The wreck was a German escort vessel built in 1936 and measures 75m long.

The F2 was a German World War Two experiment, and ended up scuttled in Scapa Flow in mysterious circumstances.

Located in water just 16-18m deep, it makes a great second dive, and can be enjoyed by those with only entry-level qualifications.

PROS: An interesting contrast to the older design of Grand Fleet wrecks. Convenient for stopping off at the Lyness Museum.

CONS: Can be crowded if there is more than one boat-load of divers on the wreck.

Biodiversity: There were loads of fish on the wreck.

Tides: Any state of the tide.

History: Though she was built in 1936 in Kiels prestige yard of Germaniawerft, she never got a name. As an experimental warship, she was called simply F2.

The first version looked very like a destroyer, but was described as a Geleitboot, or escort vessel. She was then of 790 tons, 249ft long, with a beam of 29ft and a draught of 11ft.

But no one seemed pleased with the experiment. F2 was a poor seaboat, and her high-pressure boilers gave great problems. So they fiddled about with her.

F2 was at first equipped with four 37mm and four 20mm AA guns. She had two larger guns of 4.1in, one in a single open-back turret at her bow and one similarly mounted at the stern.

None of her crew of 121 officers and men seem to have liked her, but they did admire her 28-knot speed, derived from twin turbines with two propellers each.
Fiddling with the boat took up the years before the start of WW2, and she finally went to war lengthened to 263ft and with weight reduced to 756 tons. By then she had become a torpedo recovery vessel, and the German Navy reduced her armament by the four 37mm AA guns.

What she actually did during the war seems generally unrecorded. She surrendered to the Royal Navy in 1945, arrived at Scapa Flow in February 1946, and there is a complete mystery about her sinking at her mooring in Gutter Sound on 30 December of that year.

This sinking is unlikely to have been deliberate, as there were no German crew on board. There is no mention of it in any Admiralty or local records, nor was there any attempt to raise her until salvage started in 1968.

The wreck had been bought by Metreck Company Engineering, which started blasting for metal recovery.

The site is a large iron ore mound with most of what remains of thew wreck either buried underneath the mound or dispersed.  You can see various features like the Bitts (sometimes erroneously called Bollards) and other parts scattered around the wreck.

Look carefully around the edge of the site and underneath the overhanging parts for congers and life.  Depth varies between 23m to 25m and can be quite silty so careful with your fining technique!

sites.name: Stora-korsnas-lInk I
sites.location: Redcar and Cleveland, North East, England
sites.notes:
This Large Roll on Roll off ferry is the most recent wreck off this coast. The wreck was dispersed, as it was a danger to shipping but there is still a lot to be seen.

I got the chance to dive the wreck quite soon after its loss and found it to be very dark. Given the type of vessel we didn't expect to see rows of shiny brass  portholes, but nonetheless its size was overbearing. It has been wire swept to reduce its height and the sea has already began to take its toll on the external hull, it is not one of the most glamorous dives but still 'one for the books'.

The seabed is at 40 metres, although the wreck can be reached at 27 metres.

Tides: It is in an area known for its strong tides and requires slack water.

sites.name: Puffin Island
sites.location: Sir Ynys Mon - Isle of Anglesey, Wales, Wales
sites.hazards: Very low visibility reported (approximately 1m).
sites.notes:
Puffin Island, also known as Ynys Seiriol in Welsh, is an uninhabited island located off the eastern tip of Anglesey in north-west Wales. The island offers numerous dive sites, with one of the main attractions being the opportunity to dive with friendly grey seals. The northern side of the island is a prime spot for seal encounters, with reefs dropping to depths of 12m-15m and featuring abundant marine life such as dead man’s fingers and kelp. It is advised to be cautious of pleasure boats passing by, especially during summer months, making the use of an SMB and having good boat cover essential for safety.

Puffin Island, or Ynys Seiriol in Welsh, is an uninhabited island lying off the eastern tip of Anglesey, an island itself off the northwest coast of Wales. When you are driving along the A55 dual-carriageway and look across towards Anglesey and see Puffin Island, it doesn’t look that big, but when you are next to it in a RIB, it is quite impressive, with the highest point being some 59 metres above sea level.

There are numerous sites around Puffin Island, but our plan was to dive with some of the friendly grey seals which call the island and its waters home. They can be encountered all around the island, but the northern side is generally the optimum spot for interactions, so this was our target drop from the RIB. Here the reef can drop to 12m-15m in places, and is liberally covered in thick coatings of dead man’s fingers and healthy kelp.

Biodiversity: Puffins and other sea birds visible above water.
