sites.name: Horsea Lakes
sites.alternativeNames: P Hausea Island, Portsmouth, UK Boat + Landrover +, Hausea Island, UK Boat + Landrover + Pontoon
sites.location: City of Portsmouth, South East, England
sites.notes:
Horsea Lakes is a former Royal Navy and Royal Engineer Diver Training Facility in Portsmouth, originally a torpedo testing lake created in 1889. The lake is shallow (6–9m) and relatively clear, with a fascinating collection of dummy and inert torpedo parts, metal plates, and other naval equipment scattered across the bottom. Access has historically required special permission. A unique underwater feature is a submerged building that divers can enter from the lake and surface inside, revealing an interior workshop used for covert diver training drills.

The lake is shallow throughout, ranging between 6m and occasionally 9m, making bottom time generous. The bottom is scattered with dummy torpedoes, inert pieces of real torpedoes, metal plates, and various naval components — something new to puzzle over every ten metres or so. A highlight is a submerged building that, from the outside, resembles a work shed; approaching from the lake and going underneath allows divers to surface inside what appears to be a workshop, likely used for covert entry and exit training drills. Entry is from the quayside.

Biodiversity: Shoals of tiny jellyfish are present seemingly everywhere throughout the lake.

History: Horsea was originally two islands — Great and Little Horsea — joined to form a torpedo testing lake in 1889, using chalk excavated from Portsdown Hill by convict labour. A narrow-gauge railway was constructed to distribute the chalk. The lake length was extended from 800 yards to over 1,000 yards in 1905, but rapid advances in torpedo design made it obsolete by World War I. It subsequently became the home of the Royal Navy and Royal Engineer Diver Training Facility, Portsmouth.

sites.name: Lochaline Pier
sites.hazards: Ships, Dangerous down currents and watch out for the fishing line here.
sites.notes:
Lochaline Pier is a shore dive located in the Sound of Mull, offering a wall dive from the surface to 90m. The site is known for its abundance of sea life including sponges, anemones, soft corals, and fish. It is a popular deep dive training location with facilities available for diving weekends, providing a great dive trip opportunity with diverse marine life to explore.

Lochaline pier in the sound of mull is an excellent wall dive from the surface to 90m covered in sea life. This wall dive is probably the best shore wall dives in the UK. Having all the facilities you need for a diving weekend in one place is rare and so makes for a very good dive trip.

At the wall to the left of the entrance to the pier walk down the stones and along the concrete path and enter the water as shown in the pictures below. If the tide is in you can do a jump entry at the corner of the pier. For an easy exit fin towards the other pier and exit at the sandy beach. If you are a rufty tufty diver you can climb the ladder on the pier. Utube

Fin to the right (facing the water) the wall is under the pier so pick your depth and explore and come back up the wall to the entry point to slowly decompress.

sites.name: The Penwin
sites.hazards: The area is extremely tidal and care should be taken as the surrounding seabed drops off rapidly.
sites.notes:
The Penwin is a granite reef located some 200 metres north of the Manacles, off the coast of Cornwall. The reef descends from around 6 metres to 35 metres or more, and features a vertical granite wall blanketed with invertebrate life. In common with the wider Manacles area, the site supports a profusion of marine life, and the greater depth can often result in improved visibility.

The Penwin is an outstanding granite reef some 200m north of the Manacles. It descends from about 6m down to 35m or more. One of the main features of the reef is a vertical granite wall blanketed with invertebrate life.

As with the whole of the Manacles area there is a profusion of marine life and the extra depth can often make for improved visibility.

sites.name: Furnace Quarry
sites.hazards: Fishing line, exit points, Men at work.
sites.notes:
Furnace Quarry is a shore dive site on Loch Fyne adjacent to a working granite quarry. Quarry blocks have created an underwater boulder slope colonised by marine life including dogfish, squat lobsters, crabs, gobies, anemones, and tame ballin wrasse. The site features the wreck of Bessa, known locally as the B200, a 12.2m wheelhouse-forward fishing vessel that sank in 1998. The wreck now rests on its port side at 43m depth, with its wheelhouse collapsed and covered in silt. Entry is via the wooden pier or cleared paths, with maximum depths reaching 55m. Divers should carry knives or shears due to accumulated fishing lines and hooks. The site is used for advanced training.

Furnace quarry is a great shore dive and wreck dive on the north of  Loch Fyne.

Good training site for advanced trainees. The ballin wrasse here are very tame and will swim up to your mask expecting to be fed. The cabin of the B200 has collapsed into the hull now.

Furnace Quarry is one of Loch Fyne’s most intriguing sites, with a shipwreck and plenty of curious ballin wrasse, which will swim right up to you. The seabed is made up of rocks and boulders, presumably from the eponymous quarry. The maximum depth on this dive is 55m, although there is plenty to see at shallower depths!
 
To dive the bay, go down the 45 degree boulder slope to 15m and turn left. This is a good site for edible crabs, some bigger fish including dogfish beneath the boulders, and sleeping congers that curl up like cats to nap on the seabed here. Smaller wildlife includes most of Loch Fyne's regulars: squat lobsters, gobies, anemones, sea squirts, starfish etc. 
 
The wreck of a small fishing boat, Bessa, lies below the pier at Furnace Quarry. She is known locally as 'the B200' as this appears to be the identification mark painted on her bow, although initial reports stated this as B2000. Bessa was registered in Belfast. 
 
The wreck is a wheelhouse-forward fishing vessel of length about 12.2m. This vessel sank in 18m while secured alongside the south corner of the pier in summer 1998 and lay inverted, oriented roughly NNW-SSE. The wreck was not stabilised, being supported by a single radar mast (a simple tube) close to the edge of a steep drop-off. She slipped off the drop off and now rests in deep water, lying on her port side, covered in silt and shrouded in darkness.
 
To find the B200, go straight down the 45 degree boulder slope to the bottom and turn right. The wreck is 5m away at 43m. It is approximately 43m to the top of the wreck and 46m to the seabed. Her propeller is missing but the cathodic protector and power block remain intact. Her condition has deteriorated in the last decade; her wheelhouse has collapsed in, and some fishing line has accumulated across the hull.
 
Dive knives or shears and good torches are essential equipment on this dive.

Biodiversity: Known for congregating dogfish. Squat lobsters spotted in and around the rocks. Large crabs also present.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide.

History: The quarry factory once employed over 200 men who hand cut granite to provide cobbles for the streets of Glasgow. It is now fully mechanised with only 4 operators, providing crushed stone and concrete.

sites.name: Queen Victoria
sites.notes: History: UKHO wreck no. 009000239. One of the more significant ships lost in Dublin Bay, the Queen Victoria was a 337-ton, 150-foot-long paddle steamer built in Liverpool in 1837. It was owned by the City of Dublin Steam Packet Company and was capable of 11 knots with 250 horse-power, diagonal compound engines. Under the command of Captain Church, the Queen Victoria departed Liverpool in fine weather on Monday, 14 February 1853, en route to Dublin with a general cargo, a voyage it had made numerous times without incident. On board the vessel were 24 crewmen, 12 cabin passengers, 75 deck passengers and one stewardess, totalling 112 persons. On approach to Dublin Bay the vessel encountered a snowstorm, which obscured the lights of both the Baily and Kish lighthouses. In spite of the poor visibility, the steamer failed to reduce its speed. It ran aground on the cliffs below the Baily Lighthouse, on Howth Head. At that point, about eight people were able to scramble ashore safely. The steamer then reversed away from the cliffs in an attempt to run the vessel ashore. This manoeuvre proved fatal, and the Queen Victoria began to sink rapidly. Confusion and panic ensued, as most of those aboard had been asleep below deck. Although there were four lifeboats on board, only the port lifeboat managed to launch successfully in the challenging conditions the crew were facing. The Queen Victoria sank slowly into the dark, cold waters, drowning most of those who remained aboard. The single lifeboat made it safely to shore with 17 rescued people, then returned to try to find any remaining survivors. By that stage, only the mastheads and funnel were visible above water, with survivors clinging desperately to the masts. The lifeboat managed to rescue five of these tenacious individuals, while the steamer Roscommon rescued the others. A further eight brave passengers were able to make it ashore by swimming. The Roscommon saved about 40 passengers in total. There are differing accounts as to how many on board were lost, suggesting that between 50 and 83 may have drowned, including Captain Church. The wreck was rediscovered by Marlin Sub Aqua Club in 1983 and has been surveyed by a number of Dublin dive clubs since then. It now lies in around 18m of water in an area of strong tides, 230m S of the Baily Lighthouse, and is orientated NW–SE on the seafloor. It measures 17.5m in length, 7.5m in width, with a maximum height of 3.4m. The remains of the vessel are largely broken up, with debris and remains of the paddle wheels and boiler clearly visible on the seabed. A number of artefacts have been recovered from the wreck site, and the ship’s figurehead is presently housed in the Maritime Museum in Dún Laoghaire, Co. Dublin. The Queen Victoria is one of less than a handful of paddle steamers that are diveable around the Irish coast. GSI ref. code 144a.

sites.name: Man o' War Cove
sites.notes:
Man o' War Cove, located next to the picturesque Durdle Door in Dorset, southern England, offers sheltered snorkelling accessed via a long steep path from the Durdle Door camp site car park. The cove provides a protected area for snorkelling, with the opportunity to practice surface dives in deeper waters near the mouth. Experienced divers can swim from Man o' War Cove around to Durdle Door, passing through the bay and enjoying the coastal landscape.

Man o' War Cove (or Man of War Bay and similar names) lies on the Dorset coast in southern England and is flanked by the rocky, steep and slightly projecting headlands of Durdle Door to the west and Man O War (or O' War) Head to the east.

A line of pronounced rocks takes up the far side of the cove at the distance of the great Durdle Door headland to the east; these partially enclose the cove, and have few submerged components and feature mostly at the east end of the bay — map-recorded as "The Man o' War". The line of exposed rocks continues, very intermittently about 100  metres from the shore as the Norman Rock, Pinion Rock and a cluster around the Ball Stone, along St Oswald's Bay. It is usually possible to walk along a thin strand of high tide, dry sand linking the cove to the rest of St Oswald's Bay an area almost entirely visible from the west side of the cove.

sites.name: The Isle of May
sites.notes:
The Isle of May located approximately 8 km off the coast of
mainland Scotland, on the outer edge of the Firth of Forth is
1.8 kilometres long and less than half a kilometre wide. The isle is a
magical mix of sea birds and seals and also home to the
unmistakeable puffin. There's a dark past here though, with monks,
Vikings and smugglers on the list of previous visitors.

The viz was around 6/7m on the dive site with some wreckage in the gullies. The gullies and large boulder field were full of squat lobster, deadmens fingers, hydroids and bryzoa. The sandy patches were home to sand masons, gobies, and huge edible crabs.

Biodiversity: Squat lobster, deadmens fingers, hydroids, bryzoa, sand masons, gobies, huge edible crabs, sponge crabs, tiny hermit crabs. Above water: dolphins, puffins, auks, fulmars, kittiwakes, various gulls.

sites.hazards:
Buoys attached to the bow of the wreck and several lobster pots usually in the vicinity. 

Port of Larne can be busy, contact harbour master on VHF 11 to get permission to exit/enter port. 

Be aware of ferry traffic (site is located very close to the Larne to Cairnryan ferry lane) and commercial fishing boats.
sites.notes:
A great dive located off Hunters Rock. The wreck lies on her port side and is broken into three sections either side of Hunters Rock, with the bow side to the SW (see seperate site page for State of Louisiana Stern end which lies to the NE of Hunters Rock). The wreck is starting to deteriorate although the ribs and boilers are still very easily distinguished. The surrounding seabed is comprised of sand and pebbles. Both parts of the wreck can be explored in one dive but given the short tidal window, it is recommended to split this into two seperate dives to allow more time on each part of the wreck. The stern is a better dive, with plenty to see, as opposed to the bow which is quite small, once you have seen it, you can return to midships and make ascent.

Biodiversity: The wreck is covered in sponges, with mobile fauna including sunstars, sea urchins and crabs. The site is home to lots of wrasse, mainly Cuckoo and Ballan.

Tides: Moderate

This site can only be dived at slack water, 30-60 minutes before HW or LW Belfast. There are buoys attached to the bow and funnels of the wreck which will appear at slack water. The window for slack water at the site is just under one hour.

sites.name: Ard Neackie
sites.hazards: Slight mid tide current
sites.notes:
Ard Neackie is a shore dive site located in Loch Eriboll. The dive begins by entering the water from the grass and shingle beach, then heading north along the gradually sloping seabed. The dive offers an array of marine life such as black sea hares, flatfish, scorpionfish, crabs, sand stars, and various types of seaweed. The seabed transitions from kelp-covered areas to stony patches, providing divers with a diverse underwater environment to explore. The site is known for its interesting topography and marine biodiversity.

Ard Neackie in Loch Eriboll is a good shore dive with a varied seabed and plenty to see.

Across the grass and shingle beach into the water.

Enter the water and head north. This takes you out along the bay keeping the shore on your right but taking you down the gradually sloping seabed. After swimming over the wrack growing near the shore at around 4-6 m you go over an area of tall kelp with large flat blades. There are sandy patches in places and it is here that I saw a number of large black sea hares with white spots, some of which were mating leaving a wiggly pink string of eggs on the weed. There were also several different types of flatfish. The kelp gradually changes to a shorter, smaller variety as you continue on and the bottom becomes stony with a variety of small types of brown and red weed. This continues down to about 20m but as it does not cover the sea floor there is plenty to see lurking about on the stony patches in-between. Scorpionfish are well camouflaged in this environment and there are all the usual velvet/shore/harbour/edible crabs. Lots of sand and sun stars. This stony slope continues down beyond 40m. Just amble around as you head out to your chosen depth, there are loads to see on this dive.

sites.name: Newtown Cove
sites.notes:
Also known as the Gullimines, this very popular swimming area offers a couple of excellent and easily accessed shore dives, suitable for both beginners and more experienced divers.

From the carpark head down to the swimming area to the right hand side as you face out to the sea.  You can enter and exit the water using the ladder at the end of the short pier then snorkel out about 20 meters before dropping down to head either south or north. The better dive is to the south  where there are large boulders, and crevices along with plenty of kelp and fish life.  Alternatively you, starting from the same point can head north for about 200m and exit at the other swimming area but this is a popular fishing area so bring a knife in case you get snagged up  - maximum depths for both dives are 10m to 12m.

sites.name: SS John R. Park
sites.notes:
This is the wreck of a liberty ship (similar to the James Egan Layne at  Plymouth), approximately 4-5 miles west, offshore from Porthleven.

The J.R. Park now sits upright in between 45-58m of water and is still quite intact. This is a deep dive for the experienced. Either use a local charter boat or contact the Penzance BSAC who have dived her extensively. In the right conditions, this is  an exhilarating dive and still yields interesting mementoes despite the recovery of the "major" items of interest.

sites.name: Elena R
sites.notes:
The ELENA R is a Greek steamship that was mined in 1939 and sunk off the Shambles near Weymouth. The wreck is very broken up with parts covered by shingle banks and sands, featuring the highest section rising 8 metres from the seabed at 27m depth. Strong tidal conditions make diving this site challenging.

Located off the Shambles about 8 miles from Weymouth. The highest part of the wreck stands 8 metres from the sea bed. Beware of the strong tides in this area.

Biodiversity: Saw a number of lobsters (all out of reach), spider crabs casually walking around the wreck, blennies posing in or around holes, a few bib and pollock swimming on the edge of visibility, and a couple of edible crabs including a large edible crab in a 1ft tube.

Tides: Beware of the strong tides in this area.

sites.name: Inger Toft
sites.notes:
2190gt, length 285.6', beam 41.5' draught 19.9'
The British steamship INGER TOFT (ex ELPHINSTON), built in 1920 by Swan Hunter, was torpedoed by U722 (commanded by Reimers) at 9.20 on 16 march 1945. The position given was bearing 270 degrees, 3 miles from Neist Point. 30 survivors were picked up by the anti-submarine trawler GRENADIER. The position is as given in German records, and also in 'British Vessel Lost at Sea 1939-45'. 'Lloyds World War 2 Losses' gives the latitude as 57 25 30N. She had been enroute from Reykjavik to Loch Ewe and London with a cargo of 604 tons of herring meal and 281 tons of cod liver oil. A number of barrels of cod liver oil were recovered in the Western Highlnds.

sites.name: MFV Fairweather V
sites.notes:
A 31-metre steel stern trawler sunk in February 1991, lying upright and completely intact in 25 metres of water in Annat Bay at the mouth of Loch Broom, off Scotland's Summer Isles. The wreck is densely covered in plumose anemones, creating a colourful display. The main deck sits at around 18 metres, with the shallowest point at 12-13 metres on the forward mast. Key features include an intact wheelhouse with captain's chair and instruments, a large winch-drum on the stern deck, propeller beneath a prop-guard, and fish-sorting equipment. The MV Innisjura wreck lies nearby to the east, making this a double-wreck dive site.

The Fairweather V is a 31m steel stern trawler lying upright and remarkably intact in 25m in Annat Bay, at the mouth of Loch Broom, off Scotland's Summer Isles. Sunk in 1991, it has become densely coated in plumose anemones, making it one of the most visually attractive wrecks in the area. Its main deck sits at around 18m, making it accessible for Sport Diver-level divers without decompression concerns.

A small marker buoy is usually tied to the forward mast — descend the buoy line to the mast at the bow. Note that nearby pot buoys and the adjacent wreck of the Innisjura may also be buoyed, so verify coordinates with an echo-sounder before descending. With typically no current, the wreck rewards careful buoyancy. A recommended route is to follow the hull to the stern first, exploring the lower part of the wreck at 25m, then meander along the deck back to the bow. At the bow, stays lead off the mast in all directions, with a small line-hauler offset winch at the tip. The anchor recess and a pair of empty portholes on the port bow side are heavily obscured by anemones, as is an old tyre fender further aft. The hull is largely featureless amidships, with patches of red anti-fouling paint visible near the keel where marine growth is thinner. At the stern — the deepest point at 25m — the propeller is in place beneath a prop-guard and the rudder is intact and pointing straight ahead. Ascending the stern reveals the classic stern trawler shape, with a roller separating hull from deck and a large winch-drum spanning the stern deck. The stern deck sits a level below the main deck. Moving up to the level of the cabins, the aft mast is coated in plumose anemones; just below on the starboard side are hydraulic control levers for the trawl gear. Entry to the wheelhouse is via an open hatch at the back on the starboard side. Inside, the captain's chair is decaying and echo-sounder and radar displays are visible; the radar antenna has fallen onto the roof. Most windows are intact and anemone-covered. Forward of the wheelhouse, a deck-hose reel sits to starboard and fish-sorting troughs to port. Further forward, hatches lead to the gear store, with a net draped from one hatch over the starboard railing. The tour completes at the anchor-winch just behind the forward mast. Ascend the mast and buoy line at the end of the dive.

Biodiversity: The wreck is heavily coated in long, delicate plumose anemones, particularly dense on both the forward and aft masts and across most of the hull and superstructure. Anemone coverage is slightly thinner near the keel. The Fairweather V has developed a notably richer coating of marine life than the older adjacent wreck Innisjura.

Tides: The Fairweather V can be dived at any state of the tide. Even at spring tide, current is at most very light, making ascents and navigation straightforward.

History: The Fairweather V was a 31m steel stern trawler built in 1976, registered in Peterhead. In the early hours of a February night in 1991, it ran onto the Carn Dearg rocks at the west end of Annat Bay while leaving Ullapool. Sister vessel Fairwind joined pumping operations but could not prevent foundering. The crew were rescued by the fast personnel-carrier Bittern and the Fairwind, with the captain last to leave as the bow reared skyward. The local tug Finch then attempted to refloat the trawler; the hull appeared undamaged, but as it was pulled clear an open stern hatch allowed water to flood in, sinking the Fairweather V upright onto a sandy slope. Commercial divers inspecting the wreck also discovered the nearby Innisjura, a 127-ton London-registered steel motor vessel that had vanished on 18 January 1921 while carrying timber poles to Ullapool.

sites.name: SMS V83
sites.alternativeNames: Wrack: V83, V 83 Destroyer, Wreck V83, GB - Schottland - Scapa Flow - V83, Scapa - V-83
sites.notes:
She lies in 8 metres at the bow, with her stern in 20 metres.

The V-83 is an easy, shallow dive lying upright on a gentle slope, with a maximum depth of 15 meters at the stern. It gradually shallows toward the beach, where the wreck is more broken up. The wreck rests on an even keel with a slight port list. Conditions are usually calm, making it ideal for beginners. Highlights include a 3.4-inch gun pointing upwards and another amid wreckage further forward.

Biodiversity: Expect to see scallops, lobster, crabs, ling, conger, and wrasse. Sometimes a local seal colony often interacts with divers near the beach.

sites.name: HMS Rose Valley
sites.notes:
A British steam drifter built in 1918 with a wooden hull and steel reinforcement, ordered to sink after her engine room caught fire while carrying torpedoes on deck. Lying in 9–15m of water, the wreck was only charted in 2001 and is occasionally visited by divers.

Though occasionally visited by divers, the wreck was only charted in 2001 and lies east–west in 9–15m of water. The stern, engine room, and bridge are fairly intact, while the bow is heavily broken. Key features include a steel propeller, concrete ballast, a galley with a cooker, a ceramic toilet, a triple expansion engine, Scotch boiler, and a broken-up bow with a capstan drum winch.

sites.name: Cwm Yr Eglwys
sites.hazards: There is a sailing club in the village so you get occasional boat traffic to an SMB is advised if you are in the middle of the bay
sites.notes:
Cwm-yr-Eglwys (pronounced 'koomer-egg-lewis') on the east side of Dinas is a very easy shore dive in the Sand, shingle and reefs around the cove.

There is a small shallow stream running down the right-hand side into the sea. On the opposite side of the cove, there is a small waterfall so the fresh water is probably helping with the diversity of sea life. You can also dive Pwllgwaelod just 1 mile away.

Entry to the beach is possible by the slipway as there is a seawall all along the front, then its a simple walk into the water.

Head out to The first reef is generally around 6metres and then to the main reef wall, it is a lovely 8m high wall with overhangs and crevices. There is a cavern section that is really just an extended archway that is about 15 metres long and pops out into a narrow gulley which is wide but shallow.

sites.name: X-craft
sites.notes:
The remains of two midget submarines lie in the middle of the sands near the low tide mark, in association with an anti-tank block (most probably used as an anchor point for the craft. The remains are still coherent, but much degraded with large rents in the outer hulls and little remaining of the internal machinery. 

Archaeological Diving Unit (ADU) investigated two X-craft. One of the wrecks is still charted as an obstruction and so it was easily located. Access is possible from the village of Aberlady and the Gullane nature reserve but the wrecks lie a mile away across the sands. Both X-craft and the remains of other unknown wooden wrecks were inspected and photographed.

sites.name: Maria W
sites.notes:
Maria W was en-route from Ghent to Scrabster carrying fertiliser when she became lost in thick fog.  She was blown stern first into Sandy Haven having struck the Skares and lost her propeller.  

A Coastguard Officer fired flares and flashed a lamp to head the motor vessel away from dangerous rocks but she was helpless and struck them in the fog.  The crew managed to free her but, in the poor visibility, she struck again and remained fast.  The wreck lay with her stern inshore, in a gully, her hatch covers off and completely awash.  She became a total loss.  Four of the crew plus the ships owner escaped on a life-raft.

Stonehaven radio received her Mayday call at 3.43am  and the Peterhead lifeboat was launched.   The lifeboat arrived t 5.20am and took 5 crew members onboard then headed back to Peterhead.  The Cruden Bay Lifesaving Company was also in attendance but their services were not required.

The wreck today is badly broken up and dispersed.

History: EX-TWIN '56. BUILT IN 1932 BY E J SMIT & ZOON, HOOSTLAND. LENGTHENED IN 1964. OWNED AT TIME OF LOSS BY J P WEBER & VERSTOEP. OIL ENGINE, SINGLE SHAFT. PASSAGE GHENT FOR SCRABSTER. WENT AGROUND AND LOST PROPELLOR IN HEAVY FOG AND BECAME CTL. (SIBI).
sites.description:
Maria W was en-route from Ghent to Scrabster carrying fertiliser when she became lost in thick fog.  She was blown stern first into Sandy Haven having struck the Skares and lost her propeller.  

A Coastguard Officer fired flares and flashed a lamp to head the motor vessel away from dangerous rocks but she was helpless and struck them in the fog.  The crew managed to free her but, in the poor visibility, she struck again and remained fast.  The wreck lay with her stern inshore, in a gully, her hatch covers off and completely awash.  She became a total loss.  Four of the crew plus the ships owner escaped on a life-raft.

Stonehaven radio received her Mayday call at 3.43am  and the Peterhead lifeboat was launched.   The lifeboat arrived t 5.20am and took 5 crew members onboard then headed back to Peterhead.  The Cruden Bay Lifesaving Company was also in attendance but their services were not required.
sites.diving: The wreck today is badly broken up and dispersed.

sites.name: Zeepaard
sites.notes: History: The Zeepaard (Seahorse) was a of 400 ton jacht built in Zeeland in 1655 for the Dutch East India Company or Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC). Between 1656 and 1663 the Zeepaard made two successful return trips from Wielingen, Holand to Batavia (Jakarta), Indonesia. On 28 October 1665 the Zeepaard set forth again for Batavia along with three other Dutch East Indiamen including the Gouden Leeuw, the Wittem Leeuw and the Zwarte Leeuw. The other three VOC ships safely made their destination in the Far East but the Zeepaard was not as fortunate and was reported as being wrecked west of Shetland in November 1665 along with its 150 crew. Recent dive survey work and historical research has confirmed that Zeepaard was not lost off the Shetlands but was wrecked in Broadhaven Bay, Co. Mayo. The location of the wreck was known about since 1969 but its identification was open to much speculation because it is located at the supposed site of a Spanish Armada wreck. The wreck site has been dived a number of time since the 1960s by various groups who were looking for the location of an armada wreck which is reputedly lost at the same location. In 1969 Sydney Wignall dived a wreck in Broadhaven Bay locating boat-shaped lead ingots, Dutch clay pipes (dating to c. 1675) and cast iron cannons (Wignall 1982, 76). The site was first reported to the National Museum of Ireland (NMI) in 1979 by Crochur O’Ceileachair, a radio officer from Belmullet who recovered a number of artefacts including which were handed over to the NMI. In 1986 members of the Leinster Divers Subaqua Club led by Leslie Lawrence began searching location and located a number of Iron cannon, boat shaped lead ingots and bellarmine Jars. In the following years up until 1991, the Leinster Divers carried out further survey work at the site accompanied by Nessa O’Connor of the National Museum of Ireland. The Underwater Archaeology Unit carried further survey work at the wreck site in 2012.

sites.name: Capernwray Diving Centre
sites.amenities: There is a small dive shop, with a filling station providing air and nitrox as well as a licensed restaurant.
sites.hazards: Water temperature in March as low as 6°C.
sites.notes:
Capernwray Diving Centre is the North-West’s premier inland dive site. It features clear freshwater with a diverse range of underwater attractions, including boats, airplanes, helicopters, a diving bell, and even a small yellow submarine. The site offers depths up to 21 metres (69 ft) and is well-known for its crystal clear water, friendly fish life, and excellent facilities. The centre caters to divers of all levels, with purpose-built training platforms at various depths making it suitable for both training and experienced divers alike. Opening primarily on weekends and certain weekdays, Capernwray Diving Centre is a popular destination for divers and schools in the area.

Used as a training centre, Capernwray has a range of depths to 21 metres (69 ft).

There are two sets of training platforms with levels at 2 metres (6 ft 7 in) and 6 metres (20 ft). As well as being stocked with fish including trout, perch and at least two sturgeon, the underwater attractions include:

- Numerous boats, including the former minesweeper Podsnap
- A medium range, twin turboprop airliner (a Hawker Siddeley HS 748), a Cessna 150 light aeroplane, Piper Navaho twin and two helicopters
- A vidor diving bell
- ISO shipping container
- Two plastic horses
- A small yellow submarine in the style of Thunderbird 4
- A devil statue
- Two plastic pigs
- Various garden gnomes

History: The quarry contains a number of artefacts deliberately sunk to provide interest for divers, including a small wooden WW2 minesweeper, HMS Podsnap, two helicopters and other assorted items.

Contact: 01524735132

sites.location: Tonbridge and Malling, Kent, South East, England
sites.notes:
Holborough Lakes in Snodland, Kent is an eight-acre, 11m-deep former chalk quarry which offers good visibility for a UK lake. The site features various underwater attractions including training platforms, boat wrecks, vehicle wrecks, statues, and more to entertain divers and aid in training. Visitors can enjoy clear, clean water along with fish species such as Pike, Carp, Perch, Roach, and tench. Male and female heated changing rooms, flushing toilets, and easy access make it a convenient spot for open water swimming practice.

Located in Snodland, Kent the lake is set over an eight-acre, 11m-deep former chalk quarry. Along with specimen marine life a number of under water attractions have been added to keep divers entertained and to aid with training. There are five training platforms at various depth, several boat wrecks and vehicle wrecks including a bus, van and lotus car, numerous statues, two huge digger tyres that you are able to swim through and lots of other surprises! The majority of attractions are roped to aid navigation and there are surface markers on all the platforms.

Contact: 0750 762 4911

Vobster Quay is an inland dive site in the UK that offers diving opportunities ideal for depth progression to 20m and beyond. Certified divers can hone their skills and enjoy diving in fresh water with depths ranging from 6-36 meters. The site is home to a variety of underwater attractions, including wrecks of boats, planes, and old mine buildings. Additionally, Vobster Quay is recognised as an 'ark' site for native white-clawed crayfish, introduced into the lake in 2009. Open water swimmers and triathletes will also find facilities and support services appealing at this location.

Ideal for depth progression to 20m as part of Ocean Diver and Sports Diver skills, but also deeper if you want it.

sites.name: Wraysbury Dive Centre
sites.location: Spelthorne, Windsor and Maidenhead, South East, England
sites.notes:
Wraysbury Dive Centre offers a diverse diving experience amidst the serene marine life of the lake. The lake features a variety of interesting wrecks to explore, such as a 737 plane fuselage, a bus, boats, cars, and even a VW camper van. With a maximum depth of 14m, this site is suitable for divers of all levels, providing an opportunity for novices and those in need of a refresher dive to enjoy the underwater attractions. Additionally, for nature enthusiasts, the lake is home to pike, perch, tench, eels, crayfish, freshwater mussels, and sponges.

This inland lake is set up for divers – which means you can always get a decent bacon sandwich – but it has arguably just as much to offer the snorkeller.

Ignore the crowds of tank carriers heading off for the training platforms and the bus: head for the far sides of the lake and you will enjoy a serene insight into the marine life that inhabit fresh water lakes. Water beetles, frogs, freshwater crayfish and some monstrous pike can all be seen lurking among the weed.
In late summer and early autumn, the water warms so much you could even comfortably do it in a 5mm wetsuit. Visibility is variable – if you want clear water, visit in winter and during the week.

Biodiversity: If your interests lie more with nature we have pike, perch, tench, eels, crayfish, freshwater mussels and sponges.

Charges: £15 per per person. No booking required.

Contact: 01784 488007

sites.notes:
Portroe Dive Centre is an inland dive site located in Ireland, offering depths ranging from 6m to 40m with good visibility for year-round diving. The site is ideal for recreational dive courses at various experience levels, as well as for technical and rebreather training. Underwater attractions include car wrecks, an underwater pub, equipment, wheels, and kayaks. The site features an underwater training platform at 5m deep for skills practice. While it is an artificial site with limited marine life, the quarry offers a reliable diving experience regardless of weather conditions, making it a popular choice for divers in Ireland.

Portroe Quarry will never replace all other dive sites but its admittedly one of the best inland dive location in Ireland. Its always divable regardless of weather conditions.

Depth range from 7-8m to 40m depending on water levels with an avarege of 18m.  Therefore its a perfect place to run recreational dive courses on all  levels of experience. Also many divers choose this divesite to start their technical and rebreather training career. Underwater training platform build at 5m deep allows for easy skills training and development. Beside training there are many places for scenic diving located at the bottom and around the quarry. Left from the entry wall / ramp the depth average 12 to 13m. You can find there 2 car wrecks and an underwater pub! Also few other attractions including building equipment, old wheels and kayak.

Charges: Admission is €20 for a day and €10 for anyone arriving after 2pm.

sites.notes:
Dive Newquay is a diving centre located in the heart of Newquay, just one mile from Newquay Harbour. As an SSI Diamond Dive Centre, it offers a wide range of diving equipment and facilities, including a heated pool and classroom. Dive Newquay provides various diving programmes, from Try Scuba Dive experiences to technical diving programmes like Extended Range and Closed Circuit Rebreather diving. The centre also offers specialty programmes such as Deep Diver, Wreck Diver, and Night Diver. With qualified Marine Biologist Instructors, Dive Newquay is well-equipped to provide localised knowledge about marine species in the area.

Welcome to Dive Newquay, based in the heart of Newquay. Our SSI Diamond Dive Centre stocks a range of the latest diving equipment, both open and closed circuit. Our onsite facilities include a classroom and 4m heated pool. We are 1 mile from Newquay Harbour, putting us in the perfect location for diver training.

Many of our Instructors are qualified Marine Biologists and active conservationists, and have up-to-date, localised knowledge about the species in the area.

Located in Newquay town centre, only 1 mile from Newquay Harbour, we are perfectly positioned to run our Dive Boat to the local reefs and wrecks - there is no better place to learn to dive! Dive Newquay offers a full range of diving programmes to suit your time schedule, such as; Try Scuba Dive experiences (half-day) and the SSI Open Water Diver programme (4 days). Enrol in our speciality programmes such as Deep Diver, Wreck Diver, Enriched Air Nitrox, Night Diver or Dry Suit Diver. Extend your range with our technical diving programmes such as Extended Range (XR) 45m & Technical Extended Range (TXR) 60m, or go bubble free with the Poseidon Closed Circuit Rebreather (CCR). Become a Dive Professional with the annual Instructor Training Course and make your hobby your profession. Your journey can begin from the age of 8 years old, enquire about our weekly Scuba Rangers kids club, run daily throughout the year. Welcome to Dive Newquay, based in the heart of Newquay. Our SSI Diamond Dive Centre stocks a range of the latest diving equipment, both open and closed circuit. Our onsite facilities include a classroom and 4m heated pool. We are 1 mile from Newquay Harbour, putting us in the perfect location for diver training.

Many of our Instructors are qualified Marine Biologists and active conservationists, and have up-to-date, localised knowledge about the species in the area.

Located in Newquay town centre, only 1 mile from Newquay Harbour, we are perfectly positioned to run our Dive Boat to the local reefs and wrecks - there is no better place to learn to dive! Dive Newquay offers a full range of diving programmes to suit your time schedule, such as; Try Scuba Dive experiences (half-day) and the SSI Open Water Diver programme (4 days). Enrol in our speciality programmes such as Deep Diver, Wreck Diver, Enriched Air Nitrox, Night Diver or Dry Suit Diver. Extend your range with our technical diving programmes such as Extended Range (XR) 45m & Technical Extended Range (TXR) 60m, or go bubble free with the Poseidon Closed Circuit Rebreather (CCR). Become a Dive Professional with the annual Instructor Training Course and make your hobby your profession. Your journey can begin from the age of 8 years old, enquire about our weekly Scuba Rangers kids club, run daily throughout the year. sites.name: Shell Beach
sites.hazards: There can be a swell as it is open to the west, but usually OK. The harbour is regularly used by big powerboats that can produce a wash. This could be dangerous if you were just exiting onto the rock slab.
sites.notes:
Shell Beach is a dive site located halfway down the Mull of Kintyre in Tarbert. Accessing the site is relatively easy via an obvious gap in the seawall, leading to a stepped rock slab at the water's edge. The dive primarily focuses on scallop hunting at depths of around 20 meters, with a flat seabed featuring sand, shingle, and small rocks. The underwater topography also includes the usual sea life, and there may be a reef at 30 meters that requires swimming a longer distance. The site offers an opportunity for an enjoyable shore dive experience, although it is important to note that there is no road access to Eilean a Chomraig, an area nearby.

Easy shore dive half way down the Mull of Kintyre in Tarbert.

Shell Beach is obviously the same site as what is called ‘Eilean a Chomraig’ in Lawson Wood’s ‘Dive West Scotland’. There is a place called Eilean a Chomraig on the map/chart, but there is no road access to Eilean a Chomraig and it is about ½ mile further south of Shell Beach.

Enter the shore via an obvious gap in the short seawall wall in front of the last house. There is a naturally stepped rock slab that takes you to the water's edge. Access is quite easy. It is best to exit where you came in, as exiting further round the point means a scramble over the rocks to get back to the carpark.

First look over the small hill behind the parked cars and you will see Shell Beach. It is a small beach about 70 to 100m around from the point. You could try and walk around, but the rocks between parking and Shell Beach are slippery and uneven. Better to fin round than to try and take gear overland.Fin round the point so that you are heading towards the small beach 100m south of the point. Once at the beach, take a break. Enter directly from the beach and swim out. This is primarily a scallop dive to about 20m. General UW topography is a flat sand/shingle/small rocks seabed. There is the usual small sea life. There may be a reef at 30m (according to Lawson Wood in ‘Dive West Scotland’) but this would require finning a long way out. Claire and Andy, who have dived this site several times, have never got deeper than 22m

sites.name: Budleigh Beach
sites.location: East Devon, Devon, South West, England
sites.hazards: Strong currents can run along the beach. The reef can be missed if heading out at the wrong angle. Entry involves steep steps and a steeply sloping pebble beach.
sites.notes:
Budleigh Salterton Beach is a long pebble shore dive in Devon offering access to a vibrant reef running parallel to the shore. Although the entry and swim out require some effort, the reef is teeming with life including lobsters, wrasse, crabs, and cuttlefish, making it a rewarding dive.

Enter from the steep pebble beach and surface swim approximately 25m straight out from shore. Drop down to the seabed at around 3m, then continue seaward until you find the reef, which runs parallel to the shoreline. The seabed transitions quickly from pebble to sand just a few yards from shore; the sand holds little of interest, so continue out to locate the reef. Lobster pots are a useful indicator of the reef's position. The reef is richly colonised and the highlight of the dive.

Biodiversity: Common lobster, wrasse, plaice, crabs, and cuttlefish are found on the reef.

sites.name: Fleet Drift Dive
sites.notes:
Take the B3156 from Wyke Regis towards Chickerell.Turn left after the Church , at the end of this road it becomes a track near an old military base and slopes down to the Fleet.

If you get the tide right, you can dive along the Fleet towards the Ferry bridge where the Fleet enters Portland harbour. The tide will take you with little effort on your part. The dive is very shallow, but there is lots to see, especially crabs, it goes along a nature reserve area. It’s a pleasant walk back along Chesil beach- providing you have dive boots – not recommended for shoe fins – you’ll soon buy boots and boots fins if you have to walk barefoot back along the beach!

sites.name: Picnic Site
sites.hazards: No major Hazards.
sites.notes:
Picnic Site is a dive site on Loch Linnhe, located seven miles south of Fort William. The site features a gentle shore entry from a small pebble beach, leading divers to a shelf at 3m and a mud slope down to a depth of at least 25m. Marine life includes scallops, queenies, anemones, and dogfish. Divers can follow an overhanging wall at 8m with diverse marine life, such as shoal of saith and leopard gobies. The site is popular for training due to easy access, good parking facilities, and ample space for groups.

Easy shore dive on Loch Linnhe seven miles south of Fort William which is often used for training.

This is a good site for a club training day, good parking and plenty of room.

Dive 1: The car park and picnic site have a path down to the glaciated rocks on the point. The entry is the small pebble beach to the right (North) of this (entry bay). Dive two: from the entry bay a pebble spit runs out 100 yards north, at low water, this is exposed. Walk to the end of this

Dive 1: Head straight out over a 3m shelf and down the slope to 6m, this brings you to the steep edge of a mud slope covered in multi-coloured brittle stars.  This continues down to at least 25m where the angle appears too shallow (though the loch is much deeper). Scallops (few), queenies, anemonies and usual burrowing worms.  Dogfish reported.  A gentle drift when lower down the slope took us southwards.  A few large dragonettes. Coming back up the slope we encountered an overhanging wall at 8m, covered in life (and mono-filament line and hooks) which we followed to the end of the dive surfacing at the point.  Shoal of saith on the kelp here as well as leopard gobies. Others reported following this reef further and surfaced in the middle of the bay to the south.

sites.name: Lyme Bay Cannon Site
sites.notes:
There dozens of targets derived from scanning the northeast part of Lyme Bay. Over 300 wrecks
have been documented as having gone in on Chesil beach alone - it's a real trap in a storm with no
place to go in a southwesterly.

Of the many cannon sites in this sector, a particular one sits in 26m.
There are two big guns sitting proud and last year a third was located 95% buried in the sand. It is
likely there are more - and some underwater metal detecting may be required. The site is in the
area where an East Indiaman is known to have sunk losing all but 4 hands. Ivory has been found
at the site. However, the site is also littered with mortar shells which would seem odd for an
inbound ship returning to the UK. There is also an anchor at the site and also found was an odd
copper pin. It would seem to be part of the vessel, but a proper site map does not exist, and it is
unlikely the full extent of the (probably fragmented) vessel is yet known.

Tides: This area has an odd, extended slack and can be double dived within certain 6 hour periods.

sites.name: South Shore
sites.hazards: None that I encountered
sites.notes:
South Shore is a dive site where divers can access the water by crossing the road to the beginning of the wall, descending a grassy slope, and navigating over rocks. The site features a fairly steep slope reaching around 12 metres before dropping steeply to 35 metres, with the wall adorned with ledges, overhangs, plumose anemones, red fingers, cup corals, sea stars, and various other marine life. Large lobsters, edible crabs, peacock worms, and sea cucumbers can also be encountered in this area. Additionally, the site offers a beautiful stretch of the loch's shore and is close to a popular Munro frequented by walkers and climbers.

Slope to 10m then vertical wall to 35m.

Cross the road to where the wall begins, then go down the grassy slope and over the rocks to enter the water. Alternatively, there is a ledge the other side of the wall and you might be able to do a big stride entry off that at high tide but I’ve got no idea how deep it gets as I didn’t go and investigate.

Swim down a fairly steep slope to start with. Not a great deal here mainly urchins and kelp. Swim down to around 12 metres. The wall then drops away steeply to around 35m. The wall is covered with ledges and overhangs often with dozens of plumose anemones growing underneath. Huge clumps of red fingers poke out from the wall which is also home to cup corals, loch anemones, various sea stars and dead men's fingers. Large lobsters and edible crabs made their homes on the large ledges, while peacock worms and sea cucumbers uncurl delicate tentacles.

Cross the road to where the wall begins, then go down the grassy slope and over the rocks to enter the water. Alternatively, there is a ledge the other side of the wall and you might be able to do a big stride entry off that at high tide but I’ve got no idea how deep it gets as I didn’t go and investigate.

Swim down a fairly steep slope to start with. Not a great deal here mainly urchins and kelp. Swim down to around 12 metres. The wall then drops away steeply to around 35m. The wall is covered with ledges and overhangs often with dozens of plumose anemones growing underneath. Huge clumps of red fingers poke out from the wall which is also home to cup corals, loch anemones, various sea stars and dead men's fingers. Large lobsters and edible crabs made their homes on the large ledges, while peacock worms and sea cucumbers uncurl delicate tentacles.

sites.hazards: Swell and northeast winds.
sites.notes:
Easy shore dives often used for training.

Use the steps over the seawall and walk down the stony beach into the water.

Head straight out keeping the finger of rock to your left and explore in and out of the kelp toped gully's that are covered in anemones and dead men's fingers. It's not a problem if you get lost here as its easy to get out the water along the shore.

sites.name: Cawsand Bay
sites.notes:
Cawsand and Kingsand Bay are both on the western side of Plymouth Sound in Cornwall and can both be done as shore dives, with parking 200m from the beach. Further out on the outcrop of Cawsand, close to the old boat slipway, is a great drift dive as the current moves out of the bay.

The seabed is comprised of a sandy bottom with rocky outcrops. There is a variety of marine life including flat fish, crabs, pipe worms and burrowing anemones.

sites.name: Beadnell Bay
sites.notes:
A shore dive at Beadnell Bay featuring kelp beds and rocky outcrops, with good sea life including lobsters, crabs, wrasse and pipefish. Best dived around high tide with calm conditions.

A gentle shore dive entered from the walled sea front that runs along the seaward side of Beadnell village. The dive is best undertaken around high tide, which occurs in the afternoon. The seabed consists of kelp and rocky outcrops. Visibility is reasonable under calm conditions, which are favoured by a light westerly breeze. Suitable for divers returning to the water or trying new equipment.

Biodiversity: Plenty of sea life in evidence, including small lobsters, numerous varieties of crabs, wrasse and some quite large pipefish.

sites.name: Black Lass Cove (Black Rock)
sites.alternativeNames: Black Rock, Toll Nighinn Duibhe South Point
sites.hazards: Visibility is typically poor and green. The silty bottom stirs up easily. The site can be disorienting if not dived regularly. There is an edge that drops deeper than planned (beyond 24m toward 30m+), requiring depth awareness.
sites.notes:
A first dive at Toll Nighinn Duibhe South Point on Loch Fyne, Scotland, recommended as a tip-off. Features a steep wall/buttress with good visibility and a variety of marine life including Norwegian lobster, squat lobsters, sea loch anemones, and horseman anemones. The site is described as surprisingly good and unexpectedly rewarding.

A first dive at this site, accessed by boat. The dive follows a steep wall/buttress. Visibility is reported as good. The layout is described as quite confusing with the diver noting they kept turning back and finding new bits. Depth reaches around 20 metres and the dive shallows out to around 7 metres towards the end. The dive lasted around 50 minutes. The water is cold. It is described as not a particularly big site.

Biodiversity: Norwegian lobster, spiny squat lobster (with iridescent colours), groups of squat lobsters, sea loch anemones, horseman anemones, dead man's fingers, crabs, and bacterial mat (white stuff on dead seaweed). Scallops have previously been collected in the nearby bay.

Tides: Typical temperate sea loch (Loch Fyne). Visibility was poor and green on the day, with lots of jellyfish and comb jellies. The silty bottom stirs up easily, reducing visibility further.

sites.name: Seal Cove
sites.notes:
Seal Cove, also referred to as Chick Rock, is a site only accessible by boat. It is a haul out spot for grey seals and one of our most popular sites amongst divers. Please note that this site can only be dived at high tide to limit disturbance to the seals.

Grey seals, kelp reef fish, anemones, crustaceans, nudibranchs, sea stars and sometimes catsharks can be seen.

sites.name: Smugglers Cove
sites.hazards: Very limited parking — arrive early as this is a popular site. Access requires carrying gear under a railway bridge, up steep steps, and along a 200m path. Not suitable for wheelchair users.
sites.notes:
Smugglers Cove is a shore dive near Dawlish, Devon, accessed via a steep and narrow lane off the Dawlish to Teignmouth road. The site features a long sandy beach with rocky reefs running out to sea, and sandstone rocks at the end of the beach with arches and caves. The spectacular and unusual topography makes it worth the effort to visit.

From the car park at the bottom of Smugglers Lane, kit up and walk down under the railway bridge, up 21 steps on the other side, then follow a level path along the railway line for 200m to the steps (22 steep steps with a handrail) that lead down to the beach. The site consists of a long sandy beach with rocky reefs extending out to sea. At the end of the beach, sandstone rocks form arches and caves with spectacular and unusual topography.

Biodiversity: Flatfish including Sole are common on the sandy bottom.

sites.name: Fairy Cove
sites.hazards: Occasional jet ski.
sites.notes:
Fairy cove is a good shore dive in a shingle and sandy bay also popular with snorkelers.

There are three shipwrecks in this area, HMS Venerable   HMS Savage and a German E boat destroyer the T189. None of these wrecks are wreck shaped, just plates strewn about the seabed. You need a few days of calm weather to get good visibility here also the nearest public toilets are Paignton Harbour Toilets.

Simple entry by walking down the steps to the beach into the water.

Fin out from the sandy beach over the small kelpy reefs and drop down over the rock shelf to the sandy bed. Swim along with the shelf on your right shoulder approx 150m at 8m and you will find parts of the T189. There is lots of life on the shelf so a camera is an ideal toy for diving here.

sites.name: Hope Cove
sites.location: South Hams, Devon, South West, England
sites.notes:
Hope Cove has lots of reefs separated by sand and good for night dives.  Webcam

Diving is not allowed in Hope Cove harbour. The Spanish ship San Pedro was wrecked here on the Shippen Rock in 1588 and some coins are supposed to be found here every now and then. HMS Ramilles was also wrecked at Hope Cove on the rocks at the base of Bolt Tail. Also, the wreck of the Maine is close by...GPS 50.12.820 N, 3.51.045 W Also the wreck of the perisher GPS N50 17.060 W3 58.070. The beach gets very crowded in the Summer months.

Enter the water near the rocks on your left as you look out to sea and exit at the same place.

Head straight out for 100m and turn right and slowly zig-zag back to the shore looking in the gullies and crevices which are separated by sand or head out to the right around the Shippen Rock. Its also a good dive site for a night dive, but It can get very crowded in the summer.

Tides: No tidal restrictions — dive anytime.

sites.name: Stoney Cove
sites.amenities: Equipment, shop, air, food hatch, changing rooms, toilets, pub.
sites.hazards: Can be busy on weekends, keep an eye out for other groups when moving around.
sites.notes:
Stoney Cove is a former granite mine turned popular dive site in the UK. With three main levels to explore, including a 6m shelf area for beginners and a 36m sump for more advanced divers, the quarry is filled with a variety of submerged objects such as boats, airplanes, helicopters, buses, and cars. Divers can also spot wildlife like pike, common carp, perch, and European freshwater crayfish while exploring the depths of this historic site.

You would be amazed what we have sourced and placed on the bed of the cove for our divers to explore, our history and the diversity of these objects are what makes us the 'National Dive Centre' of the UK and what keeps our hundreds of divers coming back for more.

Three entry points: the bus stop, the quayside and by the pub. Shelf at 7m with a single wooden platform, otherwise you're on the rocks or gravel bottom. Dropping off the shelf is a wall down to 20 to the majority of the quarry where most of the attractions are. To the west is a dark silty 35m pit.

Biodiversity: A slightly odd looking pike and Nessie the dinosaur.

Tides: As an inland quarry/lake, there are no tides. Visibility is significantly better in colder months — up to 20m on still, bright days — compared to the average of around 5m, which varies with algae blooms and disturbance.

History: The Leicestershire quarry was dug mostly for granite around the 1920s. Diving started there in 1960, and as the years went on the sport gained in popularity. In September 1999 a new access road and entrance were completed, opening the site to more divers. Stoney became the National Diving Centre. The Stanegarth wreck was brought to the site in part because of DIVER magazine and sunk on 6 June 2000, blessed by a chaplain. It is the biggest inland wreck in the UK.

Charges: Diving at Stoney Cove costs £25 for each diving session for visitors, and £18 for Diverlog card holders. Prebooked parking is £10 and requires Diverlog membership.

Contact: 01455 273089

sites.name: Ansteys Cove
sites.hazards: Occasional boats and swell from easterly winds.
sites.notes:
Ansteys Cove, between Babbacombe and Torquay, is a safe shore dive in Lyme bay with lots of life.

Easy entry/exit down the stairs and a short walk into the water.

Head out to 5-6m and turn right along the shore and back or out into the bay and explore. The seabed is rocky and covered with different types of seaweed and occasional snakelock anemone with broken shell in between. This is good for fish to hide under and you will see catshark gliding between the rocks and ballin wrasse over the top. This like Babbacombe bay is good for seeing cuttlefish gliding between the rocks and under the seaweed.

sites.name: Jenny Watt’s Cove
sites.hazards:
Private boat traffic including occasional anchoring at Jenny Watt’s Cove. 

Other water users including sea swimmers, SUP boarders and kayakers. 

Anglers and discarded fishing line. 

Slippy entrance when diving at low tide.
sites.notes:
There are 2 seperate areas to explore at this site: 



Fin north of entry. Descend onto mixed weed and rock. Continuing north moving onto areas of sand. Further north there are some large rocky areas with Rosy feather stars Antedon bifida, worms, sea squirts, crustaceans and juvenile fish. Good practice to deploy a SMB due to likely boat traffic.

Descend and fin west. Numerous gullies to explore including a small swim through. Again, soft corals, sea squirts and numerous crustaceans. Look out for octopus!

Biodiversity: Rose feather stars Antedon bifida, starfish, sea squirts, including the invasive leathery sea squirt Styela clava, soft corals, anemones, crustaceans, worms including the bootlace worm Lineus longissimus, nudibranchs e.g. Polycera faeroensis and juvenile fish. Curled octopus are often spotted here and on an evening or night dive, look out for the bobtail squid Sepiola atlantica.

Tides: Weak, but subject to surge

Best about an hour prior to HW Belfast. Brompton can be dived anytime but is best avoided at LW due to entry and exit hazards (slippery pebbles, boulders and kelp).

Descend and fin west. Numerous gullies to explore including a small swim through. Again, soft corals, sea squirts and numerous crustaceans. Look out for octopus!
sites.biodiversity: Rose feather stars Antedon bifida, starfish, sea squirts, including the invasive leathery sea squirt Styela clava, soft corals, anemones, crustaceans, worms including the bootlace worm Lineus longissimus, nudibranchs e.g. Polycera faeroensis and juvenile fish. Curled octopus are often spotted here and on an evening or night dive, look out for the bobtail squid Sepiola atlantica.
sites.tides:
Weak, but subject to surge

sites.name: Chesil Cove
sites.hazards: Swell and exiting the water up the pebble slope. This is not for the faint hearted it can be very hard work getting out of the water if there is any swell. The waves hit you on your back and knock you forward and, as each wave retreats, there is a vicious undertow.  If you can get help take it as cameras etc can get damaged. This cove gets very busy especially at bank holiday weekends.
sites.notes:
Chesil Cove is a well-known shore dive site in Dorset, England, offering a reasonably shallow dive with an interesting selection of marine life and flora. It is located at the southeast end of the 29-kilometre Chesil Beach, forming part of the Jurassic Coast. Divers can explore the remains of the shipwreck Prevetza in around 6 meters of water, as well as other wrecks further offshore. The sea off the Chesil beach is primarily shingle interspersed with areas of rock and reef, providing habitat for rays, flatfish, cuttlefish, and squid. Care must be taken due to strong waves and currents in the area.

Chesil Cove is a curved steep bank forming the south-east end of 29-kilometre (18 mi) Chesil Beach in Dorset, England. It is thus part of one of three large shingle structures in Britain, extending from West Bay to the Isle of Portland (Portland Bill), the latter acting more firmly as a great barrier (groyne) which stops tidal action from washing the beach away and leads to the high depositions by wind and tide action forming the grand curved bank of this "cove". The "cove", bill and much of Chesil Beach give shelter from the prevailing winds and waves for much of Weymouth Bay, the town of Weymouth and the village of Chiswell. It forms part of the Jurassic Coast.

Chesil Cove is a popular site for scuba divers. It has become one of the best known shore dives in the UK. The cove is a reasonably shallow shore dive, and has an interesting selection of south coast marine life, as well as an abundance of flora and fauna. Although there have been many shipwrecks in the cove, few significant divable remains exist close to the beach due to its exposure to strong waves.

Biodiversity: The sea off the Chesil beach is primarily shingle interspersed with area of rock and reef. It’s a great place to find rays, flatfish, cuttlefish and squid.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of tide but is best avoided in south or westerly winds above Force 3, as swell makes the pebble exit hard work.

History: Many ships have met their end on this part of the coast, leaving a considerable amount of wreckage around the cove.

sites.name: Prussia Cove
sites.hazards: No major hazards here except the long walk to the shore.
sites.notes:
Prussia Cove is a picturesque dive site in Cornwall, consisting of three coves - Piskies, Bessys, and Kings. Accessible only on foot, the nearest parking is approximately half a mile away, creating a peaceful atmosphere. The site is known for its sandy seabed with rocks and seaweed, as well as a diverse marine life including Tompot Blennies, Squat Lobsters, and Cuttlefish. Additionally, Prussia Cove features the wreckage of HMS Warspite, a Queen Elizabeth-class battleship. The clear shallow waters and rocky gullies make it a popular spot for snorkelling and diving, with notable sightings of jellyfish and marine species such as Dogfish and Pollack.

One of the prettiest coves in all of Cornwall, this is actually made up of three coves – Piskies, Bessys and Kings. Prussia Cove can only be reached on foot, the nearest parking is about half a mile away – which keeps it fairly quiet. There is not much beach, especially at high tide, and what there is consists mainly of pebbles.

The steep climb down from the car park will reward you with a beautiful expanse of shallow water. There’s lots to see in a rugged and stony area with many gullies to explore. The site is particularly notable for its jellyfish, which sometimes occur in dense masses, saving you a trip halfway around the world to Palau to snorkel in Jellyfish Lake!

The beach is a long walk from the car park so drive as far down to the beach as you can and drop off your dive kit then take your time and two trips to carry your kit to the shore. Its an Easy entry into the water by walking down the beach...

Keep to the east which is your left facing the sea and swim in and out all the gully's and return the same way. The seabed is sandy with rocks and seaweed. This dive site is famous for Tompot Blennies, Squat Lobsters, Rocklings, Squid, Cuttlefish, Dogfish as well as the usual wrasse and Pollack. In the centre of Prussia Cove, there is the wreckage of HMS Warspite a Queen Elizabeth-class battleship which sank under tow to the breakers yard.

sites.notes: From the car park take the footpath towards the small cove. Enter the water here before snorkeling out about 120m to drop down and dive around the rocks at the head. Try to return on a filling or slack tide – the journey would be quite tiring on an outgoing tide, and make sure you bring your snorkel, its a long trek to the dive site and you do not want to arrive with a half empty cylinder. Expect to see lots of starfish, anemones, and urchins.

When the current is strong, you can drift between the two rocks and swim back on the seaward side. Lots of life including wrasse and starfish.

sites.name: Big Rock
sites.notes:
Big Rock is a pinnacle from 3-45m. This scenic site is best dived on the South Eastern tip. It is covered with plumose anenomes and many other filter feeders. There is a lot of macro life to be found here, including carpets of brittlestars, with nudibranchs and sea hares. This is a great dive for scallops which are plentiful on the northern plateau, and makes an ideal last dive on the return journey to Ardrishaig or Lochgair.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide.

sites.name: Portnagh Rock
sites.notes:
Two excellent shore dives can be accessed from some steps leading to the water near the lighthouse. As these dive sites are on the eastern side of the Peninsula, they will usually be sheltered from prevailing winds and swells.

The stony sea bed here means visibility will usually be pretty good. The site is sheltered to the west and the north so should be diveable in anything other than a bad southerly swell.

The first (and the more popular) is to Portnagh Rock, the rock is usually (but not always) visible from the shore – getting to takes a few minutes of snorkeling before before dropping down to depths of 25 to 30 meters, lots of rocks, holes, gullies and crevices to explore here and usually plenty of marine life to keep you company.

sites.name: Bell Rock Lighthouse
sites.notes: History: The Bell Rock Lighthouse, off the coast of Angus, Scotland, is the world's oldest surviving sea-washed lighthouse. It was built between 1807 and 1810 by Robert Stevenson on the Bell Rock (also known as Inchcape) in the North Sea, 11 miles (18 km) east of the Firth of Tay. Standing 35 metres (115 ft) tall, its light is visible from 35 statute miles (56 km) inland.

sites.name: FM Rock
sites.hazards: Visibility can be very green and murky near the surface. Divers have experienced vertigo on good visibility days when hanging above the drop-off. Air consumption can be high at depth.
sites.notes:
FM Rock (also known as Adam's Reef) is a boat dive site in Loch Fyne, Scotland, featuring a rock wall covered in sea loch anemones, peacock worms, nudibranchs, and lobster holes. The rock tops out at around 8 metres and drops to 37 metres, offering interest at multiple depths.

FM Rock (also called Adam's Reef) is a boat dive from a club RIB in Loch Fyne. The rock tops out at about 8 metres and drops to 37 metres. The reef is sloped at one end, with the face running northwards; the top of the face becomes shallower as you go further north. Staying on the main rock gives a nice dive all the way up to 8 metres. There is an additional edge off the main rock at around 28 metres. The dive typically reaches around 28–35 metres at the deepest. Visibility can be green/low near the surface but improves with depth. The site is angular and more interesting shallower than the comparable Stallion Rock. The rock is pinnacle-like and fissured when viewed from below. A safety stop is typically done before surfacing. Dive duration around 40 minutes on a 12-litre steel tank.

Biodiversity: Sea loch anemones cover the wall. Peacock worms visible and open. Globular sponge similar to Stallion Rock. Lobsters in several holes. Swimming crabs (mating pair observed). Nudibranchs including Limacia clavigera (orange-clubbed sea slug) and egg masses. Cod on the main rock. Pollock. Feather stars on the reef.

sites.name: Thumb Rock
sites.hazards: The main boat route between the harbour and the Head passes over the deep end of Thumb Rock — dSMBs are essential.
sites.notes:
Thumb Rock is a highly regarded shallow-water dive site located just a 2-minute boat ride from Mullaghmore harbour, before reaching the headland. The top of the rock is visible above the surface at low tide and is marked with a buoy. It is considered one of the best shallow water dives in Ireland, with plenty of marine life and a depth range that makes it suitable for trainee divers.

The rock stretches diagonally out from the headland. You can choose your depth, ranging from around 10m near the mainland down to 25m as you follow the rock out to sea. The site is comparable in character to the wall at Johns Point. The buoy marks the top of the rock visible at low tide, making it easy to locate.

Biodiversity: Plenty of life reported, comparable to Johns Point.

sites.name: Lizard Point
sites.notes:
Lizard Point is the most southerly point of England. Lizard Head is the remains of a once much larger bluff, which has left many offshore reefs and rocks, stretching almost half a mile due south, which offer tremendous diving conditions and many wreck remains. On the edge of the reef the bottom drops away quickly especially on the south eastern corner where it reaches 45m.

Tides: Neap tides only.

sites.name: Auliston Point
sites.notes:
This pretty dive has some of best life to be seen in Loch Sunart. This site is situated where the fast tides bringing nutrient-rich water divide to flow on down the Sound, or into Loch Sunart, creating the perfect environment for diverse sealife to thrive. In the shallows the wall is fairly kelpy, but this quickly gives way to more diverse life at around 6m.
 
The wall drops almost vertically to 40m and the cracks offer shelter to fish and crustaceans. The wall is covered in plumose anemones and it is also great for red fingers, peacock worms and other filter feeders. This is an ideal dive for keen photographers as well as people that enjoy spectacular dives.

Tides: Best done on the ebb tide it is a gentle drift dive.

sites.name: Beadnell Point
sites.hazards: Don't go past the point except at slack water as the currents can make getting back in hard work.
sites.notes:
Beadnell Point offers a diverse dive experience with a wreck exploration of the Yewglen steamer on the north side and the possibility to dive on the south side as well. The wreck site features remains such as the boiler, anchor, and a section of the forward hull spread across a sizable area. The surrounding reef extends for approximately 150 metres, showcasing abundant marine life and growth. Additionally, divers can explore gullies and a small wall, making this a popular shore diving location in Beadnell. Facilities such as toilets and showers are available at the car park.

Beadnell point is a great shore dive with gullies a wreck and a small wall.

Toilets and showers available at the car park, There is also a wreck called the Mistey on the south side of the point but it's not dived often (info to follow)

Enter the water with the main reef out to the point on your right about halfway along the point between the high and low tide marks, and you almost jump onto the wreck itself.

Keep a couple of meters at least from the surface at high tide to avoid being pulled over the top. There are lots of cracks and overhangs to explore and the wreckage of an old steamer called the Yewglen can be found on the north side of the point and although it is well broken up and spread over a large area, there are still interesting sights such as the boiler, anchor and a section of the forward hull.
sites.description:
Beadnell point is a great shore dive with gullies a wreck and a small wall.

Toilets and showers available at the car park, There is also a wreck called the Mistey on the south side of the point but it's not dived often (info to follow)
sites.diving:
Enter the water with the main reef out to the point on your right about halfway along the point between the high and low tide marks, and you almost jump onto the wreck itself.

Keep a couple of meters at least from the surface at high tide to avoid being pulled over the top. There are lots of cracks and overhangs to explore and the wreckage of an old steamer called the Yewglen can be found on the north side of the point and although it is well broken up and spread over a large area, there are still interesting sights such as the boiler, anchor and a section of the forward hull.

sites.name: Strone Point
sites.hazards: silt, depth
sites.notes:
Boat Dive, Shore dive (but a long walk from the parking)

This site slopes down fairly steeply, with bedrock and boulders down to 8m, then silty pebbles and gravel down to 25m. Weed and Kelp cover the boulder slope to around 10m, thinning to coarse sand, then sand and mud/silt mix.  
 
The life in this area is diverse, possibly because of increased water movement off Strone Point. The calcareous tube worm Protula tubularia is common here, as are the usual Long Clawed Squat Lobsters, dogfish, sea squirts, and hermit crabs. Less common species which can be seen at Strone Point include the sea squirt Corella parallelogramma, the Cushion Star Porania pulvillus and the Velvet Swimming Crab Necora puber. Fireworks anemones are plentiful between 15-30m depth, and Pachycerianthus multiplicatus anemones can be seen decorating the sea bed.
 
Visibility is frequently around 10m.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide.

sites.name: Garron Point Maerl
sites.hazards: Tidal swells
sites.notes:
Flat sandy seabed, occasionally grooved, with patches of cobbles and pebbles, overlain with patches of maerl and often brittlestars.

Biodiversity: The seabed here is very colourful due to the presence of a patchy maerl bed, often covered in brittlestars. Maerl is a coralline algae that forms reefs which support a diversity of marine life. For this reason, maerl beds are listed as a priority marine habitat in Northern Ireland waters. A diversity of crustaceans, sea squirts, sea urchins are found at the site.

Tides: Anytime
