sites.name: Orlock Point
sites.hazards:
Entry and exit over slippery boulders can be quite difficult causing a slip and trip hazard.

There can be strong currents further from the shoreline.

Due to possible surge, there is a slight risk of being pushed against the rocks.
sites.notes:
Orlock Point is a diverse shore dive located off the coast with interesting features such as boulders, rocks, sand, mixed seaweed, soft corals, anemones, and crustaceans like velvet swimming crabs. The dive includes a unique swim-through with walls covered in abundant baked bean sea squirts, giving it a reddish glow under torchlight. There are also opportunities to see spiny squat lobsters and other crustaceans. The swim-through is approximately 5m in length, reaching a linear depth of around 6m. Following the swim-through, the remainder of the dive usually involves heading south towards the point and then east for a slippery exit over boulders.

A really interesting and diverse shore dive. Finning out east to ‘the point’ there are boulders, rock, sand and mixed seaweed. Heading north from the entry point (at 54.671221, -05.574086) there is a lovely wall at a slightly acute angle towards the seabed. At the top of this wall is kelp. Further down there are numerous sea squirts, soft corals, anemones and crustaceans such as velvet swimming crabs. Finning north, there are further points of interest with smaller walls and a seabed that is generally sandy with large and smaller pebbles. At ~54.671540. -05.574155 there is a swim through. This can be difficult to find even in good visibility. Look out for a sandy seabed with large and smaller pebbles and sea spaghetti dipping into a dark cave entrance. The entrance is ~1m across and ~1m high. The main ‘chamber’ of the swim through is ~1.5 wide and 1.8m high. The swim through walls and ceiling are covered in highly abundant baked bean sea squirts, giving the main chamber a reddish glow under torch light. There are also crustaceans such as spiny squat lobsters and velvet swimming crabs. The swim through is ~5m in length at a linear depth of ~6m. At the end of the swim through there are silty boulders and a chimney (vertical) exit to ~2m of fairly open kelp. The swim through has quite a silty seabed with smaller pebbles and sand. If you are the first diver there, it is fantastic, however the visibility quickly deteriorates due to finning and disturbance of the silt. The remainder of the dive is normally heading south to the point and then east to a slippery exit over the boulders at 54.670990, -05.575001 (from my experience, a good time to remember to keep your mask on and reg in, until you’re on dry land!)

Biodiversity: At the walls and swim through there are soft corals, numerous crustaceans, wrasse, anemones (including the white striped anemone Actinothoe sphyrodeta) and large, dense colonies of the baked bean sea squirt Dendrodoa grossularia. A white variety of elephant’s hide sponge Pachymatisma johnstonia is found on the cave walls.

Tides: Weak close to shore but can have some surge

For a shore dive, 1 hour before HW Belfast

sites.name: Farganlack Point Gullies
sites.hazards: Strong tidal currents, eddies and overfalls occur all around Rathlin Island
sites.notes:
A steep basalt bedrock wall beneath Farganlack/Lack Point with many gullies. The wall drops dramatically from 17 metres down to 163 metres.

Biodiversity: The site supports a diversity of marine life, especially sponges, with 22 species recorded here in 2019, including the rare Phorbas plumosus, a southern species. Keep an eye out for the aeolid nudibranch Aeolidia filomenae, also recorded from this site.

Tides: Strong

Slack

sites.location: South Hams, Devon, South West, England
sites.notes: A complex area of gullies with a steam pinnace wreck on the inside in shallow water.  Known locally as the Dartmouth Needles.

sites.name: Falling Rocks (aka Stybarrow Crag)
sites.hazards: A good torch and back up are essential as the water is usually very dark and peaty.  Boat traffic, paddle boarders and swimmers can be encountered, so a DSMB should be deployed if surfacing in anything but very shallow water. The road is usually very busy, so great care should be taken when crossing.
sites.notes:
Falling Rocks, also known as Stybarrow Crag, is a dive site suitable for divers of all levels with a gentle slope underwater. Located in Ullswater, an inland freshwater lake in the Lake District, the site offers depths to suit most divers. Access is from a car park on the A592 with entry into the water from large boulders on the shingle beach. Divers can explore the boulder slope and venture down to depths of up to 40m. Another dive option is The Wall, where divers can encounter a wall varying in depth from 15-20m by heading north from the beach. There are cafes and pubs in nearby Glenridding for refreshments after the dive.

Ullswater is an inland freshwater lake. It is 145 metres above Sea Level with a maximum depth c60m. It’s not an altitude site but not far off. But it is accessed by high mountain passes. There are cafes and pubs in nearby Glenridding.

Suitable for all levels of qualified diver as it’s a gentle slope down underwater. Depths to suit most divers. Many other dive sites exist along the shore from most laybys and particularly by boat.

The car parking layby on the A592, just over half a mile north of Glenridding. GR 123 456. It is a popular parking spot for walkers and lake users particularly in summer and it fills up quite early.

Site Access: Kit up in car park alongside busy A592. Carefully cross the main road and follow a gentle grassy slope to a couple of stone steps taking you down to shingle beach. Entry into the water is from two large boulders to the southern end of the beach.

Diving: Swim out and down to 6m then south to the boulder slope. Follow these down to desired depth up to 40m and work your way across and back up the craggy / bouldery slope

The Wall – A second dive from the same location, heading north – 50m further north along beach enter water and descend gradually north/ north-west along shore. Stones and shale
give way to silty bottom. A wall will soon be encountered which varies in depth from 15-20m

Biodiversity: The south facing the rock face attracts marine growth, trout, perch at 10 m – Sticklebacks and eels slightly deeper.

sites.name: Hendon Rocks
sites.location: Sunderland, County Durham, North East, England
sites.notes:
Hendon Rocks is a shallow drift dive featuring rock formations full of marine life. Once heavily silted from coal dumping, the ecosystem has recovered well and now supports a rich variety of species.

A drift dive on shallow rocks at a maximum depth of 14 metres. The rocks have eroded over time creating lots of holes and cracks full of life. More of a 'fish and flowers' dive than a wreck dive.

Biodiversity: Lots of nudibranchs and the stalked sponge Clathrina lacunosa, which isn't very common on the east coast. Rocks are full of holes and cracks which are full of life.

sites.name: Platcock Rocks
sites.hazards: Surge and waves from the northeast.
sites.notes:
Shore dive on the point of North Berwick.

It's best to dive here when there have been two weeks of low winds. Otters are often spotted here so maybe someone could get an u/w shot.

Enter the water at the end of the path to the point and exit in the same place or up the steps at the back of the pier.

You can explore around the point and head south to the pier or explore around the point heading east into the gully and back.

sites.name: Bognor Rocks
sites.location: Arun, West Sussex, South East, England
sites.hazards: There can be a swell here
sites.notes:
Bognor rock is a shallow dive on rocks with seaweed on them set on a sandy seabed, You will know if you get to the correct location since, at Bognor rocks, there is a long line of beach huts running beside the beach and the parking area.

West park public toilets are 250m north-west of here. Rocks pepper the beach and are visible at low tide. These rocks are full of fossils and under the right conditions, the sea sweeps away the sand to reveal the fossil-filled clay underneath.

After finning out head south-east and you will find the Bognor rocks they usually have a coating of seaweed and plenty of fish swimming about including wrasse, dogfish and cuttlefish with crabs and lobster under and around the rocks.

sites.name: Jan Van Ryswyck / Whirl Rocks
sites.hazards: Extremely strong tidal currents; the slack water window is very short on spring tides. Turbulent up and down currents in open water after slack. Conditions can deteriorate rapidly as the tide turns. Only realistically diveable at slack, ideally low water neaps.
sites.notes:
A challenging offshore site at the easterly edge of the Farne Islands featuring the wreck of SS Jan van Ryswck scattered across a rock shelf at approximately 20 metres depth. The wreck includes notable features such as an anchor, propeller shaft, engine block, pistons standing around 5 metres proud of the seabed, and boilers. Divers descend onto rocks, follow a gully down to the wreck, and can ascend along small cliffs at around 10 metres. This exposed site experiences very strong tidal currents and can only be dived during perfect weather conditions and slack water, typically limiting dive time to around 60 minutes.

The wreck of the Jan Van Ryswyk lies at the base of Whirl Rocks, a submerged reef East of the Knivestone, which is the furthest out island at the Farnes. This is an exposed site with very strong tides, and it can only be dived when the weather conditions and slack water are perfect.

As such it is not dived very often! The sea was calm and low water slack was predicted to be around 10:20am. Because of the big spring tides, the slack window would be short, allowing for only one wave of divers from a RHIB.

The site features a submerged reef with steep-sided gullies. Descend the shotline to reach the reef outline below, then drop into the gully where the walls glow orange from dense aggregations of jewel anemones. White dead men's fingers appear as outcrops among the anemones. Even the rocks on the seabed are carpeted with anemones. At 12 metres the kelp streams outward into open water — this is the top of the reef from where divers ascend. Notably, the nearby wreck of the Jan Van Ryswyck on the same reef shows none of the jewel anemones; instead those walls are covered with dead men's fingers soft coral. Large fist-sized barnacles cling to the rocky surfaces. Endless shoals of fish pour over the reef edge. The exit involves inflating an SMB and drifting off the top of the reef into the current.

Biodiversity: Jewel anemones (Corynactis viridis) in orange, green, and pink cover the gully walls and seabed rocks in profusion — unusual for North East coastal waters. Dead men's fingers (white soft coral) appear as outcrops. Large barnacles thrive on the rocky surfaces. Shoals of fish are plentiful, feeding in the fast-moving water.

Tides: This is an exposed site with very strong tides, and it can only be dived when the weather conditions and slack water are perfect.

History: BUILT IN 1907 BY CRAIG TAYOR & CO. TWO BOILERS, TRIPLE EXPANSION ENGINE OF 210 HP, SINGLE SHAFT. STRANDED ON THE 'IN BUS' OF WHIRL ROCKS IN THICK FOG. PASSAGE ANTWERP FOR GRANGMOUTH. GENERAL CARGO OF MAINLY PIG IRON AND STEEL INGOTS. VESSEL BROKE HER BACK, THEN INTO TWO HALVES AND SPILLED THE CARGO. STERN HALF SLIPPED OVER THE S EDGE AND DOWN INTO DEEP WATER.

sites.name: Tor Rocks
sites.notes: These rocks lie to the north of Inistrahull. The north face drops steeply from 10m to 27m to meet a series of gullys on the bottom that run out in a north westerly direction. They provide a safe haven from strong tidal currents for marine inhabitants. Shoals of Pollack and Bib are common sights.

sites.name: The O’Doherty Rocks
sites.notes:
This is an underwater reef running for hundreds of metres to the east of the Garvan Isles. There is a large system of potholes in the reef, at an average depth of 20m. They were formed by wave action rotating large boulders on a softer base rock. They can be up to six metres in diameter and some have joined up to make canyons.

You should plan to get into and stay within the system for the entire dive (to shelter from any tidal currents). The visibility is better than in open water and the sea life is excellent and varied.

sites.name: Ondine Rocks
sites.notes:
An offshore pinnacle just outside the entrance of Loch Inver to the north, rising from the seabed at 40m to within a few metres of the surface. The seaward side features rock faces festooned with jewel anemones.

The rocks rise from the seabed at 40m to within a few metres of the surface. Mooring on the 10m plateau provides a gentle introduction to diving offshore pinnacles. Descent is through kelp at 10m then over the edge onto stepped walls. The kelp line is clearly visible at 20m (below which there is none). The best life is found on the seaward side where rock faces are festooned with jewel anemones.

Biodiversity: Rock faces on the seaward side are festooned with jewel anemones. Kelp present above 20m.

sites.name: Picton’s Reef
sites.hazards: Strong tidal currents, eddies and overfalls occur all around Rathlin Island
sites.notes:
Picton’s reef is part of a submerged ridge protruding from the east coast north of Doon Point and into Arkill Bay . Whilst the west side of the reef slopes up fairly gently towards the coast, the south, north and east sides drop off steeply. The top of the reef is at approximately 18m with the base at around 36m. A vertical bedrock wall surrounds the reef with patches of large boulders.

Biodiversity: The top of the reef is covered in foliose red algae whereas the sides are dominated by a bryozoan, sponge and hydroid community, including the hydroid species Polyplumaria flabellata, Diphasia alata (both Northern Ireland Priority Species) and the white cluster anemone Parazoanthus anguicomus.

Tides: Strong

Slack

sites.name: Skokholm Reef North
sites.hazards: Strong currents, particularly on spring tides. Current splits near the site. Always carry a delayed SMB.
sites.notes:
A reef system on the NE side of Skokholm Island extending about 100m from the island in a N/NE direction. Depths of 15–25m (with a maximum of around 30m) through fantastically cut alleyways and gullies. A great diversity of fish life, crustaceans, gorgonian sea fans, dogfish, and nudibranchs.

The reef extends out from the NE side of Skokholm in a N/NE direction, reaching about 100m from the island. Depths range from 15m to 25m, though 30m is achievable; the best features are between 15m and 20m. The reef is cut with fantastically shaped alleyways and gullies. Head back eastwards during the dive — slightly west of here is where the current splits as it hits Skokholm. Always carry a delayed SMB as currents during safety stops can carry you anywhere.

Biodiversity: A huge variety of fish life and crustaceans, gorgonian sea fans, dogfish, and nudibranchs.

Tides: Currents can be significant, especially on spring tides. The current splits slightly west of this site where it hits Skokholm. Check where the current is splitting before diving and head eastwards during the dive.

sites.name: Elk Reef
sites.hazards:
When diving on the Elk you should be aware that the wreck lies less than 200 metres outside the limits of the Dockyard port of Plymouth. It is also at the end or beginning (170/250° leg) of the Western Deep Water Channel with the result that large warships, auxiliaries and ferries pass almost directly over the dive site. Though not a legal requirement, it is strongly recommended that those wishing to dive on the Elk inform Longroom Port Control on VHF Ch 14 or 01752 663225 to receive a movements sitrep. Be aware that programmes can change at short notice and so supervisors should keep a good visual lookout and listening watch on VHF Ch 14/16. If you should have concerns regarding a vessel’s movements call the ship on VHF Ch 14 or Longroom Port Control.

Be aware that from the perspective of a large ship, with concerns for navigational safety, a RIB with a Flag “Alfa” may not be seen until at short range and marker buoys even closer.
sites.notes: The Elk reef has a wide variety of marine life.  A 3 min fin SW from the stern of the HMT Elk takes the diver to an excellent reef that goes up to about 12m. A very good way of decompressing but also combining a wreck and reef dive. But needs good boat cover.

sites.name: Seal Reef
sites.hazards: None
sites.notes:
Seal reef on Loch Fyne is a boulder slope which is a great dive for trainees and photographers because of the abundance of sea life and it has an easy entry/exit.

Very easy entry and exit except for the steps between the trees.

Enter the water and go straight out to 12m and turn right, the boulder reef starts here and goes down to 24m. For a short dive (30 mins) stay on the first reef. For a longer and deeper dive head past the first reef up the loch (look at U/W map) and the reef here goes down to 40m. Look under the bigger rocks and you will probably see conger eels. Look upwards on the reefs as you get shoals of fish here. In July there are plenty of different types of fish here (look at the U/W pictures).

sites.name: Limestone Reef
sites.notes:
A limestone reef, with a wall going from 5-14 metres which leads to a sandy, gravelly seabed at the base with boulders.

sites.name: The Old Wall
sites.notes:
Approximately a mile offshore from Killigerran Head begins a reef system known locally as the Old Wall. The best diving in this area is found at the north-eastern edge of the reef where it runs a little deeper, but  forms a series of semi isolated pinnacles. These can only be reliably  found with GPS/Decca, so talk to your charter skipper or to the local  dive centres.

The top of the reef here begins in 20-24m, which then drops off dramatically via a series of sheer faces and gullies to around 35m.

Biodiversity: The rock faces are densely covered with dead mens fingers, gorgonian corals, jewel and plumose anemones and sponges Where the rock meets the heavy  sand, seabed angler fish are often encountered and large shoals of pollack  and pouting are common.

Tides: The area is exposed to tidal movement and currents can be very strong, especially during spring tides, so choose to dive here at slack water or perhaps drift on a neap tide.

sites.name: Lochaline Wall
sites.notes:
Lochaline Hotel Beach offers a unique dive experience, with a shallow basin leading to a steep wall dropping to depths of over 80m. Divers can explore a diverse range of marine life, from sea scorpions and flatfish in the shallow section to crabs, squat lobsters, and light bulb ascidians along the impressive wall. This site is ideal for both novice divers seeking training opportunities and experienced divers looking for deep dive challenges. The location between a working pier and a ferry route adds an element of caution to ensure safe diving.

The sandy beach in front of the hotel shelves gradually off onto a steep wall. The shallow lagoon area makes a good training site for inexperienced divers.

The reef and proximity of the wall, with a drop off to in excess of 80m offer contrasting environments and consequently a diverse range of life all in one dive.

The initial dive is in about 1-2m depth over inter-tidal rock pools if the tide is in, or a careful walk if the tide is out. From there the sandy bed drops off to about 6-9m before dropping off on a sheer wall which drops down about 100m. Pick your depth, as far as recreational diving is concerned. Look out for little sea scorpions which hide in the rock pools in the shallow section, and in the sand section watch for tiny flatfish scattered all over the place. The wall is very impressive and seems to show similar life whatever depth you’re at, so in the name of long dives there seems to be no reason to go much below 20m. Keep an eye out for the light bulb ascidians, and for crabs and squat lobsters fighting over choice jellyfish.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide although slack is preferable due to the possibility of up and down currents.

sites.name: Kentallen Wall
sites.notes:
This is a good Wall dive in Loch Linnhe, and a scenic dive rolled into one. The top of the wall has large boulders and lots of life swimming about. The fin out to the wall has a silty slope covered in sea pens The boulders on top of the wall are good for the U/W photographers

From the slip swim around the pier and swim towards the green buoy at the other side of the loch (north) exit at the slip.

From the end of the pier head out towards the green buoy in the distance,  300 degrees, as you head out the underwater terrain changes from small rocks to silt and then back to rock at the top of the wall. The depth here is 15m and if you drop to the bottom of the wall its 34m and head along the wall. It does not matter which way you go as its 5mins from one side to the other side.

sites.name: Inch Island Western Wall
sites.notes:
Along the west side of Insh Island runs a deep, sheer sided channel. At  the WSW comer of Insh this channel comes to within 50m of the shore. A dive at this place leads you down to 30m on a steep rocky slope. At 30m the bottom disappears. The sheer cliff extends past 50m. At 45m there is a slight overhang which adds to the excitement of such a cliff. There is rich marine life to be found on both the cliff and the steep slope.

Steep slope in shallows followed by a wall

Biodiversity: Some unusual sponges, which look a bit like the bracket fungi which adorn trees, can be seen scattered over the vertical section of the cliff.

Tides: It is advisable to dive this site on slack water as some tidal streams can be experienced in this area.

sites.name: Skokholm Wall
sites.hazards: Strong currents at times. Very sheer wall to 30m requires careful buoyancy control. Heading westwards with the current takes divers towards open water/Ireland. Always carry a delayed SMB.
sites.notes:
A steep submerged wall below the lighthouse on Skokholm Island, dropping to 30m and sheltered from N & NE winds. The site features remnants of a wreck called 'The Bury', gullies with abundant marine life, and wreckage from at least two other wrecks along the wall. An excellent drift dive heading eastward.

Drop in just right of the lighthouse, about 10m from the cliffs, and drift eastwards along the wall to locate the wreck known as 'The Bury' — you'll find an anchor, a propeller, and an area strewn with bricks. The submerged wall drops sharply to 30m, so watch your buoyancy carefully. The wall is also covered with wreckage from at least two other wrecks. Cool gullies with an abundance of life add variety to the site. Heading eastwards with the current makes for an excellent drift dive; heading westwards takes you towards open water. Always carry a delayed SMB as you could end up anywhere during safety stops.

Tides: The current can be quite strong at times, making for an excellent drift dive if heading eastwards. Check current strength before diving. In W or S winds the site may be too rough to dive.

History: Remnants of a wreck known as 'The Bury' are present at this site, including an anchor, a propeller, and an area strewn with bricks. The wall is also covered with wreckage from at least two other wrecks.

sites.name: Unknown "Blind Harbour Wreck"
sites.notes:
History: In 2007 the Underwater Archaeology Unit (UAU) of the National Monuments Service received a report regarding the discovery of two previously unrecorded cannon on the seabed in Broadhaven Bay, Co. Mayo. A two-day dive and metal detection survey carried out by the UAU in August 2009 identified 6 iron cannon at the site. The UAU returned to the site in 2010, 2011 (Excavations 2011, No. 456) and 2012 to carry out further survey work to map the known extent of the wreck site. A small-scale rescue excavation was also carried out in 2011 and 2012 to try and ascertain the date and identity of the wreck and to retrieve artefacts in danger of being lost or washed away. The site is located at the north-eastern end of the Mullet peninsula on the west side of Broadhaven Bay at the entrance to Blind Harbour in approximately 4-8m of water.
To date, the underwater survey and excavation has resulted in the discovery of twelve iron cannon, a spread of concreted cannon balls, eight boat-shaped lead ingots, pewter bottle tops, bricks, two wooden barrels and a number of smaller artefacts. No structural remains of the ship have been discovered thus far. The heavily concreted cannon lie scattered and dispersed over a 40m stretch of the seabed in an apparently haphazard layout on the seabed. Some small-scale excavation and detailed survey work was carried out around some of the cannon in an attempt to record their form, calibre and to establish if any distinguishing marks or diagnostic features were present. All twelve cannon are cast iron muzzle-loaders varying in length from 2-2.48m. However, most of the guns are of similar size, being in or around 2.2m in length which indicates that they are likely to be small-medium sized guns, possibly ranging from minion to saker if English in origin, or 3 to 8 pounder if they are of the Dutch continental system. One of the guns may be a finbanker – a type of gun cast in Sweden mainly for the Dutch market, and the largest guns appears to be a 12-pounder gun measuring 2.48m long. Initial analysis of the cannon indicates that they are likely date to the mid-to late 17th century. Eight boat-shaped lead ingots were also found during the course of the survey (see entry in Excavations 2011). The presence of the ingots, the pewter bottle tops and other artefactual evidence all point towards the wreck being that of a mid-17th-Century Dutch East Indiaman. The discovery of such a wreck in Irish waters is a unique find and there is a strong possibility that the records of the Dutch East India Company may contain the entire story of the ship and its loss. Further research and investigation is planned for 2013 to further determine the nature, extent and, if possible, the true identity of this wreck and to assist in the formulation of a definitive long-term management strategy for the site.

The UAU returned to the site in 2010, 2011 (Excavations 2011, No. 456) and 2012 to carry out further survey work to map the known extent of the wreck site. A small-scale rescue excavation was also carried out in 2011 and 2012 to try and ascertain the date and identity of the wreck and to retrieve artefacts in danger of being lost or washed away. The site is located at the north-eastern end of the Mullet peninsula on the west side of Broadhaven Bay at the entrance to Blind Harbour in approximately 4-8m of water.
To date, the underwater survey and excavation has resulted in the discovery of twelve iron cannon, a spread of concreted cannon balls, eight boat-shaped lead ingots, pewter bottle tops, bricks, two wooden barrels and a number of smaller artefacts. No structural remains of the ship have been discovered thus far. The heavily concreted cannon lie scattered and dispersed over a 40m stretch of the seabed in an apparently haphazard layout on the seabed. Some small-scale excavation and detailed survey work was carried out around some of the cannon in an attempt to record their form, calibre and to establish if any distinguishing marks or diagnostic features were present. All twelve cannon are cast iron muzzle-loaders varying in length from 2-2.48m. However, most of the guns are of similar size, being in or around 2.2m in length which indicates that they are likely to be small-medium sized guns, possibly ranging from minion to saker if English in origin, or 3 to 8 pounder if they are of the Dutch continental system. One of the guns may be a finbanker – a type of gun cast in Sweden mainly for the Dutch market, and the largest guns appears to be a 12-pounder gun measuring 2.48m long. Initial analysis of the cannon indicates that they are likely date to the mid-to late 17th century. Eight boat-shaped lead ingots were also found during the course of the survey (see entry in Excavations 2011). The presence of the ingots, the pewter bottle tops and other artefactual evidence all point towards the wreck being that of a mid-17th-Century Dutch East Indiaman. The discovery of such a wreck in Irish waters is a unique find and there is a strong possibility that the records of the Dutch East India Company may contain the entire story of the ship and its loss. Further research and investigation is planned for 2013 to further determine the nature, extent and, if possible, the true identity of this wreck and to assist in the formulation of a definitive long-term management strategy for the site.

sites.notes:

There are golden eagles nesting in the hills above the Lochside here and the locals are very protective of these, as people have tried to steal eggs in the past. Should you be in the area for any length of time you may find that someone will stop and chat to check what you are diving for. The flame shell beds are protected as they one of the few sites that exist in the uK and are much larger than those up at Loch Carron.

Enter the water on whichever side of the pier looks easiest for you.

There several ways you can dive this site as there is plenty to see.

sites.name: Eastbourne Pier
sites.location: Eastbourne, East Sussex, South East, England
sites.hazards: The end of the pier can be dark underneath and there's lots of old wreckage including nets to be aware of. Fishing is no longer allowed so that hazard has been removed but be aware of paddleboarders and kayakers if ascending under the pier.  A DSMB is recommended in case you get separated.
sites.notes:
Simple shore dive under and around the pier legs.

There are toilets 10m from the pier on the boardwalk, Visibility varies from 4/5m to zero depending on the weather so keep an eye for prolonged periods of calm hot weather and not on an easterly wind.

Its a very easy entry/exit at the right side of the pier as shown in the picture below. Its short sloping shingle giving way to flat sand. Best to paddle out to one of the legs and descend there to give yourself bearings as it's quite easy to dive straight through with the current.

Stay under the pier where there is most marine life, we did an evening and night dive, there was a big shoal of bass, probably because no-one is fishing anymore. We found flatfish, dabs and sole and crabs aplenty including hermit crabs. On our way back in we swam through a shoal of whitebait with mackerel and whiting chasing them.

sites.name: Trefor Pier
sites.hazards: Keep a lookout for any fishermen - they will cast their rods directly out there now and you don't have the protection of the pier anymore.
sites.notes:
Trefor Pier, located on the Llyn Peninsula, is a notable dive site due to its historical significance and diverse marine life. Originally constructed in 1912 to facilitate the export of granite, the wooden pier extends approximately 75 metres into the sea, offering a unique underwater environment. Despite its closure to commercial traffic in 1971, the structure has remained a point of interest, particularly for divers. With an underwater visibility that can reach up to 10 metres, Trefor Pier is sheltered from southerly winds but exposed to westerly winds. The site features old pier legs and cobbled seabeds that support a variety of marine fauna. However, visibility can be affected by weather conditions and seasonal variances. The site is accessible from the shore, with points of entry that vary depending on tidal conditions. Safety precautions such as using a Surface Marker Buoy (SMB) are advised due to fishing activity and other water surface uses.

Trefor pier is a shore dive where the old wooden pier used to be.

Use an SMB if there are fishermen about.

Kit up on the breakwater, by the picnic tables, unless you’re diving on low tide the steps here lead straight into the water (If you are diving on low tide, you’ll have to walk out along the bottom of the breakwater wall and put your fins on when you get to water!)

It is a case of compass work now - nice and simply North out, south home. There are a few rotted pier legs on the seabed, with lots of life attached, although the majority have been cleared away. Some cobbles and pebbles - good for a little mooch. Swim back to the harbour wall and ascend or follow the wall back underwater - take care as usually kids crabbing!

Biodiversity: eryri-bywioleryri-bywiol
snowdonia-activesnowdonia-active
For such a small area, the marine-life is diverse and plentiful, but only for those divers
prepared to look carefully. Freshwater eels, octopus, lobsters, edible-crabs, pipefish,
swimming crabs, squat lobsters, spiny spider-crabs, dragonets, tiny flatfish, dogfish,
bib, sea-scorpions, two-spotted gobies, sand gobies, pollack, corkwing wrasse and
ballan wrasse have all been seen on a single dive. Plumose anemones and dead-men's
fingers grow on the wooden supports, while every single crack in the breakwater wall
seems to have its own resident prawn or tom-pot blenny. Kelp and bootlace weed grow
on the supporting legs and on the many wooden beams and blocks of cut-stone which
litter the seabed.

Carcases of dead fish are often seen, presumably having been caught and thrown back
by the anglers on the pier. Watch carefully, as the fish, crabs and lobsters all congregate
to feed off this unexpected bonus. Another way to create a mini feeding-frenzy is to
simply waft away the sand and watch how the fish move in, hoping for an easy meal.

Tides: The best dives are at local high-water, which is about two hours earlier than high-water
at Liverpool. On spring-tides, there will be a maximum depth of about 7 or 8 metres
under the pier, but on low-water, only about 4 metres.

sites.name: Exmouth Pier
sites.location: East Devon, Devon, South West, England
sites.hazards: Strong currents.
sites.notes:
Shore dive beside the pier.

The slipway and dock entrance is out of bounds and divers must use an SMB.

Walk down Mamhead Slipway or giant stride off the pier (high tide only) Exit at the slipway.

Enter the water just before high tide to make the most of the slack water period. Lots of wildlife including wrasse, blennies, gobies, tunicates and sponges. The old collapsed pier creates an overhang where lobsters and scorpion fish lurk, also two old cars which are interesting to explore. A great night dive where numerous conger eels can be seen.

sites.name: Charleston Pier
sites.notes:
Charleston Pier is an easy shore dive located on Loch Gairloch. Divers should be cautious of large fishing boats using the pier and stay underneath it during their exploration. The site features plumose anemones, dahlia anemones, elegant anemones, mussels, spiny and common sea stars, various types of crabs, sea squirts, cup corals, long spined scorpion fish, humpback prawns, and juvenile fish swimming throughout the area. Toilets are conveniently located 50 yards from the pier.

dive: Charleston pier is an easy shore dive around the pier on Loch Gairloch

There are also toilets 50yrds from the pier

This is a busy harbour and it is important that you are aware of where you are all the time. Large fishing boats use this pier so you must stay under the pier itself. It is up to you how you explore but I adopted a zigzag pattern down to the end of the pier, then the same back again but higher up at around 5/6m. This was so that I could look at all the plumose anemones growing higher up on the pillars and the dahlia and elegant anemones that were growing on some of the structures that were hanging down mid water. On the bottom were heaps of mussels and feasting on these were dozens of spiny and common sea stars. There were crabs of various sorts’ shore/velvet/edible/long legged scorpion/scorpion/hermit and squat lobsters. Also decorating the pillars were dozens of tiny white sea squirts with cup corals dotted here and there. Various other sea squirts where growing on the bits of debris that littered the seabed. Long spined scorpion fish lay confidently camouflaged. Humpback prawns were everywhere but hard to distinguish amongst the debris. There were also large shoals of juvenile fish swimming up and down and around.

sites.hazards: Cold and reduced viz if there are a lot of divers.
sites.notes:
Boddam Quarry is an easily accessible dive site with no tides or currents, making it suitable for all experience levels. The site features two pits at depths of around 13m and 23m, adorned with decorations such as Halloween masks, a chequered board, and even a motorcycle. There are also marine life sightings including rainbow trout, perch, stickleback, and pike. The site is commonly used for training purposes and as an alternative dive location in adverse offshore conditions. In the summer, visibility may be reduced due to algae growth.

Boddam quarry is a site often used for training and when you get blown out offshore.

In summer it can become very green with algae reducing the viz to 3-5m. There are rainbow trout, perch, stickleback and a pike.

Very easy entry and exit. No tides or currents.

Just explore not too big so you won't get lost.

sites.name: Vivian Quarry
sites.notes:
Vivian Dive Centre, located in the picturesque Snowdonia region in Llanberis, is an old slate quarry offering a maximum depth of 22 meters, suitable for both novice and experienced divers. With dramatic vertical walls and various entry options, including a giant metal cage and a 3m drop, this site provides a unique diving experience. Facilities include a confined water training cage, changing rooms, and kit hire. The site boasts exceptional visibility due to minimal silt, making it a popular choice for divers year-round.

Vivian Dive Site is an old slate quarry, located in the stunning Snowdonia, Llanberris. The site offers fantastic visibility all year around, as unlike most dive sites, there is little silt. Vivian is probably the most picturesque dive site that you will find and whilst you are off diving, there are lots of other fun things for the family to do, including walks, museums and riding the rail line up Snowdon.

The dive site itself offers a maximum depth of 22 meters, making this the perfect location for novice divers, as well as the more experienced.

Charges: Day entry £15
Year membership £15, then day entry is £10

Contact: 07375 113576

sites.name: Bonawe Quarry
sites.hazards: Be aware that vessels may come and go from this harbour tho' it will probably be only pleasure boats looking in for a look see. On no account should you leave the harbour when any tide is running as there's a fierce current on the outside by the walls. You won't have the air to do so anyway.
sites.notes:
Bonawe Quarry is a dive site located on the North side of Loch Etive in a natural harbour with man-made features. Divers enter to the right of the Armco, walking down to the water's edge. The site offers good visibility, with a mooring line leading towards the harbour mouth where a wreck can be explored. The area features large quarry rocks, marine life like Pouting and Pollack, and a variety of underwater flora. Divers should be cautious of unstable rock boulders and fishing lines. The seabed is silty, so divers are advised to stay off the bottom.

Natural harbour with man-made features. On the North side of Loch Etive, follow the road all the way to the end. It gets narrower as you approach Bonawe itself, a wee hamlet consisting of a few houses and a pretty school.

The seabed is silty so stay off the bottom.

The entry point is to the right of the Armco and you can walk down to the water's edge to where there's been some rock clearing to create a small gravel slipway.

Basically, you will be heading to the right edge of the natural harbour and fairly far out towards the mouth of the harbour. Drop down into 5-8m over the edge of the gravel "slip" and locate the mooring line that heads off towards the harbour mouth. Occasionally you may need to lift the line to show it's position but do so only gently as the silt is very fine and lifts as clouds. You won't believe the viz, even after you've lifted the line. As you fin out, you'll first come across the Fore Derrick from a fishing boat on your right, don't waste time here, keep going. It's only 15m max in the harbour but you will want all your bottom time, either to explore the wreck that will loom up and become visible about 3 mins after the derrick, or to continue past the wreck and follow the rock base past some thick hawser wire looped in and out of the sandy bottom. You'll come across very large quarry rock piled up on the left of a narrow harbour entrance. On the right is the natural rock wall. Here you'll find a shoal of Pouting and above them some Pollack. Be careful peering into the rock boulders as they do look somewhat unstable but very inviting. There's a veritable city of Flabellina lineata mooching around these rocks, feeding on and laying eggs on the hydroids that live on the rocks. Also, beware of the yards and yards of snagged fishing line here. Watch your time, as it's still easy to run into deco (even at 15m!) or indeed out of air, mooching about here. It's a long surface swim back to the entry point from here and there's not really anywhere to exit if you come up at the harbour entrance here, the rocks are huge!

Occasionally you may need to lift the line to show it's position but do so only gently as the silt is very fine and lifts as clouds. You won't believe the viz, even after you've lifted the line. As you fin out, you'll first come across the Fore Derrick from a fishing boat on your right, don't waste time here, keep going. It's only 15m max in the harbour but you will want all your bottom time, either to explore the wreck that will loom up and become visible about 3 mins after the derrick, or to continue past the wreck and follow the rock base past some thick hawser wire looped in and out of the sandy bottom. You'll come across very large quarry rock piled up on the left of a narrow harbour entrance. On the right is the natural rock wall. Here you'll find a shoal of Pouting and above them some Pollack. Be careful peering into the rock boulders as they do look somewhat unstable but very inviting. There's a veritable city of Flabellina lineata mooching around these rocks, feeding on and laying eggs on the hydroids that live on the rocks. Also, beware of the yards and yards of snagged fishing line here. Watch your time, as it's still easy to run into deco (even at 15m!) or indeed out of air, mooching about here. It's a long surface swim back to the entry point from here and there's not really anywhere to exit if you come up at the harbour entrance here, the rocks are huge!

sites.name: Dosthill Quarry
sites.notes:
Dosthill Quarry in Tamworth is Britain's oldest inland dive site, operational since 1958. Nestled in the heart of Dosthill, the spring-fed freshwater lake is easily accessible from the M42 and M6. Visitors can encounter a diverse range of aquatic life, including roach, perch, carp, pike, and more. The quarry has historical significance, being the center of Dosthill and mentioned in the Domesday Book post the Norman conquest of England in 1066. Owned by Ian Forster since 1988, Dosthill Quarry offers basic facilities, a maximum depth of 24m, and various submerged objects for exploration such as vans, barges, and cars.

Britain’s oldest & prettiest inland dive site. This, the first of the National Inland Dive Sites, has been operating since 1958 and is popularly known as Dozzi.

sites.name: Swithland Quarry
sites.hazards:
The quarry itself is shaped like a round bottomed, narrow necked flask so you can find yourself in an overhead environment with a roof of tree roots - so not a novice dive at all.

The water is clear about 10m below the surface debris and rightly should be classed as a deep night dive. Swithland Wood Quarry is a very unusual and challenging dive, as long as all of the safety precautions mentioned are followed and diving at depths exceeding 45m is planned and conducted safely.
sites.notes:
Swithland Quarry is a challenging dive site with dark conditions due to overhanging trees, making it suitable for experienced divers. The quarry is shaped like a round-bottomed flask with an overhead environment of tree roots, not ideal for novices. Divers need to swim over a 50m section to access an 8m deep shelf. Permission from Bradgate Park Trust is required for access, and parking is limited. The quarry, formed through years of quarrying for slate dating back to Roman times, has a depth of 50 metres with visibility ranging from 5 to 20 metres.

There is no public access to the quarry and it is surrounded by substantial boarded fencing reinforced with razor wire. It is a bell-shaped quarry occasionally used for sub-aqua diving but only by special permission and only for expert divers. It is 100 metres (300 feet) long, has a depth of 50 metres (165 feet) with underwater visibility of 5 – 20 metres (15 – 65 feet).

Due to the overhanging trees it gets very dark very quickly - the first 10m has detritus and leaf litter so below this, treat it as a night dive.

The quarry itself is shaped like a round bottomed, narrow necked flask so you can find yourself in an overhead environment with a roof of tree roots - so not a novice dive at all. There is a large 8m deep shelf on the opposite side to the entry point but you have to swim over the 50m bit to get to it.

We dive it with O2 on site and a decom station set up in the water with the shot tied in to one of the waterside trees. I believe there is a Jaguar car down there at the bottom but most people are that narked they are not sure. Water temperature is cold at any time of the year as there are no currents to mix up the water. Expect 4 degrees below 10m.

History: This is the largest quarry in Swithland Woods. Swithland slate was highly prized as a roofing material by the Romans and was used for important buildings in Leicester and at East Bridgford in Nottinghamshire. The first written evidence of slate quarrying in the area is in early 1300s and the actual listing of the Swithland quarries appears in 1343, when the quarries at Swithland and Groby Park are referred to in the Borough of Leicester Records. In 1377-8, work on Leicester Castle included “2000 slates bought from John Bareman with cartage from Swithland, for 3s 1d a thousand.” In the same year, builders at Frith Lodge purchased 1500 slates from Swithland at the same price. Bradgate House, once the home of Lady Jane Grey, was also roofed with Swithland Slate.

Operating through the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries, the Swithland quarries were taken over by the Ellis family sometime during the period 1852-65. In 1859 they reopened the most southerly of the quarries in Swithland Wood apparently using ‘modern methods and Machinery’. The best bed of slate in the quarry was only 5 metres wide and almost vertical. As a result, the quarry was worked to a depth of more than 60 metres at its northern end, which presumably earned its name of The Great Pit. The Swithland Wood quarries were shut in 1887.

Charges: Found that the price had gone up from £40 to £100 (27/06/2009), as you sign a disclaimer to use the site and need you own insurance. Nice quarry but robbing costs to dive a hole in the ground. Better off with NDC Dive Centre.

sites.name: Brogborough Lake
sites.notes:
Brogborough Lake is a former clay pit in Marston Vale, situated just off the old A421 between Milton Keynes and Bedford. Once part of a large brickworks, the lake formed when the old workings flooded after the pumps were switched off. MK Scuba School have arranged access with the site owner and offer training courses and casual dives. Depths average around seven metres, dropping to approximately twelve in places, making it suitable for training and recreational diving. The lake bed is largely soft mud and clay, and the site features notable scour gullies running north to south, as well as a considerable amount of submerged debris including tyres, vehicles, ironwork, and sanitary ware. Large pike have also been observed by divers.

The expansive lake at Brogborough has recently been opened up to paying scuba divers, thanks to the persistence of a local dive outfit.

Situated just off the old A421 road between Milton Keynes (MK) and Bedford, Brogborough was once home to a large brickworks – in common with many towns and villages along this part of Marston Vale. Where the brick workings once stood is now only empty spaces and lakes, which formed when the clay pits filled with water after the pumps fell silent.

Although once a large industrial site, today Brogborough is a largely secluded site and wildlife haven, accessible only via narrow country lanes and hidden from view as your drive around. It’s primary draw is for anglers, although there is a sailing and windsurfing club on site with areas marked out on the water with flags and buoys.

MK Scuba School have agreed terms with the site owner and are now offering training courses and pay-as-you-go dives at the site.

I dived it in July 2020, and again in April 2021 just after the winter 2020-21 lockdown eased in England. At an average depth of about seven metres dropping to about 12 in places, it’s an ideal spot for training, warm-up dives or just to get wet for fun. Entry is at the eastern side of the lake via a step into waist-deep water, which then drops down into a gulley full of debris at about 6m.

We have to talk about those gullies, or perhaps more correctly, scours: these are long troughs running north-south which make for interesting buoyancy challenges if you’re moving east-west. One minute you’re at six metres, the next up to only one or two, and then down the other side into the next.

The bottom, where it reveals itself, is largely soft mud and clay-like sediment.

And we also have to talk about debris, because there’s absolutely tonnes of it. Mainly discarded tyres, but also cars and vans, fencing, ironwork, pipes, baths and toilets… and presumably plenty more yet to be discovered. Jackie (of MK Scuba) said after some investigations they had also discovered a hut or building of some description in the northeastern corner, and that there was a ‘pit’ or deeper area to the west as yet unexplored.

In 2020 visibility had been poor, so it was a relief to discover 8-10 metres of decent vis this time around. Myself and buddy Tony followed the rope to the training platforms and were rewarded with the company of half a dozen very large pike hanging lazily about. They seemed less shy than before, perhaps having forgotten what divers looked like during the lockdown… or simply more confident to take us on now the water had cleared.

Charges: £5 per person

Contact: MK Scuba School (Jackie 01908 473132)

sites.notes:
The wreck of the MV Loch Erisort, which sank on 27th May 1981 off Kirkaig Point. Wreckage is located in 9-12m of water in white sandy gulleys on the NE side of Kirkaig rock, with little remaining other than wood planks and rusted machinery.

Wreckage found in 9-12m in white sandy gulleys on the NE side of Kirkaig rock (position 58 08 346N, 005 17 818W). Not much remains other than a few wood planks and some badly rusted machinery covered in nets and ropes. The surrounding gulleys are quite scenic.

sites.hazards: The tides roar through here like a steam train, the flattened kelp in the middle and rows of heaped up sand across the channel are all evidence of this. One to be avoided on springs. Be aware of what the tide is doing all the time, don’t get so immersed in taking photos etc that you miss the tide picking up and end up with it running so fast it pushes you past your exit.
sites.notes:
An exceptional shore dive in Loch Carron, West Scotland, accessed directly from a harbour slipway. The site offers flame shell beds, walls of anemones, and encounters with dolphins. Three dive options are available in the area, all offering superb marine life.

A shore reef dive with entry directly from the harbour slip — one of the easiest possible shore entries. The site offers three distinct dive options in the area. Features include flame shell beds and walls of anemones. Nudibranchs are present and make good photographic subjects.

Biodiversity: Flame shells, anemones, nudibranchs, dolphins.

Tides: Best dived on neap tides. Strong currents on springs.

sites.name: Loch Wasdale
sites.notes:
The wreck is highly degraded and mixed in with the remains of the Constant Star which also ran aground on Skerry Rock.  All that remains of the Loch Wasdale is her boiler, winch and anchors.

History: The Aberdeen built trawler, Loch Wasdale was built for White Star Steam Fishing Co of Aberdeen Ltd.,  but requisitioned in October 1915 by the Admiralty for minesweeping service which she performed until 1919.   In 1939 her ownership was transferred to Malcolm Smith Ltd, Aberdeen.

She was stranded on Skerry Rock, off Boddam in a gale and sent a distress signal to Peterhead coastguard in the early hours of the morning.  The lifeboat was called out but her usual coxswain, J B McLean was recuperating from an operation and could not man the boat.  Instead, the Harbourmaster, Capt. James Winter, admitting he hadn't been at sea for some time, took charge of the lifeboat.

The lifeboat was launched at 4.20am in rain and pitch dark and with heavy seas from the strong south south easterly gale .  She reached the Loch Wasdale at 4.35am.  The trawler was down at the stern and the waves were breaking over her and her crew who were gathered at the bows.  Captan Winter manoeuvred the lifeboat alongside the sinking vessel and managed to keep her in place in the 4m waves, coming close enough to allow each of the crew to jump aboard until all of them had been rescued.  The last survivor landed awkwardly and fell between the vessels where he was crushed.  He was taken to hospital.   

By 5.15am the rescue was complete and the lifeboat was back on station.   The Loch Wasdale by then had caught fire and quickly sank beneath the waves.

Captain Winter later received an RNLI Bronze medal for the rescue.

sites.name: Devil's Bridge
sites.location: South Lakeland, Cumbria, North West, England
sites.hazards: The bridge also witnesses illegal "tombstoning" (bridge diving), which has caused at least one death, of a 22-year-old man in 2012.
sites.notes:
Devil's Bridge is a dive site located on the River Lune near Kirkby Lonsdale. Divers can enjoy a drift dive in clear water between two bridges, observing fish and exploring underwater rock formations. Access to the dive site is relatively easy from the shingle beach upstream of the old bridge. Diving is permitted at certain times of the year, and all divers must contact the local Tourist Information Office in advance. The site is known for its deep rock pools, good visibility, and the presence of various fish species such as trout, eels, and occasionally salmon.

The river beneath Devil's Bridge is popular with scuba divers due to relatively easy access and egress, deep rock pools (about 16 ft in a low swell) and good visibility.

Get kitted up and then walk through a narrow gate and down on to a small beach upstream of the bridge.

The current is at its strongest here so jump in and drift down under the first bridge. After the bridge, the current slackens and you can spend time looking at the fish and in the cracks between rocks for eels. The River shallows rapidly just before the road bridge and after the bridge, there are two areas to exit one above the bridge and one between the bridges.

Biodiversity: Spring and summer see migratory trout and salmon in the river as well as fresh water eels and sticklebacks.

History: The town is noted for the Devil's Bridge which at one time carried the Skipton to Kendal road over the River Lune. It dates from around 1370 and is constructed of fine gritstone ashlar. It has three spans, the western two measuring 54.75 feet (16.69 m) each and the eastern one 29 feet (8.8 m), or 45 feet (14 m) from river to parapet. The piers are hexagonal, measuring 60 feet (18 m) around and extend upwards to provide pedestrian refuges. At the eastern end is a sundial in the form of a square block on an octagonal column. The bridge was probably built by monks of St Mary's Abbey, York.

The roadway on the bridge is only 12 feet (3.7 m) wide, insufficient for modern traffic. As vehicle numbers increased the bridge was closed to vehicular traffic in 1932. Traffic instead crosses the river by the Stanley Bridge, 490 feet (150 m) to the south, which was built in the 1930s. It is a grade I listed structure and a Scheduled Ancient Monument.

Charges: Parking and diving are both free.

sites.name: Covenham Reservoir
sites.location: East Lindsey, Lincolnshire, East Midlands, England
sites.notes:
The reservoir is situated between Grimsby and Louth in Lincolnshire. The reservoir hosts a watersports centre offering sailing, waterskiing and diving with a perimeter walkway open to the public.

The diving club forms part of covenham water sports association, and as such has  designated water times. Winter times Sunday mornings; dawn-11.00am, summer times Tuesday afternoon 16.00hrs to dusk.

History: Covenham Reservoir, located in East Lindsey is a 200-acre reservoir and treatment works constructed between 1963 and 1978 by W. & C. French. The reservoir was built next to the Louth Navigation canal and acts as a pumped storage reservoir from the canal, and can be supplemented by transfer schemes from Great Eau and Long Eau rivers.

sites.name: Netherton Reservoir
sites.amenities: The reservoir now hosts watersports including scuba diving, yachting and water skiing. The Dudley Water Ski and Yacht Club began as an informal society in 1963, and negotiated with Dudley Council to allow them to use the reservoir for their activities. Changing rooms and a clubhouse were built, and the use of the reservoir was shared with two diving clubs, although they remained independent of the original club.
sites.notes:
Netherton Reservoir - otherwise known as Lodge Farm Reservoir or locally known as The Rezza is a canal feeder reservoir in the Netherton district of Dudley, England. It opened in 1838, and is now used for watersports, as well as supplying water to the canal system.

The ‘Rezza’, as it is affectionately known, has an underwater rope course so that divers can find their way around the various ‘attractions’, including several training platforms.

History: The reservoir, which was built between 1835 and 1838, acted as a storage reservoir, so that when water was plentiful, as a result of rain, it could be pumped from the canal into the reservoir, and then released back into the canal through sluices near the tunnel when it was required. The engine was installed in 1840, and drove a scoop wheel. A cottage was provided for the sluice keeper.

With the nationalisation of the canals in 1948, ownership of the reservoir passed from the Birmingham Canal Navigations, with whom the Dudley Canal had amalgamated in 1846, to British Waterways. They sold it to Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council in 1966, who wanted to improve the leisure facilities within their area, and have since developed it for watersports, although it still supplies water to the canal.

Charges: You can purchase air fills on a one-off basis (£2.50) or alternatively buy a 10-fill card for £25.

sites.name: Gorton Reservoirs
sites.notes:
Gorton Reservoirs are two reservoirs on the boundary of Tameside and Manchester in the North West of England. They are Gorton Upper Reservoir and Gorton Lower Reservoir. The upper and lower sections are separated by a road supported by a stone bridge consisting of a series of arches. They are owned and maintained by United Utilities.

History: The reservoirs were completed between 1825 and 1826. Able to supply almost 1 million imperial gallons of water per day to the city of Manchester and the surrounding area; they were used until 1963.

sites.name: Old Swimming Pool
sites.hazards: Swells with a Northeast wind.
sites.notes:
Old Swimming Pool is a shore dive site accessed by walking across rocks for a jump entry or swimming in from the shore. The site features a system of gullies along the reefs seaward side, with highlights such as the coral canyon and a large hollow at 15 meters depth. Divers can explore various nooks and crannies for marine life like crabs, fish, octopus, and lobster. The site offers an excellent rescue-training venue during high tide with shallow reefs teeming with critters and interesting gullies. However, it is recommended to dive here only after a week of calm weather due to its exposed location.

There are quite a few steps, but the walk is still considerably shorter and easier than the hill at Petticowick. Furthermore, the old baths fills at high tide (best at springs), located on a sheltered beach, which makes an excellent rescue-training venue, and the shallow (approximately 10m) reefs around the immediate shore have lots of critters and interesting gullies.

Two ways to access the dive is either walk across the rocks and jump entry into about 4-6ms, following the rocks on your right-hand side until you come to exit point or swim in from the shore crossing over the small wall over a sewer pipe (no longer used), this leads you into a gulley, turn left and follow the rocks, keeping them on your left-hand side. To exit, it can be a bit disorientating, the first gulley that looks like it will take you back to shore is a dead end, follow on for a couple of minutes to the next gulley, this will take you back to the pipe, then over a small wall back into the old pool area, then a short walk up the steps, this is murder as they are different heights, take your time.

There is a fantastic system of gullies all along the reefs seaward side, as well as some on the shore side. On the north-west side of the reef you'll come across a break in the reef, called coral canyon, around the back of this there is a large hollow at 15mtrs. Look carefully into all the nooks and crannies for small crabs, fish, the occasional octopus and lobster. Swim for 30 mins depending on your air and turn back.

Stern only remains, broken up.

sites.name: Bard's Cave
sites.alternativeNames: Cave of the Bard, Orkneyman's Cave, Orkney Man's Cave
sites.hazards: Deep cave penetration — a good torch is a must.
sites.notes:
This huge natual opening is very close to the Giants Legs on the island of Bressay. So large that a local tourist boat actually moors up inside the cave, there is always air above you and daylight is always visible – so technically not a true cave dive. However, it does offer a unique environment for flora and fauna, with a very paranoid seal usually resident at the back of the cave.

Amazing topography with smooth large boulders and blocks tumbled seaward. The right hand wall shone orange from colonies of Baked Bean sea squirts. The boulder slope as we exited the cave was also covered in marine life.

Biodiversity: The floor is washed by the powerful southerly swells, so all life tends to be the smaller things – anemones, dead mens fingers, nudibranches, all of which love this high energy site.

History: The cave is named after an Orkney man who sheltered there while running from the Pressgang. The King's men did not dare pursue him into the cave, and he was eventually rescued by sympathetic Shetlanders. One account describes the Orkneyman sailing into the cave with his boat, taking refuge on rocky ledges, but forgetting to secure his boat which was washed out by the sea swell. A storm then trapped him in the cave for two days before he swam to a small rock outside and climbed to the top of the cliff to escape.

sites.name: Fingal's Cave
sites.notes:
Fingal's Cave is a sea cave on the uninhabited island of Staffa, in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, known for its natural acoustics. The National Trust for Scotland owns the cave as part of a national nature reserve.

The cave has a large arched entrance and is filled by the sea. Several sightseeing cruises organised from April to September by local companies pass the entrance to the cave. In calm conditions, one can land at the island's landing place (as some of these cruises permit) and walk the short distance to the cave, where a row of fractured columns forms a walkway just above high-water level permitting exploration on foot. From the inside, the entrance seems to frame the island of Iona across the water.

History: Fingal's Cave is formed entirely from hexagonally jointed basalt columns within a Paleocene lava flow and is similar in structure to both the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland and Ulva.

In these locations, cooling on the upper and lower surfaces of the solidified lava resulted in contraction and fracturing, starting in a blocky tetragonal pattern and transitioning to a regular hexagonal fracture pattern with fractures perpendicular to the cooling surfaces. As cooling continued these cracks gradually extended toward the centre of the flow, forming the long hexagonal columns we see in the wave-eroded cross-section today. Similar hexagonal fracture patterns are found in desiccation cracks in mud where contraction is due to loss of water instead of cooling.

sites.name: Sugarloaf Caves
sites.notes:
Sugarloaf Caves is a picturesque dive site offering a unique underwater experience. The site features caves such as the 'Cave of Birds' and the 'Fairy Hall' which are teeming with marine life including anemones, hydroids, and sponges. The walls are adorned with jewel anemones, creating a colourful underwater landscape. Ideal for a second dive, the site is known for its friendly seals and stunning rock formations, making it a must-see dive spot.

Not true caves as the tops are open to the air. The walls are carpeted in jewel anemones. Ideal second dive and certainly unique.

Very, very picturesque and well worth witnessing. Start at the ‘Cave of Birds’ working your way to the end where yu can circumnavigate a large rock at the end (not good for the claustrophobic!). Swim back to the entrance (look up and see the suns rays streaming down into the cave), then follow the cliff face of the right through a narrow gorge created by a large rock, known as the ‘Anvil’, on your left. Hidden amongst the kelp is a narrow entrance to the ‘Fairy Hall’ (a marine biologists paradise!). Full of anemones, hydroids and sponges. At the end currents have scoured out a huge amphitheatre in the rock at the base of the Sugarloaf.

Biodiversity: In the summer guillemots and kittewakes nest on the rocks.

sites.name: Chirk Caverns
sites.hazards: Poor light levels, very dark water, and an extremely silty bottom make this a hazardous site. A guideline and redundant equipment are essential. Silting out is a serious risk without good buoyancy control and horizontal trim. The site is privately owned and access requires prior permission.
sites.notes:
Chirk Caverns is a privately owned cavern dive site within Chirk Granite Quarry, located just off the B4500 south of Glyn Ceiriog in North Wales. It is a challenging, non-beginner site with poor light levels, dark water, and a very silty bottom, suited only to divers with appropriate skills and equipment.

The site consists of caverns within Chirk Granite Quarry. The caverns have poor light levels and dark water, so a guideline is essential for navigation. The bottom is very silty, demanding excellent buoyancy control and horizontal trim to avoid disturbing the sediment. This is not a site for the everyday diver — redundancy in equipment and complete confidence in your kit and buddy are required. The site is located in a private back garden, so prior permission from the owners must be obtained before visiting.

sites.name: Watcombe Caves
sites.notes:
Watcombe Caves is a reef dive in Lyme Bay, suited for new Open Water divers thanks to its shallow maximum depth and easy navigation. The site features swim-throughs and large caverns eroded into the cliffs, with crevices hosting prawns, crabs, and occasional lobsters. Seals are frequently seen on the rocks near the caves.

The site features swim-throughs and large caverns eroded into the cliffs along a section of coastline, giving it its name. Crevices in the reef provide shelter for marine life, and the seabed sand is fairly coarse as lighter sand is washed away. The maximum depth is 12m, making navigation straightforward. Seals are often seen on the rocks near the caves.

Biodiversity: Prawns, crabs, and occasional lobsters make use of the reef crevices. Seals are frequently present and can often be seen on the rocks by the caves.

sites.name: Gouliot Caves
sites.notes:
A small swim-through cave system that is full of jewel anemones. Most areas of the system do have natural light and direct access to the surface.

Tides: Tide conditions must be perfect. A great place to explore at low tide on foot.

History: The Gouliot caves are located on the west coast of Sark in Gouliot passage which is a narrow stretch of water between Sark and Brecqhou Island in the Channel Islands. A small network of caves which are tidal and dry on low tides. The caves were discovered for the first time in 1835 by the then Seigneur of Sark Mr. Le Pelley. It was designated a Ramsar site on the 9th April 2007 site number 2276.

sites.name: The Caves
sites.hazards: Fast cars on A814, Depth, Darkness (this can be a spooky dive) the entry/exit can be difficult through the tunnel and down to the water.
sites.notes:
The Caves is a dive site located on the south side of Loch Long along the A814 in Scotland. The site features a steep boulder slope dropping to approximately 35m with crevasses and rock formations that create the appearance of caves for sealife. Plumose and sealochs anemones cover the rocks, with common sightings of conger eels and wrasse. The tops of the rocks are often covered in plumrose anemones, and there are Fireworks Anemones towards the sandy bottom. Popular for Edible Crabs and various fish, the site is also used for shore fishing, making it important to watch out for fishing lines. Access to the water involves a scramble down a steep track but is considered a rewarding shore dive for enthusiasts.

The caves in Loch Long is a steep slope and large boulders (no caves) in Loch long.

Carefully step down the side of the bridge and walk under the road (easy for the vertically challenged) there is sometimes a rope here to hold onto when getting down the steep bit to the water. (see pictures below)

Entry/exit the water on a steep slope and descend to the left and you will come to a small cliff, follow the bottom of the cliff till it reaches 30m and turns left. You are now at the bottom, follow the bottom of the cliff and large boulders till you come to a broken shell slope upwards, (should take 10 mins). Here is where you turn back and ascend diagonally to 15m and follow the tops of the large rocks, which can have large groups of plumose anemones on top of them. Keep heading back to the exit point until the large boulders change to a steep shingle slope, here is where you exit the water. There is a big rock at the water's edge which is good to sit on to remove your fins.

sites.name: Roa Island and Piel
sites.amenities: There are public toilets on Piel Street.  Also a fish & chip shop and ice cream!
sites.hazards: Possibility of strong currents if the timing of the dive isn’t right.  Boat traffic in the deeper water of the channel.  The small Piel Island ferry regularly comes to the jetty on the east side, so diving to the west side should avoid this.  Fishing line is a possibility.  It’s difficult to exit the water back onto the jetty.  If exiting onto the shore, the cobbles and pebbles are often covered in seaweed and can be slippery.
sites.notes:
Roa Island and Piel is a dive site located near Roa Island Pier and Sailing Club in the UK. Divers can access the site at slackwater, ideally on a neap tide. Street parking is available near the rocky beach, with access down a steep banking. Divers can head out into the channel from the pier and turn north, exploring the shallow waters close to the shore to avoid boat traffic in the deeper channel. The site is known for its abundance of sea life, and it is recommended to dive one hour before low water on a neap tide to avoid strong currents.

sites.name: SS Tonis Chandris
sites.notes:
A Greek steamship that ran aground on Vere Reef in 1940, now lying on a sloping kelp-covered seabed with an impressive engine block, boilers, prop shaft, and an emergency ship's wheel still upright on the seabed.

The wreck lies on a sloping kelp covered seabed. Much of the wreckage lies hidden under the surrounding seabed and kelp. The impressive engine block rises several metres off the seabed. Boilers are still in place as is the prop shaft. Close to the end of the propeller shaft is a small ledge dropping onto a sandy seabed. An impressive emergency ship's wheel was found upright on the seabed in around 26m of water. Provides a good rummage dive with great photographic opportunities and plenty of recognisable wreck features.

The site lies within the Ballycastle – Rathlin ferry channel and recreational boat traffic can also be busy (surface marker buoy and vigilant boat cover essential)
sites.notes:
A mixed sediment seabed comprised of mud, broken shell, unsorted sand, cobbles and some small boulders.

Biodiversity: The site supports a diverse faunal community, which includes the sea beard hydroid Nemertesia antennina and Ross coral Pentapora foliacea. 18 species of nudibranch were recorded here in 2019 by the Rathlin Dive Expedition team, including the rare Knoutsodonta oblonga. Other species of interest recorded here include the imperial anemone Capnea sanguinea and the Bryer’s nut crab Ebalia tumefacta.

sites.name: Cape Cornwall Bank
sites.hazards: Strong currents exceeding 1 knot at depth; current shear at around 15m. Grainy visibility due to spring bloom. Remote offshore location, 15 miles from Hayle.
sites.notes:
An offshore granite reef bank 6 miles from Cape Cornwall, rising to 25m from a 40m seabed. A challenging drift dive with strong currents, featuring ledges of fractured granite split by gullies of sand, with good marine life coverage.

The seabed consists of ledges of fractured granite between 30 and 36m, split by gullies of sand and the odd higher block of rock. Visibility was a grainy 6-7m on the visit. The bottom current was well over 1 knot and stronger than a diver can swim against. Diving strategy involved working from shelter to shelter without losing too much ground to the current. A no-stop dive. A delayed SMB is recommended. There is a shear in the current at around 15m. Best suited to small groups — with more than one pair of divers, surface cover from a RIB would be impossible. Accessed from Hayle, drifted on the ebb tide.

Biodiversity: Marine life consists of clumps of hydroids and dead men's fingers, small patches of jewel anemones and plenty of ross coral (a bryozoan). Perhaps a healthy 50% coverage, with bare granite showing through in places.

Tides: Drifted on the ebb tide. Current at the surface appeared to be just 1 knot with no signs of overfalls, but bottom current was faster. There is a shear in the current of perhaps 45° at around 15m.

sites.name: Dalky Sound
sites.notes:
A convenient evening shore dive for anyone living in the Dublin Area.

Accessed thorough Dillons Park just south of Dalky village. Park on the road, unpack and head straight down towards the shore -  easiest access point is in front of the houses to the left of the park (facing the sea). Enter the water on here, keep close to the shore as currents in the sound can quickly catch out an unsuspecting diver. Access / exit is not easy here, a lot of slippery rocks to negotiate is easiest at high tide. This is a popular spot for fishing so bring a knife in case you get tangled up -  The dive bottoms out at about 10 to 12 m on a sandy seabed – expect visibility of 5 to 10 meters in good conditions.

sites.name: Plymouth Sound Drop Off
sites.notes:
Plymouth Sound Drop Off is a dive site located a couple of miles off the coast of Plymouth, featuring a diverse underwater landscape with dense forests of sea fans, cliffs up to 4 meters high, large boulders housing congers, and a variety of marine life including sunset corals, sea squirts, and anemones. The seabed at this site drops suddenly between 30 and 40 meters to reveal a 5-10 meter wall and boulder slope, making it suitable for experienced divers due to depths exceeding 40 meters. The site showcases the submerged cliff line where the sea once reached over 10,000 years ago.

The submerged cliff line off Plymouth Sound is just that, where the sea came to over 10,000 years ago. Dive anywhere along the 30m depth contour and you find it. But depths can be well in excess of 40m, so not for novices.

Plymouth Sound Dive club usually drives the RIB over the cliff line, turns back towards Plymouth and drops a shot when just inshore of the slope. You will be amazed at the dense forests of sea fans at the top of the cliff but don’t idle there, go south over cliffs up to 4 m high standing out like buttresses guarding the canyons leading back inshore.

At the base of the cliff are large boulders providing homes for congers but sparsely colonised by attached marine life especially when compared with the gaudy and bizarre species attached to the cliffs. Here be spectacular scenery, nationally rare sunset corals, football sea squirts, yellow and white cluster anemones and all sorts else.

Biodiversity: Toward the Western end the depth slopes quite steeply between 30 and 40m over a boulder field which harbours some of the largest Conger Eels and Lobster. On the top 30m plain there is a variety and density of fan corals and soft sponges.

Tides: This site has excellent visibility and can be dived in all states of the tide. This is an excellent slow drift with minimal energy expended.

History: The same tectonic plate movement which threw up the Mewstone seems to have created this drop off with the shifting of the plates.

This is an exhilerating dive but as a rule of thumb, is only open to BSAC Advanced Divers or above with experience of drift diving.

Tides: The Jack Sound Drift is diveable 4h after HW (6h after HW Milford Haven) but is dependant on little wind from any direction.

sites.name: Holmes of Uyea Sound
sites.notes: The dive of the day was on the Holmes of Uyea Sound, which I was hoping would be sheltered, and this proved to be the case. The site was excellent as we dropped down the cliff wall through a shoal of encircling saithe. A mid-water guillemot darted past, followed by a gliding thornback ray on the seabed. Incredible, all in just five minutes. It was such a good dive with so many choices. As you headed out of one gully, there were two more! At the end of the dive, an octopus made an appearance, which is always good to finish on a high.

sites.name: John Connel Sound
sites.notes:
The John Connel Sound is a drift dive along a remote but stunning wall. The wall is alive with all manner of creatures including dead man's fingers, anemones, lobsters, squat lobsters, and edible crabs living in the cracks. Fishlife includes wrasse, ling and potentially even John Dory. A rocky pinnacle emerges from the sea above the northern wall. Both walls extend down to 40m.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide.
