sites.name: Shuna Island Sound
sites.hazards: Very silty bottom that is easily disturbed, reducing visibility. Visibility is poor further down, better near the surface.
sites.notes:
Shuna Island Sound is a scenic shore dive with easy access for dive training. Divers can enter the site from a layby, walk down a concrete path over rocks into the water, and exit conveniently near the car park. The dive involves a gentle descent to 15m, offering encounters with sea pens, Thorny skates, Gobis, and various marine life. The site features interesting artifacts such as old bottles and shipwreck timber, with an electrical cable visible underwater. Suitable for trainees, the site provides an opportunity for an enjoyable dive experience.

A muck dive in the Sound of Shuna, off the island of Shuna in Scotland, undertaken to find all three British sea pen species (slender, phosphorescent, and tall) in a single dive. The site features a silty, soft bottom at 15–17 metres and is a sheltered sound accessible as a shore or boat dive.

The site is located just off the island of Shuna in the Sound of Shuna. It is a very silty, soft-bottom muck dive site. Sea pens are found at around 15–17 metres depth. Visibility is not the best, particularly closer to the bottom — better nearer the surface. The silty bottom is easily disturbed, making buoyancy control important. The dive described was 15 minutes at 17 metres. Sea pens are found here at shallower depths than typical — normally you have to go to 30+ metres to find them.

sites.name: Shamrock Pinnacle
sites.hazards:
Very strong tides that can easilly sweep divers off the pinnacle if the dive is mistimed.

 Small pinnacle with steep walls on all sides – divers must have delayed surface marker buoys and other signalling equipment. 

Vigilant boat cover required as tide likely to be running when divers are ascending. 

Divers should be comfortable with free ascents and doing safety/deco stops while drifting. 

The pinnacle should be shotted prior to the dive to ensure that the desired depth is obtained, to check the tidal flow and to provide a reference point for divers.
sites.notes:
Shamrock Pinnacle is one of a series of submerged pinnacles lying between Scotland and Northern Ireland. It is approximately 10km north-west of Rathlin Island. The minimum depth of the pinnacle is 15 m below chart datum (BCD) with the majority being deeper than 30 m. The north side of the pinnacle is a sheer wall which drops to over 140 m, the south and east faces slopes more gradually to around 75 m before a similarly sheer wall. The pinnacle is situated in the full flow of the North Channel tidal stream, experiencing up to 3 knots of tidal current on spring tides. At the position given (on the north-west corner) there is a small stack which is covered in plumose anemones. Information about diving around Shamrock Pinnacle is available from the Shamrock Pinnacle Survey Report 2009-2011

Biodiversity: The bedrock of the pinnacle is strongly tide-swept. It is dominated by hardy species such as the oaten pipe hydroid Tubularia indivisa, dead men’s fingers Alcyonium digitatum, and the elephant hide sponge Pachymatisma johnstonia. Species of particular interest include the sea squirt Synoicum incrustatum and the white cluster anemone Parazoanthus anguicomus

Tides: Strong

HW or LW Slack (15-20 minute window eitherside of both)

sites.name: Pete's Pinnacle
sites.hazards: Currents can be very strong around this site; it should be dived during or just before slack water. Do not swim to the north of the pinnacle as the boat will not be able to see you.
sites.notes:
Pete's Pinnacle is a scenic dive site near Lundy featuring impressive vertical rock faces and a boulder field, with depths ranging from 12 to 30m. The site also has two historical boilers lying on the slope, making it an interesting mix of natural and wreck features. Strong currents make timing critical.

Start at the given coordinates (51 11.94'N, 04 40.20'W) and swim down the slope to the east to find a boiler at around 18m — if not found, head slightly north. From there, swim east-north-east to locate a second boiler at around 25m. The pinnacle itself is approximately at 51°11'59.9″N 4°40'09.8″W, and features impressive vertical faces. A boulder field lies below the pinnacle at about 30m, with the base of the pinnacle at around 25m. It is recommended not to swim to the north of the pinnacle.

Tides: Slack time is LW-2 to LW+2.

sites.name: Mewstone Ledges
sites.location: South Hams, Devon, South West, England
sites.notes:
Mewstone Ledges is a dive site located a ten-minute RIB ride south of Plymouth Sound. The site features gradual depths ranging from 15-30m, making it ideal for divers with depth restrictions. The area is characterized by fingers of rock stretching into gullies of light-colored sand, providing a scenic backdrop for underwater photography. Marine life such as Dogfish, Pollock, Spider crab, and Lobster can be observed in the area's rocky gullies, offering a diverse diving experience. The site generally has good visibility due to its predominantly rock-based terrain.

A ten-minute RIB ride south from Plymouth Sound’s breakwater, the Mewstone is an island that was once joined to the nearby shore. It’s now an isolated and impressive sight as it rises high above the surface of the water. No less impressive below, the Mewstone slopes 15-30m in places.

The site is great for scenic dives and especially for divers with a depth restriction shallower than 30m including for upping the experience levels of novices. The gradual increase in depth means it’s easy to have a controlled environment in which to further a diver’s exposure to depth. With fingers of rock stretching out into gullies of light coloured sand combined with prolific marine life, the Mewstone makes an ideal spot for the underwater photographer.

Mewstone Ledges are a favorite for Plymouth Sound Dive Club evening dives or when it gets a bit choppy and a trip much further down the coast could lead to green faces.

Biodiversity: Around the 20-25m mark there are some lovely deep gullies full of Urchins and the occasional Monkfish. The area supports a variety of marine life including Dogfish, Pollock, Bull-Huss (Like large Dogfish) Spider crab and Lobster.

Tides: 3Hrs after HW Devonport

History: In 1744, a local man who had committed a minor crime was sentenced to live on the island for seven years. His daughter later chose to stay, married, and raised a family there. The remains of a house can still be seen in the rocks.

sites.name: Low Lee Ledges
sites.notes:
Low Lee Ledges is a dive site in Penzance, located 3km south of the town and approximately 1.3km Northeast of Mousehole. The reef, adopted by Penzance BSAC, features a nature trail with a guide rope encircling the area. Divers can explore the remains of the SS Primrose wreck, including the collapsed bow still home to sizable shoals of bib, an iron cannon of unknown origin, and what remains of the stern. The site is suitable for divers of most experience levels, with the base of the reef at around 20m depth.

A small reef 3km south of Penzance and about 1.3km Northeast of Mousehole. A very scenic dive with both wreck and reef in a sheltered position. Suitable for most levels of experience as the base of the reef is in about 20m.

The reef has been adopted by Penzance BSAC and made into a nature trail with a guide rope circling the reef. The trail is buoyed and the line takes you down onto the bow of the SS Primrose, which unfortunately collapsed last winter but is still home to sizable shoals of bib.

Following the line from the Eastern side of the bows you leave the wreck and move onto the reef, look out for a line off to the right which is a short circular route back to the bows.

There is also a line off to the left that takes you to an iron cannon of unknown origin. Back on the main line if you follow this to the other end of the reef you can find what remains of the stern of the primrose. Follow the line back to your starting position.

Biodiversity: There was plenty of life with lots
of ballan wrasse, cuckoo wrasse, rock cooks and spider crabs. The
shallower rocks had kelp on them, but were covered in dead man's
fingers deeper.

History: There was a small wreck at the bottom
which was the SS Primrose which sank in 1906.

sites.name: Triple Reef
sites.alternativeNames: Twin Reef, The Ledges, South Gortein, South Gortein(Triple Ter. Reef)
sites.hazards: Entry and exit climbing up and down the rocks
sites.notes:
Triple reef on Loch Fyne is a shore great dive on three reefs.

Follow the path down onto the rocks be careful climbing down the rocks as it can be slippy. Entry and exit can be made difficult at low tide and if there is a bit of a swell.

The first reef lies directly off of the shore and drops down to about 12m. The second reef lies slightly further north and runs from 15-25m. The third reef lies about 35m and is quite featureless. The best life is found on the top reef.

Biodiversity: Scallops (including large ones), velvet swimming crab, squat lobsters, leopard spotted goby, edible crab, sea urchins, spider crab, nudibranch (Limacia clavigera), highland dancer (sea slug/nudibranch), prawns, conger eel, corkwing wrasse, tadpole fish (occasionally), cod, pollack, dead man's fingers, anemones, buccinum (whelk) eggs.

Tides: Any state of the tide

sites.name: Shoal Ground Drop Off
sites.location: South Hams, Devon, South West, England
sites.notes:
This can be an exciting dive but good supporting boat cover is important. As the name suggests, the Shoal Ground attracts surges of water depending on tide, wind and weather. It is an extensive mound of rock that rises up from over 44m to 22m. On the east side of the mound there is an impressive drop off that is coated with colourful squidgies.

A good dive plan is to drop a shot on the eastern edge of drop off in 45m and get divers to dive on the moving ebb and drift over to the Shoal Ground. This way they can dive the drop off in the best way.

sites.name: SS Snowdrop
sites.notes:
The SS Snowdrop is a 685-tonne steamship lost in December 1886 with all 14 crew, found 20 miles south-east of Portland Bill in 57m. The wreck is broken but retains many recognisable features including boiler, compound engine, rudder, propeller shaft, and bow fittings, and is home to abundant marine life.

The dive typically begins on the high point of the boiler. A distinctive steam collection device rises about a metre above the single boiler. Moving aft leads to a two-cylinder compound engine roughly as large as the boiler, with congers and crabs among the con rods. Following the propeller shaft reveals plates, winches, and derricks typical of a late-1800s coaster. At the stern, the rudder stands proud and a massive secondary steering position lies to starboard. Two of the four propeller blades are buried in the sand. Swimming back forward, past the engine and boiler, you pass over the broken bridge area — the bell has been recovered but the area is worth investigating. The bow is very broken; its presence is indicated by an upturned winch, two piles of chain, two hawse pipes protruding from the sand, and one anchor visible on careful inspection.

Biodiversity: Shoals of bib are commonly found around the boiler. Congers and crabs live among the engine con rods and other engineering.

History: The SS Snowdrop was a 685-tonne steamship that departed the River Tyne with a cargo of coal and was last seen passing Dover on 6 December 1886, en route for Kingston, southern Ireland. She was lost with all 14 crew, probably overwhelmed by severe weather. The wreck was eventually found in 57m, about 20 miles south-east of Portland Bill.

sites.name: South Gare (The Training Ground)
sites.location: Redcar and Cleveland, North East, England
sites.notes:
South Gare, known locally as 'The Training Ground' by Teesside BSAC (Club 43), is a shore dive site near Redcar, Teesside, featuring a concrete pier and submerged timber structures with a blue guide rope, making it well-suited for beginner and training dives.

Known locally as 'The Training Ground' (Teesside BSAC 43). There is a gated slipway, and a short distance to the east a concrete pier which has seen better days. A blue rope runs from the end of the pier to some offshore timbers, presumably once part of an extended pier structure. The rope then continues in a loop around the timbers providing a route to follow. Options for getting to the rope include: swimming along the shore to the end of the concrete pier and then following the rope out to the timbers, or taking a bearing from the slipway and going direct to the timbers and picking up the rope. A depth of 6 metres was reached around the timbers. Visibility was not great, which was thought to be largely due to a falling tide. The site is well suited to training and beginner dives.

Biodiversity: Several species of crab, numerous lobsters, a scorpion fish, and a small cuttlefish were observed around the timbers.

Tides: Visibility was not great, largely attributed to a falling tide. Early in the day a depth of 6 metres was reached around the timbers.

sites.name: St Chamond
sites.hazards: Strong tidal currents due to a large tidal range. The site is exposed to a heavy Atlantic groundswell. The harbour entrance at Hayle is tidal and involves a sandbar that can be hazardous, particularly when returning through breaking surf.
sites.notes:
The St Chamond, also known as the Train Wreck, is a French cargo steamer sunk by a German U-boat in 1918 approximately 1.5 miles off St Ives on Cornwall's north coast. The wreck lies at depths of around 20–24m, with the hull largely flattened across a pebble seabed. Its most distinctive feature is its cargo of steam locomotives — at least six, each weighing around 82 tons — which remain scattered across the site, some upright and some on their sides, alongside steel pipes, wheel tyres, pipe couplings, and the remains of the ship's propulsion machinery.

The St Chamond is a WWI wreck lying off Cornwall's north coast, around 1.5 miles from St Ives, at a depth of 20–24m. The wreck is famous for its extraordinary cargo of steam locomotives — at least six, possibly seven — still visible on the seabed, making it a uniquely compelling dive for history enthusiasts and wreck divers alike.

The wreck lies with its bows pointing north-west on a seabed of pebbles with low ridges of rock. The highest points are the locomotive boilers, rising just a couple of metres above the seabed. The hull is largely flattened, with just a few scraps rising upward. The shallowest section, around 20m at low water, is at the bow end; the stern lies in approximately 24m.

Descending on the shotline, you are likely to land on the first locomotive, which lies on its left side with the shotline draped over it. Each loco has four large driving wheels per side and two pairs of smaller wheels forward of the drive wheels. Nearby, the main hull section contains cargo including steel hoop wheel tyres and pipe couplings. Steel pipe in clusters is found throughout the wreck.

Moving towards the centre, the propeller shaft lies exposed — apparently shifted slightly off the centreline to port — with only a few curved steel ribs remaining of the shaft tunnel. The remains of a triple-expansion steam engine are spread to starboard from the crank. Further forward along the centreline is a large pile of steel pipes. To port lies a second locomotive on its side, within the hull outline.

One of the ship's two boilers stands upright just off the port side; the other is not visible. The bow is marked by a pile of anchor chain and a pair of anchors still in their hawse-pipes. The anchor winch has fallen forward a few metres off the bow tip, slightly to starboard.

On the starboard side heading aft, a large puzzling steel dome can be found, possibly cargo. A pair of locos follows: one with its chassis upright but the boiler entirely gone, and a second resting on its side. A reported third loco may be hidden behind these or may have shifted. Further aft is a small pile of steel pipe, then a fifth locomotive pointing aft and tipped just outside the hull outline. Alongside it on the centreline are a pair of broken winches. A sixth loco lies a little further aft in a similar orientation. The wreck then fizzles out with another small pipe pile, and scattered wreckage continues across the pebble seabed.

The stern is well off to starboard: a section of propeller shaft projects from a small V-section of keel, leading to a steel propeller partly buried in the seabed, with the remains of the rudder just aft.

Tides: There is a big tidal range along this coastline, resulting in strong currents. Slack water occurs at high water and low water Hayle. The site is also exposed to a significant Atlantic groundswell. The harbour at Hayle is tidal, inaccessible for a couple of hours either side of low water, which restricts departure and return times.

History: The St Chamond was a 3,077-ton French steamer, 94m in length. In late April 1918, she was loaded at Glasgow with five 75-ton British steam locomotives as deck cargo, destined for St Nazaire to support the Allied war effort on the Western Front. The locomotives were intended to supplement the overstretched French railway network, which could not cope with the volume of supplies required for the planned summer 1918 offensive. On 30 April 1918, while within a mile of Cornwall's north coast near St Ives, she was torpedoed by U-60, commanded by Oberleutnant Schuster — his 41st confirmed sinking. Capitaine Doln and his crew abandoned ship without loss.

Further aft is a small pile of steel pipe, then a fifth locomotive pointing aft and tipped just outside the hull outline. Alongside it on the centreline are a pair of broken winches. A sixth loco lies a little further aft in a similar orientation. The wreck then fizzles out with another small pipe pile, and scattered wreckage continues across the pebble seabed.

The stern is well off to starboard: a section of propeller shaft projects from a small V-section of keel, leading to a steel propeller partly buried in the seabed, with the remains of the rudder just aft.
sites.tides: There is a big tidal range along this coastline, resulting in strong currents. Slack water occurs at high water and low water Hayle. The site is also exposed to a significant Atlantic groundswell. The harbour at Hayle is tidal, inaccessible for a couple of hours either side of low water, which restricts departure and return times.
sites.history: The St Chamond was a 3,077-ton French steamer, 94m in length. In late April 1918, she was loaded at Glasgow with five 75-ton British steam locomotives as deck cargo, destined for St Nazaire to support the Allied war effort on the Western Front. The locomotives were intended to supplement the overstretched French railway network, which could not cope with the volume of supplies required for the planned summer 1918 offensive. On 30 April 1918, while within a mile of Cornwall's north coast near St Ives, she was torpedoed by U-60, commanded by Oberleutnant Schuster — his 41st confirmed sinking. Capitaine Doln and his crew abandoned ship without loss.

sites.name: Trail Island
sites.hazards: Strong tidal current — unexpectedly strong current made swimming very difficult, with the diver unable to make headway and at risk of being swept past the island. Lifting off the bottom results in being caught by the tide. Divers should plan carefully for return to the boat.
sites.notes:
Wrasse a few crabs, evil-looking jellyfish as well as the possibility to see seals while many gulls cormorants watch snorkellers while sunning themselves on the rocky outcrops.

Wall dive to about 50m. There are shelves at many different depths on this dive - just pick your depth and go explore.

Biodiversity: Cuckoo wrasse, Ballan wrasse, pollack, velvet swimming crab, Devonshire cup coral, moon jellies (jellyfish in crevices of rocks resembling anemones), and abundant fish life generally noted. Kelp present on the reef.

Tides: Strong unexpected current was present during this dive, making swimming difficult and forcing an early exit. The current whips over the top of the reef and picks divers up as soon as they lift off the bottom. The tide was also dropping during the surface interval, causing concern about relaunching the boat from the slip.

sites.name: Highball Bouncing Bombs
sites.alternativeNames: High Ball Trail, The Bouncing Bombs
sites.hazards: Very poor visibility on Day 1 required circular search patterns to locate features. The side charge was approached with caution as it had never been confirmed as inert ("Live" status uncertain). Significant depth requiring decompression stops.
sites.notes:
An underwater museum dive site in Loch Striven featuring Highball Bouncing Bombs from WWII testing. These spherical bombs, designed by Barnes Wallis for use against the Tirpitz, were tested by de Havilland Mosquitoes but never used in combat. The bombs on the seabed are filled with concrete and cork, not live explosives. The dive includes a large anchor at 30m and a chain leading to the bomb locations.

The dive begins by descending a shot line to a large anchor at around 30 metres (origin unknown). Divers swim along a chain to locate the Highball bombs. The depth increases to around 36 metres at the bomb cluster. Visibility is 2-3 metres in dark conditions with green but light coloured water at shallower depths (4-5 metre visibility), darkening around 20 metres. The bottom is very silty requiring perfect trim to avoid disturbing sediment when photographing. The bombs have a fine layer of silt on them.

Biodiversity: Soft corals, squat lobsters, Queen scallops and crabs.

Tides: Best time to dive is April as the waters do not get that cold over winter and April is out of the windy winter with cleaner visibility.

History: The Highball Bouncing Bombs were less famous than the cylindrical "Upkeep" Bouncing Bombs used to destroy German hydro-electric dams (made famous by the Dam Busters film). The spherical Highball bombs were developed as an RAF weapon for use against the Tirpitz, anchored in Norwegian Fjords. While Upkeep bombs were deployed by larger Wellington Bombers, the Highball bombs were deployed by smaller de Havilland Mosquitos. The Highballs were never used in anger. The bombs in Loch Striven are not live, filled with concrete and cork. In recent years, divers recovered two bombs which are now on display at the Brooklands Museum in Surrey (home to a collection of Barnes Wallis artifacts) and the de Havilland Aircraft Museum in Hertfordshire.

sites.name: Eccleston Delph
sites.notes:
Eccleston Delph, also known as Eccleston Quarry, is a dive site located in Lancashire, a mile south of Eccleston. The site offers various entry and exit points, including shore entry with concrete slipways and steel deep entry points with steps. Divers can explore a range of underwater attractions including speedboats, tanks, containers, training platforms, and a gnome garden. The site is well stocked with a variety of fish, including koi carp. Visibility is typically poor, and ropes have been installed to aid navigation. Much effort has been made to improve visibility in recent years.

Eccleston Quarry is a mile south of Eccleston, Lancashire. It is also called Eccleston Delph and Eccy Delph (pronounced "ekky"). It is an old stone quarry that flooded. It is a popular site for scuba diving. Visibility is generally very poor and ropes have been strung between each underwater 'feature' to aid navigation, since traditional compass methods are all but impossible in the murky waters. Much work has been undertaken to improve visibility in the recent past, and by 2010 the visibility was much improved.

There are many entry and exit points including shore entry with concrete slipways, sturdy steel deep entry points with fin friendly steps. Most have railings with chain linkages.

There are many things for divers to explore including speedboats, a Jet Provost, armoured personnel carriers, a light tank, containers, a concrete tube, and a gnome garden, and a playground. As well as these there are training platforms at various depths from 3m to 9m. All are marked by surface buoys.

The Delph is well stocked with a large variety of fish including koi carp: bags of food can be bought to feed the fish. Angling is not allowed there.

History: Eccleston Delph has been known as the Eccy Delph, or Hurst House Delph for the last century, and was mined by 12 local quarrymen producing stone for Blackpool Promenade and thin slates to cover the local barns and roofs.

Contact: 01257 450663

sites.hazards: Chesil Beach can be challenging (and at times, dangerous) to get in and out of if there are waves breaking onto the beach. As a rule anything over a Force 3 blowing from the West or South West should prohibit diving here. For safety, this site should really only be dived on Easterly winds whereby the water usually remains calm. Check the daily conditions here Facebook On the wreck itself the main hazard is fishing line. ALWAYS carry at least one cutting tool.
sites.notes:
The Landing Craft site is a WW2 wreck located on a pebble beach. Divers can easily access the wreck by following specific directions from the beach. The site is the remains of a large landing craft, measuring 114 x 32 ft and displacing 285 tons. The wreck, originally known as LCT 454, holds historical significance as it was leased to the UK and then back to the Americans for D-Day. A dive at this site offers the opportunity to explore a piece of military history from World War II.

Originally known as LCT 454, this Mk5 Landing Craft was launched in New Jersey in September 1942 and leased to the UK in November and renumbered as 2454. It seems we then added some additional armour plating and leased it back to the Americans for D-Day!

She is a large landing craft, measuring 114 x 32 ft and displacing 285 tons - with the capability if carrying a further 150 tons.

After kitting up, walk to the top of the pebble beach. Turn around and line up all the concrete blocks into a straight line. From this point walk in a Northerly direction approximately twenty-five paces, then face the sea. Walk directly to the shoreline from this point.

After entering the water swim straight out over the pebble terraces to a depth of 12-14 metres. In good visibility, it should not take long to locate the wreckage. In lesser conditions, a short search either North or South should reveal her remains, but do make sure not to go below 15 metres, as this will probably be too far beyond the wreck.

sites.name: Doris Mor
sites.notes:
Doris Mor is likely be a drift dive, whatever state of tide it is dived at. Divers will enter at either the north or eastern side of the wall depending on which way the tide is running. As they enter the drift, they will be carried around the northeast corner to finish on the other side to where they started. There is lots of kelp in the shallows, but divers can pick their depth down to a maximum of 45m where there is a rocky seabed. Look out for elephants ear sponges.

Tides: Slack water only due to whirlpools and strong tides.

sites.notes:
The Kendal Castle is a steamship wreck sunk in 1918 after being torpedoed. The vessel lies upright with a broken open bow, featuring a 2 metre scour on the west side and covered with old fishing nets.

The vessel lies upright with the bow broken open. There is a 2 metres scour on the west side of the ship. Lots of old fishing nets are present on this wreck. In the vicinity of this vessel are three other wrecks: the Dudley Rose, the Bleamore and the Beustan.

History: The Kendal Castle was torpedoed killing all crew. The vessel was part of the James Chambers Line. Pottery has been recovered from it, which provided the identity of the wreck.

sites.name: Lady Alice Kenlis
sites.notes: History: The hulk of the Lady Alice Kenlis lies on the east bank of the River Deben, opposite Woodbridge. It comprises the remains of a 38m long iron vessel designed by Hercules Linton and launched in 1867. The vessel served as a cargo ship for 46 years before being converted to a steam dredger. It went on to function as a dredger in Bristol and Suffolk for a further 19 years before being deregistered and partially scrapped in the 1930s. The hulk has lain in its present position since the late 1930s or early 1940s.

sites.name: Sheringham Chalk Gullies
sites.alternativeNames: Norfolk's Great Chalk Reef, Chalk Gullies
sites.hazards: Vis here is very weather dependent, and can drop to zero immediately after onshore winds, but remaining clear into the Autumn if SW winds continue.
sites.notes:
Sheringham Chalk Gullies is a unique shore dive site located in Norfolk, UK. Accessible from the Esplanade or Cliff Lane car parks, divers can enjoy an easy entry-exit by walking down the beach straight out from the shore. The main reef, known as the Cromer Shoals Chalk Bed, is just 400m offshore and stretches over 20 miles, making it the longest chalk reef in the world. This diverse marine landscape creates a habitat for a wide array of sea life, including sponges, anemones, starfish, and unique species like the Atlantic ancula sea slug and the blush-red strawberry anemone. The reef has been designated as a Marine Conservation Zone to protect its valuable ecosystem.

Dubbed ‘Britain’s Great Barrier Reef’ the Cromer Shoals Chalk Bed, created when dinosaurs ruled the earth, has been found to be the longest in the world – and it’s so close to the shore you could skim a stone out to it.

At over 20 miles long, the 100-million-year-old reef is one-and-a-half times longer than the Thanet Coast chalk reef in Kent, the former record holder.

Discovered less than ten years ago, the reef is just 25ft under the sea’s surface and has now been made a Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ) by the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs. With an area of 315sq km it’s larger than the Broads National Park.

And it's part of the chalk seam that stretches across England and includes the White Cliffs of Dover and the White Horse Hill Carvings in Wiltshire.

The reef, with dramatic features such as towering arches and deep chasms made during the Ice Age, has one of the most diverse and spectacular arrays of sea life around Britain – the composition of the reef meaning the water is actually quite warm.

The bed of the North Sea is mostly soft sand and mud, so the hard rocky chalk features create a habitat that attracts all kinds of life.

The marine haven has many species, including sponges, burrowing piddocks, sea squirts, anemones, starfish, brittlestars and fish including shoaling horse mackerel and bass. Three species never before recorded on the east coast have been found: the Atlantic ancula sea slug, the blush-red strawberry anemone and leopard spotted goby.

The MCZ means that sea life will now be protected, such as the Little Cuttlefish which can change colour for camouflage, including to metallic gold when it hides in the sand, along with hundreds of species including crabs and lobsters that colonise the soft chalk beds.

So now you know why Norfolk has the tastiest, most succulent crab and lobster you’ll find in the UK – they have a very special habitat to feed on.

Easy entry-exit walking down the beach straight out from the Esplanade or Cliff Lane car parks.

Surface swim straight out from the beach at the breakwater about 40m drop down and head north-west. The main reef is 400m out from the beach. Return to the same place to exit or straight to the shore and walk back to the esplanade or cliff lane.

Biodiversity: Life in and around the gullies is prolific, at depths of 4-8Mtrs there is plenty of time to take in all that is on offer.

Tides: This is a dive that is best undertaken on a drift between slacks.

sites.name: Wishing Well
sites.notes:
The wishing well is a good shore dive on the Isle of Cumbrae great for small groups of divers.

You can also dive Clashfarland point near here.

Entry in at the left-hand side facing the sea and there is a cleared pathway into the rocks.

You can go right which is mainly sand and rubble and depths of anywhere up to 30mtrs. If diving to the left work your way down to about 8 meters and then fin over 500 yards, at a depth of around 8-10 meters there are some nice rocks formations holding crab, squat lobster, wrasses, lobster and around that rocky area and down to about 12 meters the Rocks continue. Passed 12 meters it more sandy/silt and the chance of squat lobsters and gurnard.

sites.name: Cantabria
sites.location: South Hams, Devon, South West, England
sites.notes:
The Cantabria is a Spanish freighter that ran aground in Steeple Cove, between Bolt Tail and Bolt Head on the Devon coast, in December 1932. Despite lying in only 35 feet of water, it is considered a remarkably impressive and underrated wreck site with a great deal to explore, including boilers, decking, a propeller, and scattered debris among dramatic pinnacle rocks.

The wreck lies at the foot of the pinnacle rocks at the base of Steeple Cove's cliffs, mostly where the Cantabria originally ran aground. The underwater rocks have broad flat bases that gently slope down to sand. The boilers, still reasonably intact, lie surrounded by rusty iron plates and broken guard-rail sections. Up on a rocky plateau sits the iron propeller, alongside a large section of decking stretching across the rocks; beneath the decking is a large debris field worth exploring, as small brass fittings such as porthole fasteners can occasionally be found. Lying across the decking, supported by another rock, are the remains of the propeller shaft, which leads over to the other side of the rocks where smaller amounts of wreckage are scattered. Much of the decking is likely the main deck and the one below compressed together; in places, holes reveal an interior going down four or five feet. A few yards from the boilers lies one of the Cantabria's anchors with chain attached. Swimming toward the other end of Steeple Cove, more small wreckage and anchor chain can be found among the jumble of rocks at the cliff base. The maximum depth is 35 feet.

sites.name: Markethill Scuba
sites.hazards: At approximately 18m depth and below, visibility drops to practically zero. Hood and gloves are strongly recommended due to very low water temperatures at depth. Distinct thermoclines are present at all times.
sites.notes:
Markethill Scuba is a disused flooded freshwater quarry located on the Coolmillish Rd, County Armagh. It offers 6-7 metres visibility and is ideal for keeping skills sharp over winter, testing new equipment, training, or recreational diving with no tidal constraints.

Entry is either by walk-in or giant stride. Divers can follow the road around and down or drop over the sheer sides to their desired depth. The terrain transitions from large spongy grass areas to white sandy sunken beaches to boulders to shear drops and overhangs. Visibility is 6-7 metres. Water temperature at depth is very low — hood and gloves are highly recommended. Distinct thermoclines are visible at all times. With no tides, diving can be arranged to suit any schedule. Ideal for skills practice, training, testing new equipment, or recreational diving. No need to wash gear afterwards as it is a freshwater site.

Biodiversity: Large amounts of perch and bream. Crayfish have also been spotted.

Tides: Freshwater quarry with no tides — diving can take place at any time that suits the group.

sites.name: Lancaster Bomber ED450
sites.notes:
The wreck site of the Lancaster Bomber ED450 is located at the base of the Plymouth Breakwater in about forty-five feet of water. Discovered in 1975, the scattered remains of the bomber include two engines and some sections of the wing. The wreckage can be easily spotted just off the sandy bottom amidst the boulders and concrete blocks that make up the breakwater. The site serves as a grim reminder of Britain's battle for survival during World War II, with the bomber being a testament to the desperate days of the conflict.

Since the Plymouth Breakwater was built in 1830 a great many ships have come to grief along it’s mile-long expanse of stone and concrete. Ships and breakwaters seem to go together, but aeroplanes? Well hardly. However, at the west end of the Plymouth Breakwater lies the remains of a Lancaster bomber. How it came to be there is a grim reminder of those desperate days when Britain was engaged in a battle for her very survival, a survival that meant the destruction of the German U-boats. By 1943 the U-boat had almost brought Britain to her knees, and despite fifty-six bombing raids, Lorient, one of the most important submarine bases in Europe was still functioning.

Today the Lancaster, or rather what’s left of it, lies at the base of the Breakwater in about forty-five feet of water. This area is made up of huge boulders and concrete blocks piled one on top of the other until they reach the surface. The division between these blocks and the sandy bottom is quite distinct, and the wreckage, situated just off the sand is quite easy to spot even if you are not right on the marks.

History: On the night of 13th February 1943 a huge bombing raid was again due to take place on Lorient. Amongst all the bombers, which also included Halifaxes and Stirlings, was a Lancaster of 49 Squadron based at Fiskerton. The bombers attacked in two waves, and this time they caused such an enormous amount of destruction that the glow from the fires could be seen 160 miles away. Later reports confirmed the devastation and described the target area as a complete mass of flames. The price of success, however, was dearly bought, and amongst many others our particular Lancaster was severely damaged. Struggling across the dark sea, the pilot was desperately trying to make an emergency landing at R.A.F. Harrowbeer (just outside Plymouth). Unfortunately the Lancaster kept losing height and the pilot must have known that he would never make it.

In a last brave attempt the pilot tried to crash land in Plymouth Sound, but by now the plane must have been completely uncontrollable, and far to low. Falling from the sky, the Lancaster hit the Breakwater and completely disintegrated killing all seven crew outright; Their bodies were never recovered, and the official account of 49 Squadron recorded them as being “missing without trace”.
sites.description: Since the Plymouth Breakwater was built in 1830 a great many ships have come to grief along it’s mile-long expanse of stone and concrete. Ships and breakwaters seem to go together, but aeroplanes? Well hardly. However, at the west end of the Plymouth Breakwater lies the remains of a Lancaster bomber. How it came to be there is a grim reminder of those desperate days when Britain was engaged in a battle for her very survival, a survival that meant the destruction of the German U-boats. By 1943 the U-boat had almost brought Britain to her knees, and despite fifty-six bombing raids, Lorient, one of the most important submarine bases in Europe was still functioning.

sites.name: Duke of Northumberland
sites.notes:
Not much remains of this wreck today. She lies in just over 50m on a muddy seabed, orientated 130/210. Only machinery and a vertical boiler remain. Much of the hull is probably buried in the mud.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide.

History: The Duke of Northumberland was a wooden paddle tug built by C Chisholm, Shields, and launched in 1856. She sank on 18th May 1858 after a collision with the SS Thistle in the early hours of the morning. The SS Thistle circled for over an hour to pick up any survivors, but saw none. This was because the crew of the Duke of Northumberland had made a quick escape in their boat, landing at Millport some 90 minutes later.

sites.name: North Landing
sites.location: East Riding of Yorkshire, Yorkshire and the Humber, England
sites.hazards: Currents at the head of the bay. Take care leaving the water if there is a swell, it's easy to get knocked over.
sites.notes:
Shore Dive in a sheltered sandy bay with rocky outcrops and the remains of the SS Rosa a steam lighter which sank in 1930.

There is a hand-painted sign saying no diving but this was put up without permission and should be ignored. confirmed by Scarborough Borough Council. Best to dive if it hasn't rained for a few days beforehand or there have not been any heavy winds because the swell picks up. Also if you are night diving you can reverse your car down to the top of the slipway and drop your kit off, remember to park it back in the car park.

The walk from the car park is not far but the steep steps are a bit of a test on the way back to the car park. Enter the water at the right of the bay in front of the disused lifeboat station and exit in the same place.

Keep to the right (facing the sea) and don't go past the head. A part of the SS Rosa's boiler can be seen at low water and other fragments of steel wreckage are visible on the rocks to the west side of North Landing

sites.name: King Kong Corner - Mingulay
sites.location: Na h-Eileanan an Iar, Scotland, Scotland
sites.notes:
This site, perhaps more appropriately to be called Twin Rocks Wall or Sloc Duhn an Duine, was named King King Corner by a group of divers who felt that the rocky headland looked exactly like King Kong's face.
 
At the south west tip of Mingulay, this site is very exposed to weather and swell, although tide does not affect it. The wall steps down to 35 metres where divers will find a boulder and rock bottom covered in life.

Tides: Whilst the site can be dived at any state of the tide, it can only be dived when there is very little swell due to the exposed location.

To find the Molesey, locate a vertical slit cave in the side of Midland Isle just south of the Crabstones. Enter the water about 10m south of the cave and swim out perpendicular to the shoreline. This should lead to the boilers at a depth of 10m. From the boat, seals can often be seen in the entrance to the cave and along the shore, but you are unlikely to see them underwater.

sites.name: Vandalia (Possibly)
sites.hazards: Strong tidal currents at depth, which can drag a grapple off the seabed and make navigation extremely difficult. Characteristically poor visibility throughout the water column, caused by high particulate load. The combination of 100m depth, strong currents, and poor visibility makes this a serious and challenging technical dive.
sites.notes:
The Vandalia (formerly the SS Anglo-Californian) is a large, largely uncharted deep wreck lying at around 100–107 metres off Pembroke in West Wales. The wreck is historically notable as the ship on which Captain Frederick Parslow won the Victoria Cross in WWI. It is believed to have been almost never dived before 2022. The site is demanding, with strong tidal currents and characteristically poor visibility, making it a serious technical diving challenge.

The wreck lies at around 100 metres depth off Pembroke. The site is large — approximately 7,000 tons — and quite broken up, with the structure presenting as a confusing, smashed-up mess of plates and ribs. The bow area is identifiable by a large winch and visible anchor flukes and chains. A notable engine is also present. Navigation at depth is difficult due to persistent poor visibility and strong currents; a shot line, distance line, and careful pilotage are essential for finding and navigating the wreck. Salps and jellyfish are abundant in the water column, particularly during decompression stops in shallower water.

Biodiversity: Salps (a type of gelatinous organism) are present in large numbers in the water column, particularly noticeable during decompression stops. Jellyfish are also encountered. Dogfish (catfish) are visible on the sandy seabed near the wreck.

Tides: The area off West Wales is known for strong currents. The site requires careful timing to hit slack water, and even a slight miscalculation results in significant current at depth, strong enough to drag a grapple off the seabed and hold it in mid-water. Diving earlier in the tidal window makes conditions at the wreck considerably easier.

History: TORPEDOED & SUNK BY GERMAN SUBMARINE U 96. TOOK JUST UNDER TWO HOURS TO SINK.

sites.name: Stoke Point
sites.location: South Hams, Devon, South West, England
sites.notes:
The seabed off Stoke Point and to the west could well be described as South Devon’s “Sponge Gardens”. When we get there, we look at the echo sounder for both depth and seabed structure -there are extensive areas of coarse sand but also lots of sticking-up bits. Don’t worry if you hit sand, you should fairly soon find one of the low reefs.

Stoke Point is a reasonably short trip in the club’s RIBs out of Plymouth. It is a typical dive for a Saturday morning, weekday or an evening dive in mid-summer.

This is a great location for photography of colourful marine life and, if the tide is running for a drift dive – that is like the end of a games show where all the goodies come past you on a conveyor belt – but you are the one that’s moving. There are depths to suit novice divers but the best rock formations and wildlife are deeper than 20 m below low water level. Pause and look where the sand covers low-lying rocks – there are many species of sponges including some rare and scarce ones.

sites.name: Highland Brigade
sites.notes:
The wreck of the Highland Brigade, located to the East of Ventnor, Isle of Wight in approximately 28m of water, offers divers the opportunity to explore a shipwreck site with a varied array of artifacts and structures. Divers can discover a pile of chain, glass bottles, shells, Royal Doulton crucibles, an engine, brass fittings, portholes, and even telephone equipment within the wreck. The stern gun, stone beer bottles, and bronze hydrant with hose take-offs can also be found at this site, providing a fascinating dive experience.

The 'Highalnd Brigade' lies to the East of Ventnor, Isle of Wight in approx 28m of water, lying almost directly in line with the tide. Her stern section sits on its port side standing 6 or 7 meters proud of the shingle seabed, her midships lie collapsed to port, and her bow is more upright and intact.

Starting from the stern, the diver comes across a huge pile of chain within the wreck, with glass bottles and 6" shells scattered around the vacinity (a 6" 'Spatter Box' was recently found here). Moving forward from here, you can drop down into an area just under the deck beams, which contains Royal Doulton crucibles and smelting pot lids. Going through the deck beams onto the seabed will reward you with the site of the stern gun, which now lies partly burried in the shingle seabed.

Moving forward inside the stern, you come across general cargo of stone beer bottles and glassware before the stern collapses down behind the engine room area. The engine can just be seen under the starboard hull plates which now lean over to port. It is possible to slip in here and swim around the engine and crankshaft without disturbing too much silt! From here, move forwards, swimming between 2 of the 3 Scotch type boilers and emerging in a very broken area to the front of the engine room. This area is littered with brass fittings and a number of portholes have been found here with haxagonal dogs (as well as brass doors on iron frames)

Moving fwd again, you come to the more intact bow section. Part of the cargo of the Highland Brigade was telephone equipment, and it is still possible to find candlestick telephones in the silt of the fwd holds. There are also numerous 'ingots' of antimony here, which look like thin silver bars with bevelled edges. The foredeck of the wreck contains a bronze hydrant with multiple hose take-offs.

History: BUILT IN 1901 BY W BEARDMORE & CO LTD, GLASGOW. OWNED AT TIME OF LOSS BY NELSON LINE LTD. FOUR BOILERS, TRIPLE EXPANSION ENGINE OF 653NHP, SINGLE SHAFT. PASSAGE LONDON FOR BUENOS AIRES. GENERAL CARGO INCLUDING (AS REPORTED) 1000 TONS GOVERNMENT CARGO, 11 HEAD OF CATTLE, TIN INGOTS AND TELEPHONE EQUIPMENT. TORPEDOED AND SUNK BY UC-71.

sites.name: Argyll Campsite
sites.hazards: Silty bottom — care must be taken not to stir up the silt.
sites.notes:
A shallower dive off the Argyll Caravan Park campsite in Quebec Bay, Loch Fyne. The site features the atmospheric wrecks of small vessels on a silty bottom at 17m, colonised by squirts, peacock worms, and a colony of over 30 fireworks anemones.

Dive entry among the many small boats moored off the campsite, following a mooring line to the bottom at 17m. Care must be taken not to stir up the silt which carpets the site. The site features wrecks of various small vessels with old rusted chains and mooring ropes.

Biodiversity: Rich variety of squirts, peacock worms, and a colony of more than 30 fireworks anemones.

sites.name: HMS Argyll
sites.notes:
HMS Argyll was one of six Devonshire-class armoured cruisers built for the Royal Navy in the first decade of the 20th century. She was assigned to the 1st Cruiser Squadron of the Channel Fleet upon completion and was transferred to the 5th Cruiser Squadron of the Atlantic Fleet in 1909. Two years later, she was detached to escort the royal yacht during King George V's trip to British India. Argyll was assigned to the 3rd Cruiser Squadron of the reserve Second Fleet in 1913.

The Navy salvaged all of the valuable items on board, including her guns, and she was demolished by the salvage team. In 1970 her two propellers were recovered by divers and sold for scrap. She remains a diveable wreck

History: During the war, lighthouses were ordered to switch their lights off for fear of assisting German U-boats in their operations, and the light was only turned on by special permission. En route Argyll sent a signal requesting the light to be turned on, but the lighthouse did not have a radio and could only contacted by boat or visual signals. Attempts to notify the lighthouse failed, but the ship was not notified of the failure and proceeded in the expectation of using the light. Soon afterwards, she ran aground at 04:30, suffering extensive damage to much of the hull and starting a fire. Two destroyers, Hornet and Jackal, were sent and rescued her entire crew without serious injury.

sites.name: Gometra Anchorage
sites.hazards: Entry is awkward — dense weed can trap legs and fill fins with shells.
sites.notes:
A shallow water dive exploring a seagrass bed (Zostera marina) in a sheltered anchorage on the island of Gometra in the Inner Hebrides, Scotland. The seagrass bed extends around much of the bay and serves as an important nursery habitat for numerous species.

A shallow water dive in a sheltered anchorage bay on the island of Gometra. The seagrass bed (Zostera marina) occupies a niche between the sandy/muddy bottom and where the seaweed starts, going all the way around the bay for perhaps 50-60 metres. The seagrass is 50-60 cm tall and forms a nearly complete bed in shallower areas, thinning to patches at depth. There is a distinct demarcation between the seagrass and the surrounding seaweed zones. The bottom is silty in places. The site was discovered after a single strand of seagrass was spotted on the beach, prompting the diver to explore just offshore.

Biodiversity: Seagrass (Zostera marina) bed approximately 50-60 cm tall. Species observed include wrasse, young edible crab, snakelocks anemone, sand star, and two-spotted gobies. The site functions as a nursery ground for numerous species, with lots of small fish darting about.

sites.notes:
The Rondo wreck is a popular dive site in the Sound of Mull, resting with the bow dug into the seabed at 50 metres and the stern rising just 5 meters below the surface. The wreck is intact but lies at a steep angle on rocks, providing divers with the opportunity to explore diverse marine life including sponges, anemones, and abundant marine creatures. The dive usually begins at the shallowest point of the wreck at the rudder post and progresses downhill to the bow, with noteworthy features such as swim-throughs and dense arrays of plumose anemones along the way.

In the Sound of Mull, standing on her bow on a steep slope. It gets interesting at 50m where everything has fallen down to.

Little structure more than 2m above the surrounding seabed remains on the Rondo. Despite the degradation, it remains an impressive site suitable for both trainee and experienced wreck divers.

Biodiversity: Colourful sponges, plumose anemones and dead men's fingers.

Tides: This can be dived at slack water or all the way through the ebb tide.

sites.name: Totland Pier and Bay
sites.location: Isle of Wight, South East, England
sites.hazards: Strong currents and boat traffic.
sites.notes:
Totland Pier and Bay is a historic dive site with abundant marine life, featuring pier structures, seagrass beds and old bottles. The sandy bottom to the South of the Pier is home to hermit crabs, while to the North sea grasses, rocky outcrops and an array of marine life can be found. The pier end is a hotspot for velvet swimming crabs, edible crabs, lobsters and various fish species like Pollock, Pouting, Bass and Bream. The site offers good visibility up to 10m in peak season and night dives can also be rewarding. Strong currents can be experienced, so caution is advised when exploring beyond the pier.

Totland Bay Pier is perhaps the island’s most dived shore dive site. Access is easy, the visibility is usually good, there is plenty of life under the old pier given most of the surrounding seabed is sand and the pier is the only thing sticking out of the seabed. Logistics are easy – you can usually park very close to the entry point, the toilets are nearby, there is a cafe and generally, as it is a bit more tucked away the site is quiet.

The concrete sea defence revetment to the east of the pier provides a handy place to kit-up independently without assistance from your buddy and the walk to the water is short. Depths are up to 6m at the end of the pier, where you do need to be mindful of the tides, though they are generally manageable.

Abundant marine life, pier structure, seagrass beds and old bottles. The bottom composition to the South of the Pier is a flat sandy bottom which is often covered with hermit crabs. North from the Pier you find a sandy bottom covered with sea grasses and rocky outcrops. If you follow the pier out through the legs on a westerly heading the depth reaches up to 6m at the end. Here you will find an abundance of velvet swimming crabs, edible crabs and lobsters. Shoals of Pollock, Pouting, Bass and Bream can be seen taking shelter under the large pier end. Many old bottles and fallen pylons can be seen. If you go past the end of the pier the tide becomes stronger and depth ranges up to 8m. The current can be strong in this area so take a DSMB with you if you plan to come out from under the pier as there is boat traffic. Visibility can reach 10m in peak season and night dives are also great here too.

Biodiversity: Lots of marine life is to be found hiding in here such as blennys and gobys.

Tides: Like most island shore dives, diving high water slack is the best time, which at this site is approximately two hours before HW Portsmouth.

History: The Pier was used for ferry docking and pleasure cruises until in 1940 it was sectioned for fear of German Invasion. Totland Bay Pier re-opened on 17th June 1951, the occasion being marked by the arrival of the 'Lorna Doone' the first steamer to disembark passengers for some twenty years. Regular visits by pleasure craft continued for many years until finally ceasing in 1969. From 1971 to the early 1990s, a succession of different owners, none of whom could provide the required funds to properly maintain the structure, led to the pier's inevitable decay. Today there is a lovely cafe at the base of the Pier and plans for renovation are still under way.

sites.name: SMS Dresden
sites.alternativeNames: Scapa - Dresden, Wreck Dresden, GB - Schottland - Scapa Flow - Dresden 2
sites.notes:
The SMS Dresden wreck lies on a slope with her bows at a depth of 27 meters and her stern at 38 meters. The ship was a light cruiser built in Kiel and launched in 1917, later sunk by a British submarine in August 1917. Sitting in 35 meters of water on her portside, the wreck of the Dresden spans 25-45 meters deep. The vessel, a significant part of naval history, boasts a well-preserved hull despite the weather deck collapsing to port, revealing buried forward armaments. The Dresden, displacing 5,600 tons and measuring 156 meters long, was scuttled in 1919. Divers can admire various elements like the anchor chain, guns, armoured bridge, range finder, and the name-ship shield.

Weighing 5500 tons this light cruiser is largely intact with the anchor chain, guns, armoured bridge, range finder and name-ship shield all worth visiting on a dive.

She lies on a slope with her bows in 27 meters and her stern in 38.

sites.name: Enecuri
sites.alternativeNames: The Spaniard, Spaniard, Portland Harbour, Spaniard/Encuri (Wreck), Spaniard (Wreck), Portland, Spaniard
sites.notes:
Enecuri, also known as The Spaniard, is a small steamer wreck located at the foot of the second arm of the Portland Breakwater in Portland Harbour. The wreck lies with its bows to the south and a heavy list to starboard. The site is best accessed by swimming down the breakwater wall and navigating to the muddy base to find the stern of the wreck, which features a large 4-blade propeller and steering gear. The wreck is upright but lists to starboard, with the midships broken up but the bow and stern distinguishable. The visibility can be poor due to silting, but in good conditions, the wreck can offer an interesting dive experience for those diving in small groups. The maximum depth is 14m, making it suitable for beginners or those looking for an easy dive site.

The Enecuri was a Spanish steamship that sank in 1900 after dragging her anchor during a southwest gale and being driven onto the breakwater in Portland Harbour. The wreck is now a tangled mass of broken plates.

The recommended method diving this wreck is to enter the water opposite number 86 on the breakwater wall and swim down the wall to the muddy base. At this point, turn left and keep an eye out for the stern of the wreck lying 4-5 meters from the base of the wall. There is a large 4-blade propeller in the stern which almost touches the wall. From here, swim around the stern onto the rear deck where you'll find the emergency steering gear and the large steering quadrant, complete with steering chains. There is a skylight in the rear deck and a hatch which allows access to stern, but is almost fully silted up.

Continuing forward from here, you come across the rear hold, with a ladder running down the rear bulkhead as far as the prop-shaft tunnel. Swimming forward along the prop-shaft tunnel, the port side of the wreck is collapsing over the divers head, eventually blocking forward access.

The wreck appears to break up at this point, and there are no distinguishing features amid the jumble of plates and girders except for a large distinctive girder which forms an arch.

Moving forward from here, you eventually come to the bow of the vessel. This has a very heavy list to starboard, the foredeck being almost vertical now. The diver can enter the forepeek and swim around, exiting either through the back of the broken bow section or through one of the holes in the foredeck. This compartment is full of silt, and visibility soon reduces to nil unless the diver is careful.

Tides: Southwest gale

History: EX-MARISTOW. BUILT IN 1894 BY SIR RAYLTON DIXON & CO, MIDDLESBROUGH. OWNED AT TIME OF LOSS BY CIA NAV VASCONGADA, BILBAO. TWO BOILERS, TRIPLE EXPANSION ENGINE OF 224 NHP, SINGLE SHAFT. PASSAGE ANTWERP FOR BILBAO. DRAGGED ANCHOR IN NW FORCE 9 AND WENT ONTO THE BREADWATER ROCKS. NEXT DAY SLID OFF AND SANK. MASTER LOST. (SIBI).

Continuing forward from here, you come across the rear hold, with a ladder running down the rear bulkhead as far as the prop-shaft tunnel. Swimming forward along the prop-shaft tunnel, the port side of the wreck is collapsing over the divers head, eventually blocking forward access.

The wreck appears to break up at this point, and there are no distinguishing features amid the jumble of plates and girders except for a large distinctive girder which forms an arch.

Moving forward from here, you eventually come to the bow of the vessel. This has a very heavy list to starboard, the foredeck being almost vertical now. The diver can enter the forepeek and swim around, exiting either through the back of the broken bow section or through one of the holes in the foredeck. This compartment is full of silt, and visibility soon reduces to nil unless the diver is careful.

sites.name: Churchill Barrier 3
sites.notes:
Churchill Barrier 3 is a shore dive site with easy entry and exit from the south shore, with the option to dive the SS Reginald and three other wrecks from the shore, while the SS Clio requires a boat. The wrecks, including the SS Empire Seaman, SS Martis, SS Gartshore, and SS Reginald, are Single Screw Steel Steamers, with the Empire Seaman being a highlight for its intact structure and numerous swim-throughs. Churchill Barrier 3 is part of the Churchill barriers and can also be used for drysuit training or dive kit checkups. 

Churchill Barrier 3 is a great shore dive on the Churchill barrier block ships.

The Churchill Barriers can be used as a drysuit course site or for dive kit checkup.

Entry/exit for the SS Reginald is very easy from the south shore by simply walking into the water and head north.

There are four shore divable wrecks and the SS Clio, which can only be dived by boat. The SS Empire Seaman, SS Reginald, SS Martis and SS Gartshore are all Single Screw Steel Steamers. The Empire Seaman is possibly the most enjoyable to dive of all the barrier Blockships. She remains relatively intact and as such provides numerous swim throughs and points of interest. The Martis is in similar condition to the Empire Seaman supporting a vast range of sea life. The Gartshore is a Blockship from WWI, she is very broken up yet the propeller, rudder and prop shaft can still be distinguished. The Reginald is the Iconic wreck which can be seen from the Barrier, The Lapland is totally collapsed and lies directly beneath the concrete causeway.

sites.notes:
Manse point is a good shore dive on the point in Loch Leven

Walk down the stony path onto the beach and out to the point. It's a longer walk when the tide is out.

Head left as you face the water and you will see small walls covered in life. If you keep the main wall to your left choose your desired depth and head along the wall, the wall gradually steps up to shallower depths. You can then turn back on yourself and follow the reef back into the bay.

sites.name: MV Pionersk
sites.notes:
With a least depth of 1m running down to the stern at 22m, this is a big wreck (longer than the Battleships in Scapa) and several dives are needed to get to grips with the whole thing.

After a careful drop off with us all looking out for any stray rocks or wreckage underneath, we descended onto the bow. The visibility was not quite as good, with a slight milky residue from the previous storms. We passed down through a dense shoal of saithe which obscured the scene ahead. The fish started to disperse, allowing a full view of the wreck. An impressive hawse pipe rested upright virtually touching the surface with the weight of a bulky anchor chain dangling down. One wonders how long this will remain in-situ.

Anchor chain generally dominated the scene where it seems to have breached the Ship’s hull. The Pionersk was covered with the usual dreaded kelp, which at times made it hard to discern wreck from rock. The high rocky walls would also form barriers to finning down the natural course of the wreck, funnelling you into the inevitable dead end, although we often found a porthole down each one!

Eventually after much searching we reached 18 metres, which I believed to be the deepest section of the wreck. We combed around the large chunks of the stern but failed to find the propeller, perhaps still hidden underneath.

Biodiversity: Yellow Ringed and Gas Mantle sea squirts, horse mussels, moon jellyfish, occasional octopus.

History: The Russian fishing vessel of the Pionersk. The bulky 165-metre-long vessel sank during the night of 31 October 1994 in south-easterly winds of Force 8, gusting to force 9-10.

In rough seas, she dragged her anchor until the fateful inevitable happened and the ship’s bow ploughed into the rocks. During that night Lerwick lifeboat crew managed to rescue the 155 people off the boat. All survived, although I expect they were a little shaken up.

sites.name: The Giants Legs
sites.notes:
The Giant's Legs are half-formed sea stacks projecting from Bard Head at the southernmost tip of Bressay Island, Shetland. The geological formation, shaped by erosion, features rock pillars with a profusion of marine life including anemones, nudibranchs, shrimp, crabs, and lobsters. A sizeable cave extends some 120 metres into the cliffs, with an air space through much of its length and a tight passage leading to another cliff face. Scattered wreckage, thought to include material from an oil rig jacket, lies at the site, and seals are occasionally encountered.

A truly spectacular place to dive, stunning above and below, this is a cave that stretches 120 meters into the cliffs under the Giants Legs.

The epic proportions of the Giants Legs are impressive – snorkelling over to the arch I certainly felt tiny. The swell was still pounding through the arch, so it was a matter of dropping down to 4m to escape some of the surface swell, followed by a forward and backward drift dive through the legs to surface on the other side.

It was certainly worth the extra effort. The light faded as we headed down, but the colours of the walls intensified, plastered in anemones. The visibility was good enough to see all the way to the bottom, although the surface was a little too frothy to see the arch above.

Biodiversity: This scenic site has a profusion of life on the rock pillars that form the cliff with nudibranchs, anenomes and all manner of fish.

History: The Giants legs are situated at the southern end of the Island of Bressay know as Bard Head.
The Old Norse name for Bressay was Breiðey and then later in 1490 the island is referred to as Brusoy, the meaning of name in Old Norse means broad island.

sites.name: HMSm E49
sites.alternativeNames: Great Britain Shetland HMS E49 Wreck
sites.notes:
The HMS E49 is a British submarine wreck located at a depth of 33 metres off the coast of Unst, North Shetland. It sank in 1917 after striking a German-laid mine in Balta Sound, resulting in the loss of all crew members, and is recognised as a war grave. The wreck is partially submerged in white sand, with the conning tower and periscope remaining visible alongside some of the submarine's gears. The wreckage is in two sections, with the tower bent to starboard. The site offers a poignant reminder of the perils faced by submariners during wartime.

Wreck of the British submarine E-49 ( war grave ) at 33m on Unst, North Shetland

E49 is slowly being swallowed up by the white sand it lies in. The conning tower and periscope are still visible, as are some of the gears responsible for maintaining trim. The conditions were favourable, and we did two dives on the site. One of the few opportunities I’ve had to make pictures of wrecks in the UK using available light.

Biodiversity: Conger, Ling, Tusk, Pollack, Poor Cod, octopus, Sunstars, Cushionstars, Dead Men's Fingers, sea squirts, hydroids.

History: 10.3.17   MINED WITH LOSS OF 3 OFFICERS AND 28 RATINGS. (WW1SL). MINE THOUGHT TO HAVE BEEN LAID BY UC 76 OFF BALTA SOUND ON 10.3.17. E49 WAS SHELTERING FROM A GALE IN BALTA SOUND. ON LEAVING THE SOUND THROUGH SOUTH CHANNEL SHE STRUCK THE MINE. (SHIPWRECKS OF N SCOTLAND, BAIRD).

sites.name: MFV Fraoch Ban
sites.alternativeNames: Great Britain Shetland Fraoch Ban Wreck
sites.notes:
The MFV Fraoch Ban is a small fishing vessel that sank on 15th August 1999, resting in approximately 27 metres of water with GPS coordinates 60° 08.194’N, 01° 02.680’W. Located near the Isle of Noss, between Bressay and North Ness, the wreck lies upright on the seabed with a 45-degree list to port. Measuring 15 metres in length and rising about 5 metres off the seabed, the steel hull of the Fraoch Ban features significant marine growth, making it an appealing site for underwater photography. Despite its modest size, the wreck offers good visibility and minimal tidal influence. Notable features include a cargo winch at the stern and intact wooden decking, with cables adorned with plumose anemones and squid eggs. Access to certain interior sections, such as the bridge, is possible, though small entrances may pose a challenge. The site provides an intriguing dive environment characterised by a variety of marine life, including plaice and diverse critter populations.

Fraoch Ban where on 15th August 1999, in calm seas the movement of the fish rushing from side to side in unison actually toppled the boat and it sank. The fishermen lost their boat, the catch of sand eels and nearly their lives. Today the ship rests on the port side rising 5m off the seabed and measuring 15m in length.

We descended the shot, hoping the GPS references were accurate and thankfully they were, as we dropped down to 20 metres and paused for a while. I had never seen such good visibility. You could actually see the silhouette of the whole ship from stern to the bow. Below us a welcoming committee of plaice were gathering.

This was surreal and the image of diving a Red Sea wreck popped into my head. The ship was certainly a picture, with Disney-esque qualities. The stern was marked by a huge cargo winch, which would have helped drag up all of those sand eels. Cables dangled down, covered in plumose anemones, along with huge clumps of squid eggs. The wooden decking is usually one of the first areas to disintegrate but the boards were still fairly intact, covered with various critters.

At midships, on the top at the starboard side was an entrance inside the wreck, although both of us felt it was just too small and not worth the risk. Next to this was the bridge, with some of the glass windows still intact. You could enter inside with care, but there seemed no need as the view through the opening showed it all. The steering wheel had gone but the steering mechanism was still in place. The floor was covered in debris, along with an old coiled phone cable.

Several plaice seemed to be following our progress along the wreck from the sea floor, so we headed onto the white sandy seabed for a gander, then headed for the bow. At midships various mast debris had fallen onto the sand, probably broken off when the vessel hit the bottom. All too soon and we were going to have to leave this wreck behind. I could have stayed down there all day, just watching the fishes.

Biodiversity: Plaice, sand eels (historic cargo).

Tides: Can be dived at any state of the tide.

History: The Fraoch Ban sank on 15 August 1999 in calm seas when a cargo of sand eels shifted from side to side and capsized the boat. No lives were lost.

Current can be very strong in area. 

Be mindful of rocks just below the surface in the area. 

Usual hazards associated with wrecks, including some deterioration.
sites.notes:
Wreck lies just off Russell Rock, to the north-east. The wreck is badly broken up but it is huge – the largest at the Maidens. It is possible to follow a trail of broken metal down to 30 metres, where you can see the boiler and as you descend you will notice a sloping wall on your right that drops to around 45 metres. There is a nice rocky reef beneath Russell Rock at ~35metres.

Biodiversity: The wreck is covered in intermittent patches of dead men’s fingers, anemones, urchins and short animal turf.

Tides: Strong

Slack water only as currents can be strong in this area. Slack water is 1 hour before HW/LW Belfast

History: Date of loss 04/01/1908. A steel tanker en route from Barrow-in-Furness to New York in ballast. LBD: 105.86 x 13.86 x 8.28; g.t. 4041. Built in 1893 by Naval Construction and Armament Co, and owned by Anglo-American Oil Co. of London. Having left Barrow on 3rd January 1908 she struck Russell Rock, on her port side, and started to take on water. The Captain ordered all the crew off but the officers, who remained. Rockets were sent up but very unluckily one fell back onto the ship and started a fire. All but two crew members made it off the ship; one falling in when he tried to board a lifeboat and another was noticed missing as they neared the lighthouses. It took them three hours to make it to the lighthouse. The surviving crew were collected from there 24 hours later. (Sources: Larn & Larn 2002; Ms. L. Keatley).

sites.name: Rutland Island Wreck
sites.notes:
History: The remains of a wooden vessel lie in the shallows of Burtonport Harbour immediately to the NE of Rutland Island, this once armed ship, that carried both ordnance and weapons, dates to the early part of the 17th century. The wreck lies c. 120m NE of Rutland Island in 3m-5m of water at low water Spring tides. 1620-1640s.  Local divers, including Liam Miller who reported the find, discovered the wreck in 2008. Subsequent Archaeological investigations on the wreck site from 2010-2013 by the Underwater Archaeology Unit (UAU) of the National Monuments Service, Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht recovered a significant quantity of artefactual finds, including munitions, pottery, leather, barrel material and a bandolier’s belt. The archaeological excavation focused on the internal limits of the wreck itself and revealed that the lower hold of the ship is preserved in situ from bow to stern, with a small section of orlop deck remaining along with a large section of transom and its rudder assemblage. The wreck itself was not removed but remains preserved in situ for future scientific investigation. The excavation was supported by the Geological Survey of Ireland and the wreck surveyed by the RV Keery in 2011. GSI Wreck No_299.
----------------------------

sites.name: James Eagan Layne
sites.alternativeNames: John Egan Layne - Plymouth, Eagan Layne
sites.hazards: Care should be taken not to move or collect radioactive discs which are 4-5 cm in diameter, and are still occasionally found on the wreck! In recent years, ammunition has also been found in the stern section.
sites.notes:
The James Eagan Layne wreck is a popular site for divers in Whitsand Bay, Cornwall. This 7,176-ton US Liberty Ship, sank in 1945 after being hit by a torpedo from U-1195. The wreck is split into two sections, with the bow pointing north, and is home to a variety of marine life such as white anemones and dead man’s fingers. Divers can explore the various holds filled with wreckage, swim through the wreck from bow to stern, and observe the collapsed stern section. The wreck is suitable for novice wreck divers, offering easy routes through the remains of the engine room and holds. While the site can get busy, it remains a popular and well-known dive spot in the UK.

This may be the best-known wreck in the UK. If you haven’t dived it, then you are possibly standing next to someone who has.

The wreck is split into two sections, the bow section being the largest is some 25m away from the stern section. The bow complete with railings points north and was very much intact until 2012. Visibility is generally good, although this does depend on the number of divers on the site.In summer it becomes very busy!

It is possible to dive the wreck at most states of the tide, as it is sheltered from the South- easterly / easterly winds by Rame Head.

Several years ago, part of the bow collapsed, opening up even more of the wreck to explore. However, one of the most impressive views of this wreck is still from the seabed – looking up at the bow towering above you!

You can swim through the wreck from bow to stern, exploring the various holds filled with wreckage. The bulkheads are long disintegrated however upright ‘ribs’ stick out from the wreckage which you can easily swim between. A favourite route for many on the Eagan Layne is to swim down the outside of the hull, which is covered in life, and come back up the middle of the ship over the holds.

Biodiversity: The sides of the Layne are covered with white dead man's fingers and soft corals. The Eagan Layne supports an enormous fish population where shoals of Pollack, Pouting and Bib mass on sections of the wreck.

Tides: Can be dived at any state of Tide.

History: The James Eagan Layne was an American Liberty ship. She sank on March the 21st 1945, after being hit by a torpedo. The ship is sat upright on a sandy bottom, in a charted depth of 24m, at position 50.19.32N 04.04.42W.It is situated about three quarter of a mile off shore, and is marked with a wreck buoy to seaward.

History: Date of loss 05/01/1867. A full-rigged composite ship of iron and wood, 52m in length. Built in 1865 in Glasgow. En route from Glasgow to Singapore with a general cargo of spirits, beer, cotton, pottery and saddlery. One of the castle line of ships. Stranded and lost with all hands. Eleven bodies were recovered and are said to have been buried in a mass grave near Layd; a large mound is said to be still visible. Relocated by sports divers in the 1970s and ‘heavily plundered’. In 1995 a survey and short excavation under license from NI Gov was carried out by Management for Archaeology Underwater (MAU) in order to obtain a representative sample of the cargo (see Breen 1996; Breen and Forsythe 2004). The wreck lies in 15m of water, 70m offshore at the base of steep boulder cliffs. This is an important wreck and a potential candidate for protection. Please do not carelessly damage the site further. Condition assessments would be welcomed by the Historic Environment Division (see ‘Record Heritage’).

Please do not carelessly damage the site further. Condition assessments would be welcomed by the Historic Environment Division (see ‘Record Heritage’).

sites.name: Portland
sites.notes:
A little dived wreck just off St Davids headland in West wales is the Portland wreck. I’ve dived it a few times and loved it.

Its a lovely wreck hidden away in the Porthlysgi Bay, only accessable by boat out of Porthclais.

Once located, the remains are sitting on a stoney reef with lots of bits to see including winches, loads of fish life and chunks of steel which have become reefs for the sealife.

Its also only in approx 10mtr of water so great as a first time dive for newbie divers and for the weekend of fun when you want somewhere sheltered.
