sites.name: Portland Underwater Curiosity Park
sites.notes:
The Portland Underwater Curiosity Park in Balaclava Bay near Portland Harbour features various attractions on the seabed, such as Admiralty anchors, statues, and concrete pipes. With minimal tidal currents, a maximum depth of 33 to 46 feet (10 to 14 m), and protection from wind by Portland Isle and the harbor breakwater, this dive site offers a leisurely exploration experience suitable for divers of all levels. The park is marked by yellow buoys from April to October.

This site in Balaclava Bay, south of the Portland Harbour breakwater, features several attractions on the seabed. We swam into the two six ton Admiralty anchors, four statues (including a diver, a shark and two Greek statues) and a smaller nymph. Somewhere nearby are several lengths of large concrete pipe to swim through – and the attractions are roped together. A great dive for newbies – 14 metres max.

The Portland Underwater Curiosity Park is located in Balaclava Bay, next to Portland Harbor. Between April and October, four yellow marker buoys denote the corners of the 53,819 square foot (5000 m²) park. The buoys are removed during the winter.

The park is an excellent dive location even — and especially — when dive conditions around the area are less favorable. The bay is protected from southerly, southwesterly and westerly winds by Portland Isle, while the harbor breakwater protects the bay to the north. Additionally, the bay has minimal tidal currents and a maximum depth of between 33 and 46 feet (10 to 14 m), with gritty sand at the bottom, perfect for some leisurely exploration dives.

History: Most of the artifacts were sunk in June 2018 and the park is aiming to add even more. The sunken objects are mostly related to, or symbolic of, Portland and the ocean. Some examples include reconstructed Roman temple ruins with statues, columns, and ancient masonry. There is also a 10-foot long (3 m) shark, numerous pipe tunnel swim-throughs (about 4 feet/1.2 m wide), an 8-foot (2.5 m) tall deep-sea diver, and two 6-ton Admiralty mooring anchors.

sites.name: SS South Western
sites.hazards: Very short slack water on spring tides with strong currents building quickly; the area is not renowned for good underwater visibility. Snagging a delayed SMB on the shotline is a risk if deployed near the boilers during building current.
sites.notes:
The South Western is a recently identified wreck of a 674-ton cross-Channel mail steamer lying approximately six miles south of St Catherine's Lighthouse, south of the Isle of Wight. Torpedoed by a U-boat in 1918, the wreck sits at 38m and offers a detailed tour of machinery, cargo gear, stern fittings, and scattered hull sections — though it requires careful timing around a short slack-water window and is not renowned for good visibility.

The wreck lies on its starboard side and has broken and collapsed further, with some sections almost rolling over. The tour begins at the boilers, the obvious shotline target. One boiler supports the remains of the hull, the other rests against it slightly aft. Turning aft, the triple-expansion engine has fallen from the hull with its pistons pointing out along the seabed; the base of the engine is now uppermost and supports a section of hull — it is possible to wriggle behind the engine between it and the hull, but only for experienced divers. Immediately aft of the engine is a single cargo winch, just visible beneath a hull that soon collapses to the seabed. Further aft, the hull is broken across, leaving the propeller shaft (broken at a joining flange) visible from both parts of the wreckage. The port gunwale rests on the seabed, and the wreck has split open along the keel, exposing the propeller shaft most of the way to the stern. At the stern, the propeller and rudder remain in place. A small swivel mount on the keel side of the wreck may once have carried the South Western's 13-pounder stern gun; tucked in close to the wreck, a broken crate holds a shell casing. Returning forward past the boilers, a large steam pipe snakes across the wreckage in an inverted U shape. The hull forward of the boilers has collapsed flat to the seabed, ending in a clean break with no sign of bow debris — the bow was blown off by the torpedo and likely lies over a mile away. Just off the deck side of the wreck lies an anchor large enough to have been a spare. A long section of hull lies almost parallel to the main body but set further out, marking the limit of wreckage on that side. Between the aft end of this hull section and the main body are steps that may have led from the forward main deck to the boat deck, and nearby is a toilet. The wreck lies with its bow to the west. To deploy a delayed SMB, move a few metres forward or aft of the boilers to avoid fouling the shotline.

Tides: Slack water is essential and occurs 25 minutes after high water Dover. On spring tides, slack is very short and can be a few minutes later. A period of calm weather is advised before venturing to the site. Strong tidal currents south of the Isle of Wight can build quickly at the end of slack water.

History: The South Western was a 674-ton mail steamer built in 1874 by J&W Dudgeon Ltd of London for the London & South Western Railway Co's cross-Channel mail and ferry service. Based in Southampton, she served routes to France and the Channel Islands. Her original two-cylinder compound engine was later replaced with a triple-expansion engine by Day, Summers & Co of Southampton. With the outbreak of the Great War a 13-pounder gun was fitted at the stern. On 6 March 1918, she left Southampton for St Malo. At 11pm, Captain John Clark spotted a surfaced submarine and ordered his gunners to open fire, but it dived before they could fire. Half an hour later the submarine reappeared 200m to starboard, and before the gunners could act a torpedo struck the forward hold. Kapitänleutnant Erwin Wassner of UB-59 reported the entire forecastle exploded; the South Western sank 20 minutes later. Of 28 crew and 6 passengers, only four survived including Captain Clark. Wassner, responsible for sinking 89 ships totalling 135,178 tons during the war, ranked 20th among successful U-boat commanders.

sites.name: Carrick Castle Reef
sites.hazards: The mud here is quite stable to there are very few site hazards that require safety measures beyond safe diving practices. There can be boat traffic but it is not heavy. DSMB is recommended.
sites.notes:
Shore Dive on a small reef just offshore near Carrick Castle

Lots of parking and suitable for all levels so great group site.

Enter via the beach in front of the public toilets as in the pic below.

Head straight out perpendicular to the shore. You will find scatterings of larger rocks. Follow them and you will come to the rocky reef. Water gets shallower again as you reach the reef to as little as 5 metres. If you find yourself on mud plains at 12 metres then you have missed the reef.

sites.name: Tynemouth Castle
sites.notes:
The Tynemouth Castle lies in 58 metres at 57 21.952N  01 47.088W orientated 0/180 degrees with the bow to the south and stern north.  She is upright and intact, but typically, the superstructure has now gone.

History: Built as the William Griffen for the Royal Navy, she was sold in 1921 and again in 1928 to A.B. Lee & Co Ltd, North Shields when she was renamed Tynemouth Castle.  In 1939 she was sold to John Lewis Ltd of Aberdeen but was lost before her fishing registry could be changed.

On the 9th December 1939 the Tynemouth Castle struck the Cruden Scares then drifted off and foundered three miles south-east of Cruden Bay.  The fate of the crew is unknown.

Another steam trawler found during the hunt for the U-1206.  In February 2007 when performing a search around the 'North-Corner' fisherman's mark, we found the wreck in a depth of around 60 metres.  It wasn't until the 2nd September that we dived the site, found it was a steam trawler and discovered the bell which was engraved 'WILLIAM GRIFFEN' -  confirmation of her identity as the Tynemouth Castle.

sites.hazards: Use an SMB as there is a yacht marina in the bay and the headland is favoured by fishermen so watch out for line / lures.
sites.notes:
A pleasant shore dive.

Heading north out of Oban take a left turn signed Castle and Dunstaffnage Marine Biology Labs. Park and kit up in the car park near the castle and walk through to the headland.

Descend down a rocky shore line keeping close to the shore, through a kelp layer, where you'll find a sandy bottom, max depth 19m, with a wide variety of life, Dogfish anemones etc.

sites.name: Abercastle
sites.notes: A very narrow bay (deep vee), lots of local fishing boats and many shore lines secured to left-hand side. A 5 minute amble round the coast path however brings you to a small pebble strewn bay which gets you past the mooring lines. Right-hand side of bay is free of mooring lines and has a cut that floods at high water, careful however, RIBs use it as a short cut at high tide. Abercastle has toilets but no shops (post office, Tea Rooms and a Pub in Mathry) and only room for a small number of cars, but a beautiful spot.

Newhaven Scuba’s training site is an ideal site to gain experience in a safe environment with areas that you can practice neutral buoyancy and watch the vast fish life. Max depth is 6 meters and the life changes dramatically at night. Join Newhaven Scuba’s club to get exclusive use of this site.

You will be able to see Cuckoo wrasse, Ballan wrasse, Mullet, and Corkwing wrasse most of the year and at certain times of the year you will be able to see pipefish, Seabass, and nudibranchs.

sites.notes:
Usual dark and silty conditions on this small wreck but when the weather gods are not helpful you have to take what is available.

Hiding from the strong SE winds this small wreck in 40 metres was the only option available. Small but complete I spent a relaxing half hour exploring some of the unusual features of this composite hulled wreck. The bottom was very silty and soon became disturbed as can bee seen in much of the video. A definite contender for the experienced open circuit air diver.

A Norwegian steamship built in 1875 that went ashore in bad weather in January 1913. Salvaged to the waterline, her remains including boiler, engine and lower hull make for a good second dive or a site sheltered from the south.

The Dovre is in very shallow water and was salvaged to the waterline however her remains including boiler, engine and lower hull although somewhat broken up, makes for a good second dive or a site sheltered from the south. The site of the Dovre was dived for the first time by Valkyrie based divers in 2009.

History: Date of loss 11/01/1910. A 77 n.t. Steam Trawler of Fleetwood which was wrecked on rocks. The crew of 11 was safe. The vessel was built in 1903. In 1980 the wreck lay in the west part of Larry Bane Bay in 20m of water. It stood to a height of c. 4m waters with the hull plating having fallen from the frames. By 1986 fishermen had reported that this wreck was badly broken up. (Sources: WA G19; AWD). AWD (Admiralty Wreck Data); WA (Wilson Archive).

sites.name: SS City Of Brisbane
sites.location: Lewes, East Sussex, South East, England
sites.notes:
The dive site known as SS City Of Brisbane is a wreck that is broken up in two parts, with the bow section steel plates and girders standing 3 metres off the sea floor and listing to port. Dead man's fingers are growing on the exterior of the wreck, providing a habitat for common crabs and various fish. The wreck lies three nautical miles south of Newhaven in 30 meters of water, standing 6 meters proud at the bows. The stern is to the North and broken up, while the bow section remains fairly intact. The wreck offers an opportunity for underwater photography on clear visibility days, with depths ranging from 22 to 26 meters depending on the tide.

Stern is to the North and is broken up. Bow section remains fairly complete but deck area is a mess of wreckage.

This wreck is broken in two parts and has a lot of dead mans fingers growing on exterior which form the home of quite a few common crabs and various fish life. This can be interesting for photo’s on a clear visibility day depth from 22 to 26 mts, dependent on tide.

Biodiversity: She has a lot of dead mans fingers and plumose anemones growing on her with a large amount of mussels.

sites.name: SS Shuna
sites.alternativeNames: Oban: SS Schuna, Sound of Mull - Shuna
sites.hazards: This is a dive that requires planning and gas to last 70 mins + Deco.
sites.notes:
The SS Shuna is a popular dive site located in the Sound of Mull, sunk in 1913 while carrying a cargo of coal. The wreck lies upright in 30 metres of water, with the deck at a depth of 16-20 metres. Despite being quite silty, the wreck is intact and features the remains of the ship's engine, winches, masts, and propellers. Marine life such as fish, sand eels, nudibranchs, tunicates, and hydroids can be found around the wreck, making it an interesting dive site for those interested in exploring wrecks and underwater ecosystems. The SS Shuna can be accessed from dive boats launching from Oban, Lochaline, or Tobermory.

Wrecked in 1913 while carrying a cargo of coal, the steel steamship Shuna, built in Holland (880 net tonnes), was discovered in 1991, and lies intact and upright in 30 metres (16 metres to the deck). The wreck is quite silty, but can be dived at all states of the tide.

The Shuna is one of the more popular dive sites in the Sound of Mull. Although not as pretty as the Hispania or Thesis she is still an interesting dive with plenty of life on. The Shuna sits upright in 30-32 metres of water, parallel to the shore, on a gently sloping seabed with the deck 16-20 metres from surface. Her main desk is at about 25 metres. Her least depth at the higher parts of her bridge superstructure is about 18 metres.
 
The Shuna rests in a bay which is sheltered from the main tidal streams of the Sound of Mull. Although the shelter means the wreck is diveable at all states of the tide, it also means the seabed is silty and silt can also build up on the wreck. Visibility can be 10 metres on a good day, but this is easily destroyed by careless finning kicking up the silt. The diving on this wreck has drastically improved since the marine farm has been moved away, leading to generally better visibility across the wreck. 
 
Much of the inner workings of the ship are still intact and the triple expansion steam engine can be seen through the doorways of the engine room. Due to the lack of extensive salvage of the ship the spare propeller is still on the aft deck along with winches and other machinery. For those more interested in life and less in metal there is also much to see; fish and sand eels shoal around her and there is lots of macro life, including nudibranchs. The shot line brings you down to a mast amidships, giving you a good view of the whole wreck in good visibility.

Biodiversity: Plenty of sea life, including scallops. Seals nearby.

Tides: The wreck of the Shuna can be dived at any state of the tide. Visibility may be better earlier in the day before too many other divers have been on the wreck. Cannot be dived in strong south-westerly winds.

History: 8.5.13      BUILT IN 1909 BY A VUIJK & ZONAN IN THE NETHERLANDS. OWNED AT TIME OF LOSS BY SCANDANAVIAN SHIPPING. ONE BOILER, TRIPLE EXPANSION ENGINE, SINGLE SHAFT. MACHINERY BY G T GREY, HOLBOURN WORKS, SOUTH SHIELDS. PASSAGE GLASGOW FOR GOTHENBURG. WHILE SEEKING SHELTER FROM HEAVY WEATHER STRUCK GREY ROCKS ON 8.5.13. ATTEMPTED TO REACH TOBERMORY BUT HAD TO BEACH ON MORVEN SHORE & SANK THE FOLLOWING DAY. CREW SAFE. (ARGYLL SHIPWRECKS, SIBI, & SHIPWRECKS OF W SCOTLAND).

sites.name: Queenie Reef
sites.alternativeNames: Seven Steps Reef - Loch Creran; Oban, 5th Passing Place on the Left
sites.hazards: Poor visibility and a silty, dark environment. Slight tidal flow can be felt at depth. The site can be deeper if venturing out into the muddy areas beyond the reef.
sites.notes:
A shore dive in Loch Creran accessed via steps from a nearby layby. The site features rolling rocky reefs at 9-15 metres with deeper muddy areas beyond. The main reef slopes down to around 15 metres, with serpulid reef formations in shallower areas at approximately 6 metres. Marine life includes plumose anemones, cup corals, crabs, fan worms, occasional thornback rays, and pipefish. Large stands of Ascophyllum seaweed are present in the shallows. A second reef can be reached by heading straight out from shore. The environment is characterised by poor visibility, dark silty conditions, and a gently sloping gravel beach entry. The fragile serpulid reefs require careful finning technique.

Queenie Reef is a silty, shallow shore dive in Loch Creran, a Scottish sea loch, named for the abundance of Queen Scallops covering the bottom. The site is relatively shallow at around 9–10 metres and features a rolling reef, with deeper muddy areas beyond.

Shore dive accessed via steps down to a burn and then onto the beach — parking is nearby. The site is about half a mile up from the bridge at the loch entrance. The reef is rolling rather than steep and sits at around 9–10 metres; it can be deeper if you venture out into the mud. Visibility is poor and the environment is quite dark and silty. There is a wall section and some rocks out in the middle of the bay, as well as a collection of old tyres. The diver swam out to where the water changes colour, then along and back in to a second reef that comes up shallower.

Biodiversity: Queen scallops (queenies) are abundant and cover the bottom — they are fairly mobile bivalves with visible eyes around the frills of the shell. Also present: variegated scallop (attaches to substrate), king scallop, live native oyster, harbour/swimming crab, sea toad, horse mussel (clabby dubh), and unspecified fish.

Tides: The loch has a fairly constricted entrance under a bridge. The tidal flow through the narrows can be quite quick but is not particularly big overall. Inside the loch the tidal pull is only slight. The silty environment is a result of the tidal and loch conditions.

sites.notes:
Steamship, struck a mine and sank 1916. 686 tons, 206 x  29

One of our favourite wrecks. The Stern is largely intact although the  site is generally collapsing. Usually excellent viz (15-20m). The wreck has a good covering of life and attracts large fish such as Ling. Bell recovered by Castaway in 1997.

History: 20.12.16      BUILT IN 1892 BY MESSERS JOHN JONES & SONS OF LIVERPOOL FOR THE SLIGO STEAM NAVIGATION CO. FITTED OUT TO HIGH STANDARD FOR SALOON AND DECK PASSENGERS. sites.name: SMS Bayern Turrets
sites.alternativeNames: Scapa Flow: SMS Bayern Gun Turrets
sites.notes:
SMS Bayern was a German Bayern-class Super Dreadnought of some 28,000 tons, scuttled at Scapa Flow in 1919 and salvaged in 1933–1934. During the raising, her four twin 15-inch gun turrets — Anton, Bruno, Caesar, and Dora, each weighing 580 tons — ripped free of the hull and remain on the seabed to this day. Lying inverted and partially buried in silt at depths of roughly 34–45 metres, the turrets are oriented east–west at Bayern's original scuttling site. The eastern turrets (Caesar and Dora) are the more intact of the four, offering views of internal mechanisms, ball bearings, ammunition lift spaces, and drive cogs, while the western turrets (Anton and Bruno) suffered greater damage during the salvage. A debris field of masts, platforms, and other structure lies between the two pairs, and the two sets are typically connected by swim lines.

The SMS Bayern Turrets dive site in Scapa Flow consists of the four massive twin 15-inch gun turrets (named A–D, Anton, Bruno, Caesar, and Dora) that separated from the Bayern battleship during a failed salvage attempt in 1934. The turrets lie inverted in 34–38 metres, offering a unique close-up perspective on these enormous weapons of war not available anywhere else in Scapa Flow.

The four turrets lie oriented roughly east–west within the depression of Bayern's original scuttling site, with the bow turrets (A & B / Anton & Bruno) to the west and the stern turrets (C & D / Caesar & Dora) to the east. All four are inverted and embedded in the seabed at 34–38 metres; the shallowest point is the top of Turret C at around 23–24 metres. None of the gun barrels are visible, but some of the barrel ports can be seen. The west turrets (A & B) appear more damaged from the salvage mishap, with little rising above the original turret ball race. The east turrets (C & D) are more complete, and offer a clearer view of their platforms, mechanics, central ammunition lift space, massive ball bearings, and the motors and drive cogs that powered their rotation. The two pairs of turrets are normally linked by swim lines, allowing a visit to all four. Between the two sets lies a debris field of masts, platforms, and other structure that was sheared off as the ship rolled and sank in 1919.

Biodiversity: Small fish, conger and ling can all be found, an abundance of dead mans fingers, sea urchins, king and queen scallops along with crabs and lobsters.

History: SMS Bayern was a Bayern-class steel battleship built at Howaldtswerke, Kiel, and launched on 18 February 1915. On the afternoon of 21 June 1919 she was scuttled and came to rest on the seabed in an inverted, east–west orientation with her bow pointing west. During salvage recovery work in 1934, the 28,079-ton battleship accidentally rose to the surface, vented, and partially sank again by the stern. During this mishap her four massive turrets, each carrying twin 15-inch guns, separated from the main hull. The hull was subsequently raised successfully later in 1934, but the turrets remained on the seabed. New sonar surveys in recent years have recorded both the original and secondary seabed depressions created by these events.

sites.name: SMS Karlsruhe
sites.notes:
SMS Karlsruhe is a Königsberg II class light cruiser sunk in Scapa Flow on 21st June 1919. Measuring 150 metres long and displacing 5,440 tons, she was completed in January 1916 at Wilhelmshaven. The wreck lies on her starboard side in 26 metres with a minimum depth of 12 metres over the port side. Heavily salvaged with the bow broken away and amidships collapsed, the stern section remains intact. Features including gun turrets, piping, armour, capstans, teak decking and brass signs are visible throughout. The wreck rests on a flat bottom populated by horse mussels, scallops and queenies, and is home to various fish life.

The Karlsruhe has been heavily salvaged with only her stern section remaining intact, however all over the still shipshaped wreck, features like gun turrets, piping, armour and capstans can be made out. A great dive in shallow water she is covered in life and home to many fish.

This Light cruiser lies in shallower water with the least depth over her port side of about 14 metres.

Biodiversity: A large white seal may be encountered, particularly around the salvage break area.

The salvaged remains of the WWI German battlecruiser SMS Seydlitz, scuttled at Scapa Flow in 1919 and raised in 1928. Now a shallow wreck at 20–22m on a silty gravel bottom, ideal for exploring scattered debris.

This shallow wreck is the salvaged remains of the WWI battlecruiser S.M.S. Seydlitz, ideal for those who enjoy exploring debris. Lying at 20–22m on a silty gravel bottom, the site features scattered wreckage, including anchors, guns, searchlights, and salvage equipment.

Biodiversity: Expect marine life consisting of shoals of saithe, conger eels, ling, lobsters, and the chance to drift for scallops.

sites.name: SMS Kronprinz Willhelm
sites.alternativeNames: VK, Scapa, SMS Kronprinz Wilhelm, Scapa Flow - SMS Kronprinz Wilhelm, Wreck Kron Prinz Wilheilm, Scapa - Kronprinz, Wrack SMS Kronprinz Wilhelm
sites.notes:
The SMS Kronprinz Willhelm, a World War I battleship wreck, lies nearly upside down at a depth of 38 meters. The wreck is a popular site for underwater photographers due to the impressive profusion of encrusting life, including dead men's fingers, plumous anemones, and fan worms in vibrant colours like pinks and yellows. Despite salvage work over the years causing confusion to the wreck's shape, much of the massive ship remains intact underwater, offering divers the opportunity to explore its substantial volume and historical significance. SMS Kronprinz Willhelm was a 177m long Koenig class vessel launched in 1914 and sank in 1919, now providing an intriguing dive experience for those interested in maritime history.

Another Konig Class, displacing 25,400 tons, she was launched in Kiel in 1914. The Kiel Canal had to be widened to get her to open sea.

Lying upside down to her starboard side, the hull starts in about 16 metres and her main guns can be seen at the seabed in 38meters.
